Derivatives are taken within $I$. No Euler equation for $B$ or $E_c$ is imposed. Section 2.2.1 assumes smooth $B$ on the physical time interval; the formalization permits continuous $B$ and a larger compact observation set. Later results require that this set contain the complete physical interval under consideration.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The prescribed gradients and preceding wave determine the setting

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
On the physical interval $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, let $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, with a nonzero transverse preceding wave, positive frozen couplings $
u,\eta$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$ and $S=\sigma/r$. The formal object requires a new transverse solution of the wave equations, starting with $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ and amplitude a positive multiple of $-E_1/S+E_2$, with attained peak $U_*$. It records $
u_+\ge
u\varepsilon/2$, early amplitude at most $e^{3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}}U_*$, and the first crossing of $\eta_+/
u_+=\varepsilon_+$ in the normalized bracket $[	au_m,2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}]$, where $2/\varepsilon\le	au_m\le3/\varepsilon$. At crossings, $\sigma_+/(\lambda U_*)$ lies between $e^{-1}/(4\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})$ and $18e^3/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. At the selected crossing, $|\log(
u_+/
u)|\le2\varepsilon$. These are required properties, not an existence theorem. The paper takes $U_*=\lambda^{-3/4}$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Records a normalized wave and its first prescribed crossing

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For an existing `GrowingCrossing` record, the delay from activation is strictly greater than $1/r$ and at most the crossing horizon divided by $r$. These inequalities come from the record’s `crossing_after_switch` and upper bracket endpoint. They do not assert that the selected time is the first crossing before the reference-turn bracket.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The selected crossing occurs after switching and before the horizon

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At a selected growing crossing, the actual first coupling is positive, the ratio of third to first coupling equals the requested `next`, and the logarithmic change in first coupling is at most twice the old ratio. These are properties of the same selected wave and physical gradient, extracted from its crossing record.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: A selected crossing supplies the next frozen couplings

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: If the supplied gradient agrees with the physical gradient at the crossing and the requested next ratio is positive, both frozen couplings are positive there. Their ratio and logarithmic first-coupling bound are unchanged. Unlike the equation transport lemma, this needs equality only at the single crossing time.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The actual gradient retains the positive crossing couplings

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For positive frequency, gains, and strength constants, an actual crossing with gain gap at least 640, strength between $c\mu^{1/4}$ and $C\mu^{1/4}L^2$, and first coupling between $\pi$ and $4\pi$ has explicit rate and delay bounds. A further lower bound on the next gain ensures delay at most $\mu^{-1/8}LNext^3$. The conclusion also gives strict time advancement, normalized delay at least $2L^2$, and weighted duration.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Physical strength and coupling give the next activation clock

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At activation, the selected covector is `scale` times the preceding third frame vector and has norm `scale` when the scale is positive. Its amplitude is a positive multiple of $-E_1/S+E_2$. The positive normalization preserves the growing direction and refers to the same crossing witness used later.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The selected wave has the prescribed launch directions

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: On an interval starting at a selected crossing, the switched rank-one gradient formula becomes the unswitched formula because the wave cutoff is already one. The finish must remain before the model endpoint. The correction `E` is unchanged, so the next physical comparison uses the same actual gradient splitting.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: After crossing the preceding rank-one term is fully active

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Restricting a selected wave to an interval beginning at its crossing preserves nonzero perpendicular data and the actual covector and amplitude equations. The supplied finish must not exceed the previous active endpoint. The previous switch equals one on the whole restricted interval because the crossing occurs after switch completion.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The crossed wave remains valid on the successor interval

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The selected wave’s affine equations on a successor interval can be rewritten with any gradient `B` that agrees there with the physical model gradient. The only additional premise is the endpoint bound for the restriction. This transports equations along an exact equality and does not estimate a discrepancy between two gradients.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The successor equations use the identified physical gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For the same growing crossing whose peak is `scale` to the power $-3/4$, positive scale and coupling ratio $(4\log\mathrm{freq})^{-2}$ imply the normalized amplitude is at most $\exp(3-4\log\mathrm{freq})$ throughout the first physical switching unit. The proof cancels the peak normalization and substitutes the chosen ratio into the crossing’s early-gain estimate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The normalized amplitude is small during the initial switch

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a physical growing crossing with old ratio given by `L` and target ratio given by `LNext`, the hypotheses $L>0$ and $640L\le LNext$ put its normalized delay between $2L^2$ and $2L\,LNext$. This combines the lower crossing bound with the explicit horizon identity. Existence of the growing crossing is assumed through the supplied object.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Successive gains bracket the normalized crossing delay

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For an actual physical growing crossing, identifying the initial ratio with the inverse square of `L` gives $2L^2\le rate\,(crossing-t_0)$. The crossing object supplies the comparison and positivity properties used by the proof. No separate positivity hypothesis on `L` appears in this theorem; the prescribed ratio is the relevant compatibility assumption.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: An actual growing crossing lasts at least the inverse ratio

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: When the prescribed peak is $\lambda^{-3/4}$ and $\lambda>0$, the strength estimate at the recorded crossing has denominator $\lambda^{1/4}$. The theorem rewrites $\lambda\lambda^{-3/4}=\lambda^{1/4}$ and applies the stored crossing-strength bounds. It retains the constants $e^{-1}/4$ and $18e^3$ and does not supply a new crossing.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The induction peak gives a quarter-power strength denominator

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: With positive wave scale, preceding gain at least one, and gain separation `640 * Lprev ≤ L`, a wave normalized to peak amplitude $\mathrm{scale}^{-3/4}$ has crossing strength between $(e^{-1}/4)\mathrm{scale}^{1/4}$ and $18e^3\mathrm{scale}^{1/4}L^2$. The hypothesis identifies the old coupling ratio with the preceding gain. These are loose bounds suited to iteration.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Crossing strength has uniform induction bounds

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Using the actual smooth periodic odd parent flow, this theorem proves the prescribed label covector is nonzero and its transported value agrees with the selected Eulerian wave vector throughout the activation slab. The model gradient must agree with the parent’s actual central gradient. Oddness fixes the origin, connecting the label trajectory to the central physical comparison.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The chosen label covector transports to the selected physical wave

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: A `GrowingCrossing` occurs after the switching delay. Therefore, for any `t` at or after `d.crossing`, the activation cutoff `waveSwitch t₀ w.rate t` equals one. The theorem uses the crossing record’s delay bound and the positive rate carried by the physical amplification data.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The switch is fully active by the crossing

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Transfers normalized comparison bounds back to a physical crossing: the scaled components satisfy $|X|\le T^2$, $|Q|\le T$, and $|Z-1|\le1/2$. Here `T ≥ 2` is the normalized window length and the evaluated time belongs to `w.activeSlab T`. Further hypotheses require a nonzero scale, clock containment, a sufficiently large comparison constant, and ratio and error smallness.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The selected wave retains its physical geometry

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: If $|u-1|\le\varepsilon\le1/2$, then $|\log u|\le2\varepsilon$. The closeness hypothesis implies $u\ge1/2$, so the logarithm is used on positive values. In the crossing construction this converts relative first-coupling control into a logarithmic bound.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: A scalar near one has a controlled logarithm

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The active slab is $[t_0,\mathrm{clock}(T)]$, namely $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$ for the positive rate stored in `w`. The definition only specifies endpoints. Inclusion in the original physical set `I` is supplied later, and positivity of the normalized length is not part of this set definition.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical interval for a normalized time window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The frame is built from the preceding wave vector and amplitude stored in `w`: their normalized directions and their cross product. On the recorded physical set `I`, `preceding_data` guarantees both vectors are nonzero and perpendicular. The abbreviation is defined for all times, so the record’s geometric guarantees should only be used on `I`.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The preceding wave supplies the moving frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For an amplification step activated at $t_0$, put $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, $\nu=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)>0$, and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$. The formal object is $t(\tau)=t_0+\tau/r$, the inverse of the paper’s normalized time $\tau=r(t-t_0)$. Nonzero preceding wave data give $\sigma>0$, hence $r>0$. The formula is defined for every real $\tau$; it supplies no wave equation outside the prescribed compact time set. The interval hypotheses of each estimate require $t([0,T])\subset I$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The affine change of time has positive rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a window with endpoint `t₀ + 2 * half`, normalized time $2r\,\mathrm{half}$ maps exactly to that endpoint, and the normalized interval maps into the physical interval. Positivity of the rate is inherited from the physical amplification structure. This is a clock identity and containment statement, not a crossing existence result.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The normalized clock reaches the physical endpoint

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Applying the physical clock to elapsed normalized time returns the original real time. The equality uses only the positive, hence nonzero, rate from `w`. It is valid for all real times, while derivative and geometric properties of the wave remain restricted to the physical window.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The inverse clock recovers the original physical time

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For $\tau\in[0,T]$, the physical time `clock τ` belongs to `activeSlab T`. The proof applies monotonicity of the clock and its activation value. This is the forward membership conversion used when moving maxima, nonvanishing and crossing estimates onto the physical slab.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: A normalized time gives an active physical time

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The affine clock sends τ = 0 to t₀. This identifies the initial slice when the physical wave equations are rewritten in normalized time.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Normalized time zero is the activation time

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Each of the three directions in the physical frame is continuous on `I`. The proof obtains their within-set derivatives from the preceding wave equations, trace-free older strain and nonzero perpendicular data, then takes continuity. No smoothness of the error strain beyond the physical record’s continuity is used.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Every preceding-frame direction varies continuously

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The older strain and error strain are continuous by the physical record, while the preceding wave paths are continuous because their within-set derivatives exist. The rank-one product of those paths is continuous as well. Adding the three terms proves continuity of the full physical gradient on `I`.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The complete physical gradient is continuous on its window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Freeze the preceding wave's strength $\sigma=|\mathbf a_p(t_0)|\,|\kappa_p(t_0)|>0$ and first coupling $\nu>0$ at its activation time $t_0$. With $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}>0$, the formal definition assigns the normalized elapsed time $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ to every real $t$. Thus the physical interval $[t_0,T]$ corresponds to $[0,r(T-t_0)]$, and the inverse conversion is $t=t_0+\tau/r$. This is a change of time variable for the central wave equations, not a new physical time interval or an existence assertion about the wave.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Converts physical time to the wave comparison variable

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Applying elapsed normalized time after the physical clock returns τ. The positive growth rate stored in the amplification data supplies the nonzero denominator.

A physical time between `clock a` and `clock b` has elapsed normalized time in $[a,b]$. The proof applies monotonicity to both inequalities and simplifies the inverse-clock identities. It is a set-membership lemma, without a claim that either interval lies inside the domain of a physical wave.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The inverse clock preserves both interval endpoints

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Every time in `activeSlab T` has elapsed normalized time in $[0,T]$. This specializes the interval-transport lemma using `clock 0=t₀`. It lets proofs reuse normalized estimates at a physical time whose membership in the active slab is known.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: An active time lies in the normalized interval

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
This reads the four-term physical error from the stored frame, older strain, strain error, initial couplings and growth rate. Boundedness of the relevant suprema is supplied by compactness and continuity in the amplification arguments.

Default-value audit (b5): The amplification record gives a compact nonempty time set and continuous ingredients, so the suprema have their intended finite values. The positive coupling and rate hypotheses exclude zero denominators.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical error evaluated on the amplification interval

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a physical window with coupling ratio at most one, bounds on the older gradient, its supplied time derivative, and the correction give the explicit comparison error estimate with constant eight. Positive rates and couplings come from the window structure. The conclusion includes nonnegativity of the actual error, not just an upper bound.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical comparison error is bounded by older gradient data

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For an existing physical crossing, positive frequency scale and sufficient smallness, choose `D` above both $252eS$ and $2/(\nu\varepsilon)$. With $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}\|a\|$, every transverse solution has relative growth bounded by `D`, and the new first coupling is at least $D^{-1}$ throughout the active slab. The estimates use the same amplitude and wave vector already recorded in the crossing.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The same physical wave meets both center estimates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
Let $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$ on a compact time set containing $t_0$, with continuous $B,E_c$, trace-free $B$, and a nonzero transverse preceding wave solving the wave equations over $B$. Freeze $\sigma,
u,\eta>0$, and put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. There is an absolute integer threshold such that, for integers $C_0$ above it, $\Theta\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ suffice. If $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$ lies in that set, $\lambda,U_*>0$, $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}\le\Theta$, a growing transverse wave exists with initial direction $-E_1/S+E_2$, attained peak $U_*$ and a first prescribed crossing after the reference turn. It includes the early-gain and crossing-strength bounds of §6.2. The threshold is chosen before all wave data. Here $\delta$ denotes the formal comparison error; its defining formula is absent, so exact agreement with (2.6) is unverified.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Constructs the prescribed wave under the comparison assumptions

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: A universal threshold produces a physical `GrowingCrossing` together with both center estimates for that same witness. Inputs include positive frequency and target peak, an admissible clock, both smallness inequalities, a positive successor ratio at most one thirty-second of the current ratio, and a horizon inside the window. The chosen `D` must dominate the explicit growth and inverse-coupling constants.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: One crossing carries the center bounds for its own wave

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For sufficiently large preceding frequency $\mu$, the prescribed logarithmic gain, lower coupling bound, and upper growth rate imply both $252eS\le\mu^9$ and $2/(\nu\varepsilon)\le\mu^9$. The threshold depends on the positive strength constant. These bounds supply one common `D` for transverse stability and positive coupling.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Both center estimates fit one parent scale

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Consider the growing wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$ on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, with nonzero transverse paths, initial direction $-E_1/S+E_2$, and frozen $\nu,\varepsilon,S>0$. For all sufficiently large integers $C_0$, assume $\Theta\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. If $\mathsf D\ge252eS$ and $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$, every transverse amplitude solution satisfies $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for ordered times in this interval, and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. Multiplying both amplitude denominators by $\lambda^{3/4}$ gives (5.5). Nonzero seed and covector make all these divisions meaningful. The result assumes the growing wave has already been supplied. Here $\delta$ denotes the formal comparison error; its defining formula is absent, so exact agreement with (2.6) is unverified.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The growth bound and positive coupling give the required control

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
On $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, take the selected growing transverse wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, starting in direction $-E_1/S+E_2$. Here $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, with positive frozen strength and couplings. For every sufficiently large integer $C_0$, assume $\Theta\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Then every transverse solution $\mathbf b$ of the same amplitude equation satisfies $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le252eS\,|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for $t'\le t$ in the interval. The nonzero seed makes the denominators positive. This proves the first estimate of (6.7), with an explicit absolute constant; the lower bound for $
u_+$ is a different conclusion. Here $\delta$ denotes the formal comparison error; its defining formula is absent, so exact agreement with (2.6) is unverified.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Controls every transverse solution relative to the selected seed

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a physical `GrowingCrossing` and sufficiently strong smallness, any two ordered times in its active slab admit a continuous linear equivalence between their transverse planes. Its norm is at most $252eS$ times the ratio of the same growing amplitude’s endpoint norms. For every initial vector the conclusion supplies a full closed-slab amplitude path realizing the equivalence, with transversality throughout.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Physical transport is an equivalence between the transverse planes

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
For a nonzero transverse preceding wave, let $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$ and $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$. The formal object is the scalar $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. It is frozen at the activation time, not the time-dependent entry $B_{12}(t)$ elsewhere on the interval. Positivity of this number is required in the amplification data. The same $
u$ is used in $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$; the error $\delta$ measures how the time-dependent entry differs from its frozen value.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The first coupling is evaluated at activation

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Given the older gradient $B$, preceding wave vectors $k_p,\mathbf a_p$, and error $E_c$, the formal object is $M(t)=B(t)+\mathbf a_p(t)\otimes k_p(t)+E_c(t)$. Here $(\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p)v=(k_p\cdot v)\mathbf a_p$. For the nonzero transverse preceding wave this equals $B+\sigma_pE_2\otimes E_1+E_c$, as in Section 2.2.1. The matrices are continuous on the prescribed compact set and the preceding vectors satisfy their ordinary differential equations there. This definition does not assert that $M$ itself is a global Euler velocity gradient or that $E_c$ is trace free.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The preceding wave contributes its rank-one gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The formal object is $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, the strength of the preceding wave at the new wave’s activation time. Both factors use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$ and are strictly positive under the amplification hypotheses. This is the fixed number denoted $\sigma$ in Section 2.2.1; the evolving strength is $\sigma_p(t)=|k_p(t)||\mathbf a_p(t)|$. Their ratio is estimated separately. The product is the size of the rank-one shear contribution when $k_p$ and $\mathbf a_p$ are perpendicular.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The initial strength fixes the time and shear scales

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The product of the preceding wave-vector and amplitude norms is positive at `t₀`. The proof applies `preceding_data` at `activation`, so nonvanishing is supplied by the physical record rather than inferred from a totalized norm formula. This positivity is used to define a nonzero growth rate and shear.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The preceding strength is strictly positive at activation

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: This helper transports a physical wave vector and amplitude to $[0,T]$ when their within-set derivatives are known only on `activeSlab T`. It uses the normalized gradient identity and the clock’s membership map. Unlike the earlier `rescale_wave`, it does not require these path equations on all of the larger physical set `I`.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Closed-slab physical paths give normalized closed-slab paths

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For the new wave, the formal object is $\eta_+=(\widehat k\times\widehat a)\cdot M\widehat a$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, $\widehat k=k/|k|$, and $\widehat a=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$. For nonzero perpendicular $k,\mathbf a$ this is the entry $E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ used in Lemma 2.7. The definition accepts arbitrary vector functions. A zero vector is normalized to zero, so the formula gives zero if either vector vanishes; the new-wave theorems establish the nonzero transverse setting in which it is an orthonormal-frame coupling. No positivity is contained in this definition.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The coupling uses the full prescribed gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a new wave vector $k$ and amplitude $\mathbf a$, the formal object is $\nu_+=\widehat k\cdot M\widehat a$, with $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. When $k,\mathbf a$ are nonzero and perpendicular, their normalized vectors are the first two vectors of the new wave’s frame, and this is exactly $E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ in Lemma 2.7. The definition itself imposes neither the wave equations nor positivity. Normalization assigns zero to a zero vector; later positivity conclusions require the hypotheses of the amplification theorem.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The coupling is a scalar entry of the full gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
With positive frozen strength $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$ and coupling $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$, the formal object is $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$. It is positive and converts physical time into $	au=r(t-t_0)$. As the paper explains, the exact rate obtained by freezing the initial two-component system is $\sqrt{2
u(\sigma-
u)}$ when $\sigma>
u$. Thus $r$ is the leading strong-shear scale, not that exact frozen growth rate. The two differ by the factor $\sqrt{1-
u/\sigma}$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The scale is the leading strong-shear growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The record’s activation strength and first coupling are strictly positive, so their growth rate $\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ is positive. The theorem derives this from the corresponding record facts. It ensures that the physical and normalized clocks are invertible and preserve time order.

The formal object is $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, where $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$ and $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)>0$ are the preceding frame’s frozen entries. Both are evaluated at the activation time, so $\varepsilon$ is constant even when $B$ and the frame evolve. Positivity is part of the data; smallness is an additional hypothesis, imposed through $C_0\varepsilon\le1$. This number determines the reference angle by $	an\varphi=\varepsilon	au^2/2$. It is distinct from the evolving successor ratio $\eta_+/
u_+$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The ratio of positive couplings determines the reference angle

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The frozen ratio is the third coupling divided by the first. Both couplings are strictly positive fields of `PhysicalAmplification`, so the ratio is positive as well. This fact validates the inverse and square-root expressions used for the reference turning interval and the successor crossing horizon.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The frozen coupling ratio is strictly positive

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Given a wave-vector path and amplitude path satisfying the affine equations on the physical set `I`, compose both with the positive clock. Under the hypotheses needed for `toNormalized`, they satisfy the corresponding equations on the entire closed normalized interval $[0,T]$. The theorem changes time units and does not assert initial data, transversality or nonvanishing for these new paths.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: A physical wave obeys the normalized equations

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
The formal object is $S=\sigma/r$, where $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|>0$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}>0$ with $
u=B_{12}(t_0)$. Therefore $S=\sqrt{\sigma/(2
u)}$. It is the dimensionless scale used in the anisotropic components of the new wave: the $E_2$ component of $k$ and the $E_1,E_3$ components of $\mathbf a$ carry factors $S^{-1}$. Large $S$ describes strong preceding shear. Its positivity follows from the data; quantitative lower bounds such as $S\ge T^2$ require the smallness assumptions.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The shear scale compares shear rate with growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The frozen shear satisfies $S=r/(2\nu)$, using $r^2=2\sigma\nu$ and the original definition $S=\sigma/r$. The rate and first coupling are positive in the physical model, so division is legitimate. This alternate form is used to compare the center growth constant with the induction parameter.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The shear scale is determined by rate and coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The map from normalized to physical time is strictly increasing because the rate is positive. The proof divides a strict inequality by the positive rate and adds the activation time. This ensures that the reference turning bracket and the first crossing retain their order after returning to physical time.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical clock preserves strict time order

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Multiplying physical time relative to activation by the positive rate gives a strictly increasing function. This inverse-clock monotonicity converts physical interval memberships and crossing inequalities into normalized ones. The theorem applies to all real times and does not itself state any wave property.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Elapsed normalized time preserves strict order

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, the formal object is $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. The preceding vectors are nonzero and perpendicular, so this is an entry in an oriented orthonormal frame. The amplification data require $\eta>0$. This fixed value enters $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$; it is not the time-dependent entry $B_{32}(t)$, whose relative variation contributes separately to the error $\delta$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The second coupling is evaluated in the preceding frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For $T\ge2$ and `C₀≥240`, this construction reparametrizes the preceding pair by `w.clock` and divides both physical strains by `w.rate`. The hypotheses `hclock`, `hsmallε` and `hsmallδ` supply interval membership and the two smallness inequalities. The output is an `AmplificationWindow` carrying derived coefficient bounds, positive ratio, nonvanishing data, and the normalized wave equations.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical assumptions supply a normalized amplification window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At a point of the normalized slab, each coupling computed from the normalized gradient equals the corresponding physical frame pairing divided by the frozen first coupling. The identity uses $2S/r=1/\nu$. It accepts arbitrary supplied `k` and `a`; the separate nonzero transverse hypotheses are needed to call their normalized directions a moving orthonormal frame.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Normalized couplings equal physical couplings divided by the frozen one

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At a normalized time inside $[0,T]$, the gradient stored in `toNormalized` equals $r^{-1}$ times the full physical gradient at the clocked time. The proof also matches the preceding-wave rank-one contribution, using nonzero preceding data. This guards against mixing the physical and normalized strain conventions in subsequent coupling estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The normalized gradient is the physical gradient divided by rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Q.text:
The coordinate $Q=S(E_2\cdot k)/\lambda$, so the second frame component of $k$ is $\lambda Q/S$. The extra factor $S$ is the scaling used to obtain the reference equation $Q'=-\varepsilon Z$. The definition supplies the coordinate only; orthonormality, nonzero scaling parameters and the wave equation are hypotheses of later lemmas.

Default-value audit (b5): The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; totalized inversion alone does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Space.text:
This abbreviation is three-dimensional real Euclidean space. Its norm is the Euclidean norm; it is distinct from the maximum norm on the auxiliary pair of amplitude coordinates.

Default-value audit (b5): This is an abbreviation for a real Hilbert space, with no equation or nonzero-vector condition. The oriented frame lemmas impose perpendicular nonzero data.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.X.text:
The coordinate $X=(E_1\cdot k)/\lambda$ in the moving frame. `scale` is the positive initial frequency $\lambda$ in the comparison theorem. This scalar is defined for arbitrary frame and vector path, so the definition itself imposes no differential equation or nonzero denominator. Those hypotheses enter the decomposition and comparison results that explain how $X$ evolves.

Default-value audit (b5): The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; totalized inversion alone does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Z.text:
The coordinate $Z=(E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$ in the preceding frame. Initial data $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$ give $Z(t_0)=1$ when the frame is orthonormal and `scale` is nonzero. The amplitude’s third coordinate will divide by $Z$, so Lemma 2.4 subsequently proves that $Z$ stays at least $1/2$ on the comparison interval.

Default-value audit (b5): The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; totalized inversion alone does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_div_le_s.text: Assuming `hS : 1 ≤ S`, proves $|a/S|\le|a|$ for any real numerator. The lower bound makes $S$ positive and permits replacement of its absolute value by itself. This is used to discard harmless inverse-shear factors when collecting the coefficients of the moving wave-vector residual.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_div_le_s.summary: Division by the shear scale does not enlarge magnitude

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_le_of_de.text: If $f(0)=0$ and the absolute derivative is at most $M$ throughout $[0,T]$, bounds $|f(\tau)|$ by $MT$ at a member `τ` of the interval. The derivative is within the closed interval. The proof first uses the sharper distance $\tau$ and then bounds it by $T$; the hypotheses themselves force $M\ge0$ on the nonempty interval.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_le_of_de.summary: A bounded derivative controls displacement from zero

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_threePro.text: If the three scalar coefficients have absolute value at most $M$, bounds the absolute value of $ax+bq+cz$ by $M(|x|+|q|+|z|)$. Each hypothesis is retained separately, and no sign assumptions on the coordinates are needed. This triangle-inequality estimate converts rowwise coefficient control into the residual bound used by the wave-vector comparison.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.abs_threePro.summary: Bound a linear combination by its coordinate sum

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.affineWaveAm.text: Multiplying the strain operator by any real scalar $c$ multiplies the affine amplitude operator’s value by $c$. The pressure correction is linear in the strain just as the transport term is. This algebraic identity also holds for zero wave vectors under the totalized definition, and is used in reversing the clock change.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.affineWaveAm.summary: Rescaling the strain rescales the amplitude derivative

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text:
Define the square-root growth rate from the preceding strength and first coupling. It converts physical time to normalized time; strict positivity is proved only under positive physical parameters.

Default-value audit (b5): The rate is zero when twice the strength-coupling product is nonpositive, under the real square-root convention. The physically meaningful rescaling assumes both parameters positive, so the rate is nonzero.

Positive preceding strength `hσ` and positive first coupling `hν` imply that $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ is strictly positive. The proof reduces this to positivity of the radicand. This supplies the nonzero denominator required to pass between physical time and normalized time; it does not itself bound the error or construct a wave.
With positive preceding strength and first coupling, squaring the amplification rate gives twice their product. This supplies the scalar cancellation in the normalized model coefficients.

The formal object is $\delta=\sup_I|B_{12}/
u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+r^{-1}\sup_I\|B\|+
u^{-1}\sup_I\|E_c\|$, with entries taken in the preceding wave’s frame and matrix norms the Euclidean operator norms. It agrees with (2.6) when $I=[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The formalization also allows a larger compact set, measuring all four terms there. The definition accepts arbitrary sets and denominators. Real suprema of empty or unbounded sets are assigned zero, as is division by zero; the amplification hypotheses supply a nonempty compact set, continuity, and positive $
u,\eta,r$, so these exceptional assignments do not enter the estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Four suprema quantify the departure from the reference setting

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text:
Let $t_0\le T$. Suppose $B$ is trace free and differentiable in time, and a nonzero perpendicular pair $(\kappa_p,\mathbf a_p)$ solves the wave equations over $B$ on $[t_0,T]$. Assume $\|B\|\le M$, $\|B_t\|\le D$ and $\|E_c\|\le E$ there. Freeze $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$ and $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$, with $0<\eta\le
u$, and take $r>0$. The formal statement gives $\delta\le8[(T-t_0)(M^2+D)/\eta+M/r+E/
u]$, with operator norms and positive denominators. It permits arbitrary valid uniform upper bounds and supplies the explicit constant eight. The imported definition of the comparison quantity $\delta$ is absent from the packet; its exact equality with the paper's expression (2.6) cannot be checked here.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Bounds comparison error by strain variation and central corrections

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: On a nonempty closed interval, an orthonormal frame with the stated axis-rate bounds and matrix, derivative, and perturbation bounds controls `amplificationPhysicalError` by $8[(finish-t_0)(M^2+D)/\eta+M/r+E_{max}/\nu]$. The scaling rate is positive and the initial couplings satisfy $0<\eta\le\nu$. These hypotheses make the denominators and real suprema legitimate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Frame-rate bounds control the physical comparison error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: If the universal threshold dominates a fixed coefficient and exponent, its finite-smallness inequality bounds that smaller polynomial times delta by epsilon. The horizon must be at least one and the quantities nonnegative.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: A fixed polynomial fits the smallness budget

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: A threshold at least two and its product with nonnegative epsilon at most one imply epsilon at most one half. This is a numerical prerequisite for the comparison estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: The epsilon bound from the universal threshold

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: Assume $T\ge2$, $\delta,\varepsilon\ge0$, $S>0$, $S^{-1}\le2\delta$, and an integer $C_0\ge240$ with $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Then $\varepsilon\le1/2$, $240\delta T^6\le1$, $T\delta\le1$, and $T^2\le S$. These are the quantitative inequalities needed to absorb polynomial errors and bound the scaled coordinates. The formal exponent $C_0$ is a natural number, so $T^{C_0}$ is an ordinary integer power. This arithmetic implication does not derive $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ from the physical gradients; that estimate is a separate input here.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: The prescribed smallness supplies four normalized bounds

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coefficient_.text: The norm of a strain controls each of its orthonormal-frame entries.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coefficient_.summary: The strain norm controls its frame coefficients

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.column_pairi.text: In an orthonormal frame, expresses the pairing of $A^*k$ with axis $j$ using column $j$ of the frame matrix of $A$ and the scaled coordinates $(X,Q/S,Z)$. Both `scale` and `S` must be nonzero. The adjoint relation moves $A$ onto the basis vector before the scaled decomposition is substituted.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.column_pairi.summary: Express the adjoint action through one matrix column

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.continuousOn.text: A jointly smooth parent on a positive closed slab has a continuous spatial gradient at the origin on any comparison interval contained between time zero and the parent endpoint. The proof restricts the joint spatial derivative along the central particle. It does not require that the comparison interval have positive length.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.continuousOn.summary: The actual central gradient is continuous on comparison intervals

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i.text: At the activation time $t_0$, assume an orthonormal frame, a nonzero frequency $\lambda$ and the initial wave vector $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$. The formal statement gives $\zeta_1(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_2(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_3(t_0)=1$, where the second projection is scaled by $S$. Under $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ these are precisely $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ after (2.3). The identity does not require $\lambda>0$, any restriction on $S$, or the wave equation. Positivity of the frequency belongs to the later amplification setting.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i.summary: Launching along the third frame vector gives the prescribed initial coordinates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry.text: For three vectors $E_1,E_2,E_3$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ and a linear map $B$, the formal entry is $E_i\cdot BE_j$. With an orthonormal frame these are the matrix components $B_{ij}$ of Lemma 2.2; in particular $\nu=B_{12}$ and $\eta=B_{32}$. The supplied formula itself does not require orthonormality or trace zero. Its coordinate positions are numbered from zero, so the first, second and third positions correspond to the paper’s subscripts $1,2,3$. No transpose or interchange of row and column is involved.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry.summary: Scalar products express a linear map in the supplied frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry_strain.text: In an orthonormal frame the added shear has just its `(1, 0)` entry.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry_strain.summary: Only one matrix entry contains the added shear

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.euclidean_er.text: The componentwise estimate gives the Euclidean estimate used in the affine-wave comparison.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.euclidean_er.summary: Component bounds imply the Euclidean error bound

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_frequ.text: There are uniform comparison and initial-frequency thresholds such that every supplied actual parent window satisfying the schedule, strength, coupling, and older-gradient bounds admits a later-wave selection. The output combines the crossing and the center estimates for one trajectory at scale `freq (j+2)`, with `D = μ^9`. The parent window itself remains an explicit input.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_frequ.summary: The schedule constructs a later wave over the actual parent

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_later.text: The actual central gradient splitting constructs a physical amplification window once the preceding cutoff equals one on the new slab. The hypotheses include nonzero perpendicular preceding data, their affine equations, continuous actual gradients, a divergence-free older field, and positive frozen couplings. Continuity of the correction is deduced from the splitting instead of assumed separately.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_later.summary: A completed preceding cutoff yields an actual comparison window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame.text: Given paths $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, the formal frame is $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, as in §1.1 and Lemma 2.2. This definition alone does not assert orthonormality: that requires both vectors to be nonzero and perpendicular. Normalization assigns the zero vector to a zero input, so a vanishing wave vector or amplitude still produces a defined triple but not an orthonormal frame. Its three positions correspond, in order, to the paper’s axes $E_1,E_2,E_3$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame.summary: Nonzero transverse vectors determine the three oriented frame vectors

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frameExpansi.text: In an orthonormal three-dimensional frame, every vector equals the sum of its three coordinate projections. This local copy of the expansion lemma builds an orthonormal basis from the frame and uses the finite dimension to prove spanning. It underlies the scaled wave-vector decomposition; it assumes neither a wave equation nor positive coordinate scales.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frameExpansi.summary: Resolve a vector along all three frame axes

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame_entry_.text: An orthonormal frame whose axes have speed at most `2*M`, together with a matrix field bounded by `M` and derivative bounded by `D`, has each frame entry vary by at most $(4M^2+D)(finish-t_0)$. Derivatives are taken within the closed interval. The theorem assumes the frame-speed bounds rather than deriving them from the wave ODEs.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame_entry_.summary: Frame coefficients vary by the gradient and frame-speed budget

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.hasDerivWith.text: Let $f$ be a vector-valued path whose derivative at $t_0+\tau/r$, relative to a time set $I$, is $v$. Suppose $s\mapsto t_0+s/r$ maps the chosen normalized time set $J$ into $I$. The formal statement gives derivative $v/r$ for $s\mapsto f(t_0+s/r)$ relative to $J$ at $\tau$. This includes the one-sided derivatives at interval endpoints used in §2.2.1. It does not require $r\ne0$: division by zero is assigned zero, making the reparametrized path constant when $r=0$. The application has $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}>0$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.hasDerivWith.summary: An affine change of time divides the derivative by the growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.later_compar.text: If the next activation lies within the first old half interval and the new half length is at most one quarter of the old one, the full next comparison slab lies inside the old slab. Nonnegativity of the new half length is explicit. This elementary interval containment allows previous wave equations to be restricted to the next step.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.later_compar.summary: The next comparison interval fits inside its parent

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_ampli.text: For a positive growth rate $r$, sends every $\tau\in[0,T]$ to physical time $t_0+\tau/r$ in $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The theorem does not require a separate sign assumption on $T$; when the source interval is empty the mapping assertion is vacuous. In the amplification application, $T\ge2$ supplies the intended nonempty window.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_ampli.summary: The inverse clock preserves the time window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_inver.text: For a positive rate $r$, every physical time in $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$ maps under $t\mapsto r(t-t_0)$ into $[0,T]$. Positivity allows multiplying both endpoint inequalities without reversing order. No positivity of $T$ is required in the statement; when $T<0$ the source interval is empty.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_inver.summary: Normalized time stays inside the prescribed interval

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_.text: At a time $t$ in a time set $I$, let $B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have trace zero. Suppose $\kappa(t),\mathbf a(t)$ are nonzero and perpendicular, with $\kappa_t=-B^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)B\mathbf a$ there, taking derivatives within $I$. Form $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$. Each $E_i$ has a derivative within $I$ whose Euclidean norm is at most $2\|B\|$. The matrix norm is the operator norm. The statement is pointwise and requires no bound on $B_t$; a uniform bound for $B$ gives the displayed interval estimate in §6.2.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_.summary: Each frame vector has speed bounded by twice the strain

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.text: Derives the three exact normalized-time equations for $X,Q,Z$ from the preceding affine wave and the new wave-vector equation. The old strain is trace free, the preceding vectors are nonzero and perpendicular, and `scale,S` are nonzero. Both strain operators already use normalized time. The error entries appear with their actual factors of $S$ or $S^{-1}$; this lemma establishes equations, not error bounds.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.summary: Wave-vector equations in the preceding moving frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.text: For a preceding affine wave and its new wave vector, proves $|X-x|+|Q+\varepsilon t|+|Z-1|\le120\delta T^6\le1/2$. It assumes $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$, $S\ge1$, nonzero `scale`, the normalized strain bounds, correct initial direction, and `hsmall : 240 * δ * T ^ 6 ≤ 1`. This is the coordinate comparison only; the separate norm comparison and amplitude estimates need further lemmas.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.summary: The scaled wave vector stays close to the reference

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_a.text: Under the clock mapping hypothesis, composing both wave vectors with the affine normalized clock preserves the ODE form with the strain divided by the rate. The algebraic theorem is total even at rate zero; its physical use has a positive rate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_a.summary: The affine wave equations after time rescaling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_c.text:
For any frame family and operator $B$, rewrites $2(\sigma/r)\langle e_i,(B/r)e_jangle$ as $\langle e_i,Be_jangle/
u$. It assumes positive $r,\sigma,
u$ and $r^2=2\sigma
u$. Orthonormality is unnecessary because only bilinearity and the scalar identity are used. This converts the normalized first and third entries into the paper’s relative coupling errors.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_c.summary: A scaled entry becomes a ratio to the coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_n.text: Transforms both new-wave ODEs under $t=t_0+\tau/r$ and rewrites the preceding rank-one shear using normalized frame axes and the relative strength. It requires `hr : r ≠ 0`, an explicit `MapsTo` condition, and nonzero preceding vectors at activation and the evaluated time. It assumes neither positivity of $r$ nor preceding-wave evolution; those facts are needed by other parts of the amplification argument.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_n.summary: Rescale the wave over the full parent gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.text: Let $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ be nonzero both at time zero and at time $t$, and let $r\ne0$. Put $\sigma=|k_p(0)||\mathbf a_p(0)|$, $\sigma_p(t)=|k_p(t)||\mathbf a_p(t)|$ and $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$. The formal identity is $(\sigma/r)(\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1=(\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p)/r$. Multiplication by $r$ recovers the preceding-wave term in $M$ in §2.2.1. This algebra does not require perpendicularity or an evolution equation. Time zero here is the chosen base time; the physical application shifts it to $t_0$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.summary: Normalizing the wave directions preserves the preceding wave’s rank-one gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.text:
Let $I$ be compact and contain $t_0$, with a continuous frame orthonormal at $t_0$, continuous matrices $B,E_c$, $\sigma>0$, and positive frozen entries $
u=B_{12}(t_0)$, $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)$ satisfying $\eta/
u\le1$. Put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, and let $\delta$ be the four suprema in (2.6), taken over $I$. The formal statement proves $\delta\ge0$, $S^{-1}\le2\delta$, and, for every $t\in I$, $\|B/r\|\le\delta$, $\|E_c/r\|\le\delta/S$, $|B_{12}/
u-1|\le\delta$, $|B_{32}/
u-\eta/
u|\le\delta$. Operator norms are Euclidean. No wave evolution is needed for this estimate; compactness and continuity make the suprema finite.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.summary: The four physical suprema bound the rescaled coefficients

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.text: Under positive growth rate and frozen strength and coupling, with $r^2=2\sigma\nu$, identifies $(\sigma/r)\|(1/r)E\|$ with $\|E\|/(2\nu)$. The identity explains the large factor introduced by scaled coordinates. It is an equality for any continuous linear error operator and does not itself impose the small error budget $\delta$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.summary: The scaled matrix error is measured against the coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.text: The normalization in time divides the full older-plus-wave-plus-error gradient by the rate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.summary: Time normalization divides the full strain by the rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_t.text: Multiplying the background operator by the reciprocal rate preserves zero trace. This purely linear identity does not require the rate to be nonzero.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w.text: Assume an orthonormal frame obeying all three equations (2.2), nonzero scales $\lambda,S$, and a wave vector solving $k'=-M^Tk$. Write the normalized full gradient as $M=B+S(\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1+E$ and use the scaled coordinates (2.3). The formal statement gives the three exact derivatives of $\zeta$, including the terms from $E$. With $E=0$ these are the equations displayed in the proof of Lemma 2.4. For $E=E_c/r$, its extra rows give the matrix $-r^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(1,S,1)E_c^T\operatorname{diag}(1,S^{-1},1)$. Derivatives are relative to the supplied time set. No smallness or nonvanishing condition on $k$ is used in this linear calculation.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w.summary: Moving-frame differentiation retains every component of the gradient error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.pairing_coor.text: For nonzero `scale` and `S`, rewrites each pairing with $k$ as `scale` times the corresponding entry of $(X,Q/S,Z)$. This is cancellation of the coordinate definitions and does not require the frame to be orthonormal. Orthogonality enters only when the three pairings are used to reconstruct the vector or its norm.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.pairing_coor.summary: Recover frame pairings from the scaled coordinates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.physical_aff.text: If normalized paths solve the equations for the strain $M/r$ on $[0,T]$, their compositions with $r(t-t_0)$ solve the physical equations on $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The amplitude may also be multiplied by any constant `c`, including zero. The theorem assumes $r>0$ and returns within-set derivatives on the closed slab, without adding a nonvanishing conclusion.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.physical_aff.summary: The inverse clock restores the physical wave equations

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.polynomial_w.text: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and $D\ge0$, with $12DT^3\le1$. On $[0,T]$, suppose $(X,Q,Z)(0)=(0,0,1)$ and $X'=-Q+r_1$, $Q'=-\varepsilon Z+r_2$, $Z'=r_3$, where each $|r_i|\le D(|X|+|Q|+|Z|)$. The formal statement gives $|X-\varepsilon\tau^2/2|+|Q+\varepsilon\tau|+|Z-1|\le24DT^5$ for every $\tau\in[0,T]$. It uses the sum of absolute coordinate errors, which bounds their Euclidean norm. This supplies the perturbative estimate behind (2.10), conditional on these residual bounds; it does not itself obtain them from the physical gradients.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.polynomial_w.summary: Small residuals give an explicit polynomial error from the triangular model

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualQ.text: Defines the remainder in $Q\prime=-\varepsilon Z+\mathrm{residualQ}$. The term $\varepsilon-2Sb_{32}-Sd_{32}$ measures the deviation of the third coupling from its frozen value, while the other terms contain the older diagonal entry and scaled error entries. Lean uses zero-based indices, so its `b 2 1` is the paper’s $b_{32}$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualQ.summary: Second-coordinate error beyond the limiting coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualX.text: Defines the remainder in $X\prime=-Q+\mathrm{residualX}$ from older-strain entries `b`, error entries `d`, and the relative preceding strength `σratio`. Its three terms multiply $X,Q,Z$, respectively. The coefficient of $Q$ includes the difference between the current and initial shear strength. This is an algebraic definition for arbitrary entries, with no smallness assumptions built in.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualX.summary: First-coordinate error beyond the limiting shear

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualZ.text: Defines the entire right-hand side of the $Z$ equation, since the reference third coordinate is constant. The expression combines the error’s first and third entries with the difference $b_{23}-b_{32}$ in the coefficient of $Q/S$. It accepts arbitrary entries and coordinates; identifying it with an actual derivative requires the moving-frame equations.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residualZ.summary: Third-coordinate error beyond a constant reference component

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residual_bou.text: Bounds each of the three residuals by $5T\delta(|X|+|Q|+|Z|)$. It assumes $T,S\ge1$, nonnegative $\delta$, entrywise bounds on `b,d,S*d`, relative-strength error at most $2T\delta$, and the third-coupling error at most $\delta$. No bound on $X,Q,Z$ is assumed. These explicit row estimates supply the perturbative coefficient bound before the bootstrap closes.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.residual_bou.summary: All wave-vector residuals satisfy one coefficient bound

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV.text: At a fixed time, let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be orthonormal and let $\lambda,S\ne0$. Define the coordinates by $\zeta_1=(k\cdot E_1)/\lambda$, $\zeta_2=S(k\cdot E_2)/\lambda$, $\zeta_3=(k\cdot E_3)/\lambda$. The formal statement proves $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$, the wave-vector part of (2.3). The assertion is pointwise linear algebra and includes $k=0$. It neither assumes the wave equation nor constructs an amplitude. Nonzero scales are required because the reconstruction cancels the divisions used in the coordinates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV.summary: Projection reconstructs the wave vector in the scaled orthonormal coordinates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.shearScale_d.text:
With positive $r,\sigma,
u$ and the defining relation $r^2=2\sigma
u$, proves $(\sigma/r)(1/r)=1/(2
u)$. This is the conversion $S/r=1/(2
u)$ used to measure the matrix error against the older coupling. All three positivity assumptions appear in the source, although the equality is algebraic once the relevant denominators are nonzero.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.shearScale_d.summary: The shear factor converts growth rate to coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strain.text:
The normalized strain is B plus the rank-one shear Sσratio e₁⊗e₀ plus E. Orthonormality and evolution of the frame are additional hypotheses when this algebraic expression is used in the amplitude equations.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a sum of continuous linear maps for arbitrary data. It imposes neither orthonormality of the frame nor trace or symmetry conditions.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strain.summary: Older strain plus the leading shear and error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.text:
The preceding wave strength normalized by its value at activation.

Default-value audit (b5): The strength ratio divides by the initial product of vector norms. Nonzero initial wave vector and amplitude are needed for the ratio to be a physical normalization.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.summary: The preceding strength relative to its initial value

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.text: On $[0,T]$, suppose $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ are nonzero, perpendicular solutions of the wave equations over a trace-free background $B$, with Euclidean operator norm $\|B(t)\|\le\delta$ and $T\delta\le1$. The formal statement proves $|\sigma_p(t)/\sigma_p(0)-1|\le2T\delta$, where $\sigma_p=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$. This is the strength estimate used in Lemma 2.4, after time normalization makes $B$ the physical background divided by $r$. The denominator is positive by the initial nonvanishing assumptions. Only relative derivatives on the interval are needed; smoothness of $B$ is not an additional hypothesis.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.summary: A small older gradient keeps the preceding strength close to its initial value

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c.text: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1/2$, $T\ge2$, $0\le\tau\le T$, and assume $|X-\varepsilon\tau^2/2|+|Q+\varepsilon\tau|+|Z-1|\le1/2$. The formal statement gives $1/2\le Z\le3/2$, $|X|\le T^2$, $|Q|\le T$ and $X^2+Q^2/S^2+Z^2\ge1/4$. These are algebraic consequences of the error bound, before any amplitude equation is used. The conclusion holds for every real $S$, because division by zero is assigned zero and the $Z^2$ term already supplies the lower bound. In the physical application $S>0$ and the last expression is $m$ in (2.3).
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c.summary: A half-unit coordinate error keeps the third component and norm denominator positive

TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold.text: For a nonnegative integer $b$ and functions $F,\mathcal B$ on the nonnegative integers, the formal condition requires, at positive indices, that $\mathcal B$ be nondecreasing, positive, at least $F$, and satisfy $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$, where $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. Values at zero are unrestricted. The function $F$ is a proposed majorant of the fixed-order analytic constants; the inequality $F(s)\le\mathcal B(s)$ alone does not identify those constants or prove that $F$ bounds them. The condition also does not itself require $b\ge1$. Those facts must be supplied in the application to the parameter choice of §1.5.
TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold.summary: Positive thresholds dominate costs and satisfy the logarithmic floor

TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector.text: For a prescribed wave vector $k$ on a compact physical time set $I$, the formal condition requires $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ and $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$ at every time in $I$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. Derivatives are taken relative to $I$. This is the amplitude vector of §2.2.1; no initial amplitude or nonvanishing condition is imposed, and the zero solution is allowed. The formula assigns zero to division by zero. Its physical use accompanies a launched wave vector that is nonzero on the active interval, so that convention does not alter the pressure coefficient there.
TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector.summary: The amplitude solves its linear equation and stays perpendicular to the wave vector

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol.text: The formal object is a smooth function $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi(\zeta)=1$ for $|\zeta|\le1$, $\psi(\zeta)=0$ for $|\zeta|>2$, and $\psi(-\zeta)=\psi(\zeta)$. Thus its support is compact and contained in the closed ball of radius two. Appendix B assumes radiality; the formal condition requires only evenness, which admits additional symbols. This is a condition on the symbol, not the definition of the operator $S_\Lambda$ or a proof of any operator estimate. No frequency parameter or field is selected here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol.summary: Records smoothness, support and evenness of the symbol

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol..text: Suppose $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is smooth, takes values in $[0,1]$, equals one on the unit ball, vanishes outside the ball of radius two, and has equal values at points with equal Euclidean norm. The formal statement shows that $\psi$ satisfies the cutoff conditions used in Appendix B. The only deduction is evenness, since $|-\zeta|=|\zeta|$; all other conditions are supplied as hypotheses. It therefore verifies that every radial symbol allowed by the paper is allowed by the formalization, without asserting that an even symbol must be radial.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol..summary: Derives the formal symbol conditions from radiality

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.cutoffSymbol_.text: This theorem supplies AppendixB.CutoffSymbol for the fixed dyadicMultiplierCutoff used in the library construction. It gathers the existing smoothness, range, unit-ball and support facts and its symmetry under negation. The paper allows a fixed radial symbol rather than naming this particular library object; this is one admissible implementation, not an identification of all choices.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.cutoffSymbol_.summary: The library cutoff satisfies the appendix hypotheses

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.text:
This requires every coefficient slice c(t,·) to be C∞ and every unweighted label-jet value set through order n to be bounded above. It is the finiteness condition for all |c|_m with m≤n. The theorem CoefficientNormFinite.fieldNormFinite transfers it to the phase-independent lift for arbitrary weights.

Default-value audit (b4): ContDiff rules out derivative defaults, and BddAbove rules out unbounded real suprema. Nonemptiness follows from the inserted zero, including when the time type is empty. The predicate asserts no temporal smoothness, no phase dependence and no positivity of external weights. No integral, inverse, square root or ENNReal conversion is introduced.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.summary: Smooth coefficient derivatives with finite bounds

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.text: If the coefficient c has smooth bounded label jets through order n, its phase-independent lift has finite mixed norm at the same order for every radius ℓ and phase width h. The proof separates words containing the phase direction, which vanish, from label-only words, whose values are scalar multiples of bounded sets. This supplies the finiteness guard that the companion expression identity does not assume.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.summary: Finite coefficient norms remain finite after adding a phase

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.text: For $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, with $X$ a real normed space, this condition requires smoothness in the label variable, bounded derivatives uniformly over the specified time set $I$, and $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ for every $m\ge0$. The sequence $(C_m)$ is an explicit input, and $q$ is a nonnegative integer. The quantity $|c|_m$ is the sum of the suprema of the coordinate derivatives with $|\beta|=m$. In Lemma D.2 the output constants are chosen before $I$, $\mathsf D$ and the fields, which supplies the paper's uniformity. This condition by itself imposes no lower bound on $\mathsf D$; the coefficient estimates separately assume $\mathsf D\ge1$.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.summary: Specifies the constants before measuring a coefficient

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.text: For any CoefficientPower certificate and any chosen n, this extracts smoothness and the boundedness conditions through order n to produce CoefficientNormFinite n c. It uses the explicit boundedness component of the certificate, not a conclusion inferred from a possibly default-valued real norm inequality. D and the coefficient exponent need no extra restriction for this extraction.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.summary: Power bounds give finite coefficient norms at every order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.FieldNormFini.text:
This is the analytic side condition for fieldNorm: every time slice is C∞ in (a,s), and every set of derivative values entering the finite sum is bounded above. It concerns only words of total order at most n, although the slice smoothness is unrestricted. It does not itself require phase periodicity or positivity of ℓ and h; the result using it states those separately where needed.

Default-value audit (b4): This predicate is the guard, not another numerical norm. Its ContDiff conjunct excludes zero-default derivatives at the measured orders, and BddAbove excludes the unbounded real-supremum default. Nonemptiness of each value set already follows from the inserted 0. If I is empty the conditions are vacuous and all value sets are {0}; that is an allowed zero-domain convention. Positive ℓ,h must still come from the caller.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.FieldNormFini.summary: Smooth mixed jets with bounded supremum sets

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.HolderFieldNo.text:
This requires C∞ label slices and boundedness of every set of supremum values and half-Hölder quotients through weighted order n. It is the finiteness predicate paired with holderFieldNorm. It imposes no temporal differentiability because the time variable is only an index of a uniform bound.

Default-value audit (b4): ContDiff excludes default spatial derivatives; BddAbove excludes unbounded real suprema. The quotient radicand is dist x y≥0, with zero numerator at x=y, so its zero-over-zero diagonal contributes only zero. Each set explicitly includes 0 and is nonempty. An empty time type is permitted and gives the trivial zero-domain case. No positive radius hypothesis is included here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.HolderFieldNo.summary: Smooth label jets with bounded Hölder quotients

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.text:
This sums ℓ^m|c|_m for 0≤m≤n. For a smooth phase-independent coefficient and ℓ≥0, the identity fieldNorm_phaseIndependent identifies it with the mixed norm of (t,a,s)↦c(t,a), for any h. This definition uses the explicit powers ℓ^m, so positivity matters if it is to behave as the paper’s norm.

Default-value audit (b4): The derivative words use fderiv and therefore can have the default zero value where differentiability is absent. Smoothness of every spatial slice is part of the corresponding finiteness predicate. hierarchyJetValues contains 0 by definition (HierarchyProductEstimates.lean:325–329), so its set is nonempty even for an empty time type. Without BddAbove its real supremum can return the default zero; the finiteness predicates supply exactly that missing guard. The empty time type gives an identically zero norm and is allowed by these general definitions; the paper applications use nonempty slabs. The real suprema are those of coefficientOrderNorm. A negative ℓ can create cancellation between different orders, while ℓ=0 erases all positive orders; the identity lemmas assume ℓ≥0 and the analytic estimates assume ℓ>0. At m=0 the convention ℓ⁰=1 correctly retains the field itself.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.summary: The weighted finite norm of a phase independent coefficient

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.text: For a smooth phase-independent coefficient and ℓ≥0, the explicit sum ∑_{m≤n}ℓ^m|c|_m equals hierarchyFiniteWordNorm with only label directions. It is the non-Hölder specialization of labelWordNorm_eq_sum, in the direction useful for replacing a coefficient norm by a word norm. Boundedness is not part of the theorem, so genuine norm interpretation remains a separate finiteness obligation.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.summary: Coefficient norms equal the weighted label word sum

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientOr.text: For a phase-independent field $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, this expression is $|c|_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{t\in I,a\in\mathbb R^3}|\partial_a^\beta c(t,a)|$, with the norm of the real normed target space $X$. A sorted list of coordinate differentiations represents each multi-index once. The supremum includes all times in the chosen set, not time derivatives; choosing $I=[t_0,T]$ gives the paper's interval. The expression uses real-valued suprema, so the separate boundedness hypotheses are needed for it to measure the derivatives. It does not assert smoothness or boundedness of an arbitrary coefficient.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientOr.summary: Sums each spatial multi-index once at a fixed order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm.text: For $f(t,a,s)$, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, the expression sums the suprema of $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf$ over $|\beta|+j\le n$, counting each pair $(\beta,j)$ once. The supremum runs over the entire chosen time set, all labels and all phases. For positive scales and bounded smooth derivatives this is $\|f\|_{[n]}$ in (D.1); for a periodic profile the phase supremum may equivalently be taken over one period. The expression itself neither requires periodicity nor proves boundedness. Smoothness and boundedness are separate assumptions in the estimates that use it, and there are no time derivatives in this norm.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm.summary: Weights label derivatives and phase derivatives separately

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_pha.text: Let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$ be smooth in its spatial variable at every time, let $\ell_*\ge0$, and let $n\ge0$ be an integer. Regarding $c(t,a)$ as a function of $(t,a,s)$ independent of $s$, the formal statement gives $\|c\|_{[n]}=\sum_{m=0}^n\ell_*^m|c|_m$ for every real phase weight $h$. Every derivative containing a phase differentiation is zero, so only spatial multi-indices remain. This identifies the two expressions used in Appendix D. Boundedness is not a hypothesis of this identity between expressions; it must be supplied separately when interpreting them as finite derivative norms.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_pha.summary: Identifies the mixed norm of a phase-independent field

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.text: For a phase-independent field $c(t,a)$, this expression is the sum over $|\beta|\le n$ of the uniform-in-time half-Hölder norms of $\ell_*^{|\beta|}\partial_a^\beta c$. Labels range over $\mathbb R^3$ and there is no time differentiation. Each half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the spatial supremum and $\sup_{a\ne b}|g(a)-g(b)|/|a-b|^{1/2}$. The coincident-point quotient is assigned zero. The customary sum of these two quantities is between this maximum and twice it. The paper does not specify that internal convention; the distinction changes constants, not the boundedness class. Boundedness of all quantities entering the expression is a separate hypothesis.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.summary: Uses spatial Hölder bounds uniformly over the time set

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.text: Let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$ be smooth in the label variable, with $X$ a real normed space, and let $\ell_*\ge0$. For every integer $n\ge0$, the formal statement identifies the finite Hölder expression with $\sum_{m=0}^n\ell_*^m|c|_{m,1/2}$. Each multi-index occurs once, and each order uses the supremum over all times in $I$ of the maximum of the spatial supremum and half-Hölder seminorm. The equality is the grouping by order stated in Appendix D. It does not establish finiteness; bounded derivative and difference-quotient families must be assumed when these expressions are used as norms.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.summary: Groups the finite Hölder norm by spatial order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNo.text: For a phase-independent field $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, the formal expression sums, over $|\beta|=m$, the supremum in time of the maximum of $\|\partial_a^\beta c(t)\|_\infty$ and its spatial half-Hölder seminorm. Each multi-index is counted once. Difference quotients use Euclidean distances between labels; the quotient at equal labels is assigned zero. The paper's notation $|c|_{m,1/2}$ does not specify whether the two parts of the Hölder norm are added or maximized. Replacing the maximum by their sum changes this quantity by at most a factor two. Smoothness and boundedness are not conclusions of the definition.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNo.summary: Measures each spatial derivative in the maximum Hölder norm

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.jetValues_lab.text: For every smooth coefficient c, every word w, radius r∈ℝ and either choice of Hölder values, the jet-value set in directions re_i is |r^{length w}| times the set in unit directions. This is a set identity before taking any supremum. It holds also for negative r or r=0 and does not need boundedness. Spatial smoothness is needed to identify the iterated derivatives with their scaled versions.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.jetValues_lab.summary: A scaled label derivative contributes one radius factor

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.labelPartial.text:
For each time and each i∈Fin 3, this applies the Fréchet derivative of f(t,a,s) in the label direction (e_i,0). Lean indices 0,1,2 are the paper’s three coordinate labels. Time is a parameter of an arbitrary type I and is not differentiated. The operation is defined on every function; smoothness is supplied by the norm-finiteness hypotheses when it is used analytically.

Default-value audit (b4): phaseDirectionalDerivative is fderiv applied to the direction (PhaseJetBounds.lean:18–26); for a nondifferentiable input fderiv may be the zero default. No differentiability is built into labelPartial itself. FieldNormFinite in Lemma D.1 includes spatial smoothness, and its positive weight makes smoothness of f/γ equivalent to that of f at fixed time. No integral, square root, reciprocal or extended-real conversion is introduced here.
