It is the kinetic matrix in (4.1), and the quadratic part of the label energy in (4.7). The transpose is the Euclidean adjoint and norms are operator norms. This definition gives nonnegativity, not a positive lower bound. If $F$ has inverse norm at most $D_->0$, the separate ellipticity estimate gives $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$.
TorusEuler.Paper.meanKinetic.summary: Define the kinetic coefficient from the flow deformation

TorusEuler.Paper.meanVorticity.text: With $F=D_aX_{0,t}(a)$ and $M=D_xu(t,X_{0,t}(a))$, the coefficient is $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. It is the pulled-back vorticity in (4.1) and supplies the term $\Omega z_t\cdot z$ in the endpoint energy. The matrix convention is $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_ju_i$, fixing the sign of $M^T-M$. The formula does not require Euler or incompressibility. Its relation $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$ uses the separately established flow identity $F_t=MF$.
TorusEuler.Paper.meanVorticity.summary: Pull the skew velocity gradient back by the flow

TorusEuler.Paper.modelEntries.text:
The formal matrix is $ igl( egin{smallmatrix}0&
u&0\0&0&0\0&\eta&0\end{smallmatrix} igr)$, so its only possibly nonzero entries are $B_{12}=
u$ and $B_{32}=\eta$. In Lemma 2.3 these are entries in the preceding wave’s moving orthonormal frame, not fixed spatial components. The definition permits arbitrary real $
u,\eta$ and contains no time variable. The model hypothesis separately requires the actual gradient to have these constant frame entries throughout $[0,T]$, with positive activation couplings and vanishing error gradient $E_c$.
TorusEuler.Paper.modelEntries.summary: The model matrix has precisely the two prescribed couplings

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8.text:
Let $B,E_c$ be continuous on compact $I\supset[t_0,t_0+T/r]$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and nonzero perpendicular preceding wave data satisfying $k_p\prime=-B^Tk_p$, $\mathbf a_p\prime=-B\mathbf a_p+2(k_p\cdot B\mathbf a_p)k_p/|k_p|^2$. Set $E_1=\widehat{k_p}$, $E_2=\widehat{\mathbf a_p}$ and $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$; $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. Physical derivatives are relative to $I$; for interval $I$, endpoint derivatives are one-sided. Put $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$, $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)>0$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, and $\delta=\sup_I|B_{12}/
u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+\sup_I\|B\|/r+\sup_I\|E_c\|/
u$. Assume $T\ge2$ and $C_0\varepsilon\le1$, $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ for sufficiently large integer $C_0$. In physical time, the new wave solves $k'=-M^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, with $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$, $\lambda>0$, and $\mathbf a(t_0)=-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$. Use $	au=r(t-t_0)$, $\alpha_1=S\mathbf a\cdot E_1$, $\alpha_2=\mathbf a\cdot E_2$, $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$, and $a_{m ref}=\exp\int_0^	au Y$ with $Y\prime=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)-\varepsilon	au\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. Assume $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le T$. The theorem gives $\eta_+/
u_+=\varepsilon_+$ at a crossing in $[	au_m,H]$, after the reference peak. With $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$, every crossing there satisfies $\exp(-1)/(4\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})\le|\mathbf a||k|/(\lambda A)\le18\exp(3)/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. It also proves $|\mathbf a|\le\exp(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2})A$ on $[0,1]$. Here $
u_+=\widehat k\cdot M\widehat a$ and $\eta_+=(\widehat k	imes\widehat a)\cdot M\widehat a$. Crossing uniqueness is not asserted.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8.summary: Every crossing in the prescribed interval retains the strength bound

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_1.text: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. Assume a smooth odd solenoidal unit-periodic parent $U$ and flow $X$, Fourier bands $2\mathsf D$ for $U$ and $4\mathsf D$ for the odd residual $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$, bounds $\|DU\|,\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. The pressure may be any smooth periodic choice satisfying these conditions. For $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$ normalized at $t_0$, the six coefficients $DX,DX^{-1},M,\kappa/\lambda,\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2,P_\kappa$ have order-$m$ bounds $C_m\mathsf D^{C(m+1)}$. A field with $\|D^mf\|\le C_m^{\prime}A_f\mathsf D^m$ satisfies $\|D_a^m(f\circ X)\|\le C_mA_f\mathsf D^{Cm}$. If $0<\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-C}$, the scaled sums satisfy (5.8). One exponent works at every order; operator norms replace coordinate sums.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_1.summary: Bernstein estimates yield the uniform coefficient bounds

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_11.text: Let $V,\Pi$ be a depth-$P\ge2$ approximation over a smooth odd divergence-free periodic parent on $0<T\le1$, with gradient and deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, velocity and residual Fourier radii $2\mathsf D,4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$. Assume (5.5), $\lambda\ge1$, $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$, small envelope and $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, where $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$. For every smooth radial $0\le\psi\le1$ equal to one on $|\xi|\le1$ and zero on $|\xi|>2$, and $\Lambda\ge1$, the theorem constructs $u=S_\Lambda V$ and its normalized Poisson pressure $p$. With $\varepsilon=\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$ and $e=C\|R_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}+K_P\varepsilon$, the velocity error is at most $K_P\varepsilon$, the summed residual and pressure-Hessian errors at most $e$, and $D^2(p-p_U)\le(C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/4}+e)I$. Both $u,R_u$ are odd and divergence free with Fourier radii $2\Lambda,4\Lambda$. Error norms may be evaluated at independent times.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_11.summary: Prove the cutoff error bounds with the normalized Poisson pressure

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_2.text: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. Assume a smooth odd solenoidal unit-periodic parent $U$ and flow $X$, Fourier bands $2\mathsf D$ for $U$ and $4\mathsf D$ for the odd residual $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$, bounds $\|DU\|,\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. The pressure may be any smooth periodic choice satisfying these conditions. For a smooth periodic phase-independent solution $B_t+MB+\mathbf d\bar q=\bar f$, require $B=DXz_t$, $\operatorname{div}_az_t=0$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. At sufficiently small fixed $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$, $\|B\|_{[n]}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|\bar f\|_{[n+1]}$ for every $n$. These are scaled label-derivative suprema on all of $[0,T]$. The exponent is chosen before the parent and order. This estimates existing solutions; it does not set $B(0)=0$.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_2.summary: The endpoint mean bound loses one source derivative

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_4.text: Assume a smooth odd unit-periodic solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, with bands $2\mathsf D$ for velocity and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, residual bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$ and $0\le t_0<T$. The nonzero central seed solves $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, is transverse, has relative forward stability at most $\mathsf D$ and normalized coupling at least $\mathsf D^{-1}$, and satisfies $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. For sufficiently small fixed $\ell_*$, the projected seed exists, and every depth $P\ge2$ admits a unique family of retained velocities and normalized pressures satisfying the mean and transverse recursions. For $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$ and $\mathsf P=\sum_{p=1}^P(\mathsf p_p+\bar q_p)$, $\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot W=0$ and the momentum residual is $R_P+R_{\widetilde\chi}$. The oscillations and their sources vanish before activation and outside the envelope; there the remainder is phase independent. Means need not vanish before activation. Smoothness is on the closed slab; no continuation across its endpoints is asserted.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_4.summary: Construct unique retained profiles and their exact remainder

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_1.text: For every common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, this theorem constructs smooth periodic velocity $u$ and mean-zero pressure $p$ solving Euler on $[0,T_\infty)$. The datum $u(0)$ is smooth, odd and divergence free, with $U_j(0)\to u(0)$ in every $C^{m,1/2}$. The velocity stays odd, and $U_j\to u$ uniformly in each such spatial norm on every $[0,S]$, $S<T_\infty$. Every maximal solution of finite lifespan from the same data lasts at least to $T_\infty$ and agrees with $u$ there. This is a conditional comparison, not general maximal-solution existence; Corollary 8.3 later proves maximality of the constructed solution. The exact numerical Hölder norm is imported from a file not supplied here.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_1.summary: Prove existence and convergence without a general maximal-existence theorem

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2.text: For a common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1 and its smooth Euler limit from Proposition 8.1, this theorem proves $\sup_{0\le t<T_\infty}\|u(t)\|_\infty<\infty$ and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. In addition, fixed real $c>0,C$ give $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\ge c\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}-C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/32}-C$ for every sufficiently large $j$ and all $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$. Thus the blow-up is not restricted to a sequence of times. The spatial domain is the unit torus, represented by periodic fields on $\mathbb R^3$; the velocity norm is its essential supremum. The quantitative estimate is stronger than the printed Proposition 8.2 and is used with crossing lengths for the later integral argument.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2.summary: Prove bounded velocity and a full terminal vorticity limit

TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_4.text: For the smooth periodic Euler limit of any common construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, this theorem proves the two limits in Proposition 8.4. Given a compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$ and an integer $m\ge0$, $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ converge uniformly on $K$ with every spatial derivative through order $m$, as $t\uparrow T_\infty$. The limits extend to $C^m$ fields near $K$. Removing the lattice means removing the torus origin, and the time derivative is taken inside $[0,T_\infty)$. The conclusion supplies spatial limits of the velocity and one time derivative; it does not require convergence of all higher time derivatives. The auxiliary note proves a stronger extension assertion for a suitably chosen construction.
TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_4.summary: Prove both local limits away from the torus origin

TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAmplitude.text: For a real function $Y$ and time $\tau$, the formal expression is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(s)\,ds)$, using the interval integral with its orientation when $\tau<0$. This defines a positive number for every input function. If the integral is not defined by an integrable function on the interval, the formal integral is assigned zero, giving amplitude one; this is not a claim of integrability. In the application, $Y$ solves (2.12) on $[0,\infty)$, hence is continuous there, and the ordinary integral gives the reference amplitude with $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$.
TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAmplitude.summary: Exponentiating the integral of the logarithmic slope defines the reference amplitude

TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle.text: The formal angle is $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ for every real $\varepsilon,\tau$. It satisfies $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, and for $\varepsilon\ge0$ lies in $[0,\pi/2)$. These specify the branch in (2.4); there is no ambiguity by integer multiples of $\pi$. The angle parametrizes the limiting direction $\tan\varphi E_1+E_3$ as the preceding shear tends to infinity. The definition does not claim that it is the actual angle of a finite-shear or perturbed wave, whose components must be estimated separately.
TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle.summary: The arctangent chooses a fixed branch for the limiting wave-vector angle

TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem.text: For every $\varepsilon\ge0$ and every real $\tau$, the formal statement proves $0\le\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)<\pi/2$. This is the branch requirement for $\varphi$ in (2.4), extended to all real times. In particular the cosine is positive at every finite time. The result concerns the explicitly defined reference angle only; it does not constrain the actual wave vector of a finite-shear configuration. Neither an evolution equation nor the smallness condition (2.7) is a hypothesis.
TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem.summary: A nonnegative coupling ratio keeps the reference angle below a right angle

TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix.text: Put $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal matrix acting on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ is $-\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi&\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Its second row therefore gives $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$, exactly as in (2.5). This definition uses the paper’s signs, unlike the intermediate matrix in coordinates $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. It is defined for all real parameters and times and is only a coefficient matrix: it neither constructs a solution nor proves that a particular amplitude satisfies the equation. Those assertions require separate differential-equation hypotheses or theorems.
TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix.summary: The matrix is written in the paper’s two scaled amplitude coordinates

TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2.text: There exist smooth odd divergence-free data $u_0$ on $\mathbb T^3$ and a smooth odd maximal Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$, with $0<T_*<\infty$, bounded velocity, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and divergent time integrals of both gradient and vorticity norms. Velocity and its time derivative converge in every spatial $C^m$ norm on compact sets away from the origin. The velocity also extends smoothly in space and time through $T_*$ away from that point. Any maximal solution from $u_0$ has the same lifespan and velocity. The extension is periodic and need not solve Euler after $T_*$. This is the existential assertion of Remark 1.2, not an extension theorem for every singular solution.
TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2.summary: The chosen singular solution extends smoothly away from the origin

TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq.text: For a real scale $S$ and vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$. When $S\ne0$ and $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ in an orthonormal frame, it satisfies $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$. This is the factor after (2.3), not the ordinary Euclidean squared norm of $\zeta$. The definition also permits $S=0$: division by zero is assigned zero, so the middle term vanishes. To use $m$ as a nonzero pressure denominator, the amplitude equations impose positive $S$ and nonzero $\zeta_3$.
TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq.summary: The scaled squared norm has a different weight in the second direction

TorusEuler.Paper.statementsS34ASolenoida.text:
This local instance makes the existing NormedAddCommGroup structure on the solenoidal HalfHolder subspace available to elaboration. It introduces no new norm formula and no additional regularity assertion about a field. The paper uses the inherited C^{0,1/2} norm on divergence-free fields without spelling out this type-class step. It is implementation support for the endpoint statements, not a separately numbered mathematical claim.

Default-value audit (b4): No analytic operation is defined here: inferInstance reuses the bundled normed additive-group structure. Finiteness of the HalfHolder norm is part of the ambient bundled space, rather than a fresh real supremum over an arbitrary unbounded function. This instance does not by itself prove coefficient continuity, integrability, or differentiability.
TorusEuler.Paper.statementsS34ASolenoida.summary: The inherited norm on divergence free fields

TorusEuler.Paper.statementsS34ASolenoida.text:
This local instance supplies the inherited real NormedSpace structure on the solenoidal HalfHolder subspace. It lets the endpoint statements use continuous linear maps, scalar multiplication and derivatives in that subspace. No solution is constructed and no coefficient estimate is proved. It is the explicit elaboration support for the paper’s use of a normed linear space of divergence-free fields.

Default-value audit (b4): The declaration only reuses an existing type-class instance. It introduces no derivative, integral, division, supremum, ENNReal conversion or square root. The presence of a NormedSpace instance is not a substitute for any field’s regularity hypotheses.
TorusEuler.Paper.statementsS34ASolenoida.summary: Scalar multiplication on divergence free Hölder fields

TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix.text: For scale $S$, ratio $\varepsilon$ and scaled wave vector $\zeta$, put $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$ and $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/m$. The formal matrix is the linear map whose first component is $-\alpha_2+\zeta_1\Pi$ and whose second is $-(1-1/(2S^2))\alpha_1+\varepsilon(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(2S^2\zeta_3)+\zeta_2\Pi/S^2$. These are the finite-shear right-hand sides in Lemma 2.3. The definition asserts no differential equation. Its use for a model amplitude requires $S>0$, $\zeta_3\ne0$ and transversality. At zero denominators the formal divisions are assigned zero, so existence of the matrix alone does not establish that this reduction is valid.
TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix.summary: Eliminating the third amplitude component gives the two finite-shear equations

TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe.text: Let $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$ and $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/m$. The formal statement proves that the finite-shear matrix applied to $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ has components $-\alpha_2+\zeta_1\Pi$ and $-(1-1/(2S^2))\alpha_1+\varepsilon(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(2S^2\zeta_3)+\zeta_2\Pi/S^2$. This verifies the algebra connecting the coefficient matrix to Lemma 2.3. The identity holds for arbitrary real inputs, including zero denominators because every division by zero is assigned zero. It is not an assertion that an amplitude solves this system; that requires the model wave hypotheses and $\zeta_3\ne0$.
TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe.summary: Matrix multiplication gives the two displayed finite-shear right-hand sides

TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure.text: For $S,\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal formula is $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/(\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2)$. In the two-entry model, with positive $S$, nonzero wave vector and the scaling (2.3), this is $\lambda S p_{\rm w}/r$. It is the pressure term in Lemma 2.3, linear in the two remaining amplitude components. The definition itself does not assume the model equations or positivity of the denominator. Division by zero is assigned zero; the lemma’s condition $\zeta_3\ne0$ ensures the ordinary pressure interpretation.
TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure.summary: The reduced pressure depends linearly on the first two amplitude coordinates

TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle.text: For all real $\varepsilon,\tau$, the formal statement proves $\tan(\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2))=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$. This is the first relation in (2.4) with the explicitly chosen arctangent branch. It imposes no sign condition on $\varepsilon$ and involves no wave equation. The additional paper condition $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ uses $\varepsilon\ge0$. Because arctangent always lies strictly between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$, the tangent here does not encounter a pole at any finite real input.
TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle.summary: The chosen arctangent has exactly the required tangent

TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1.text: There exist smooth odd divergence-free periodic data $u_0$ and a smooth odd maximal Euler solution $u,p$ on $[0,T_*)$, with finite $T_*>0$. Velocity remains uniformly bounded, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and the time integrals of $\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty$ both diverge. For every compact set away from the torus origin and every $m\ge0$, velocity and its time derivative converge in $C^m$. The formal statement further spells out the classical uniqueness implicit in the paper: every maximal solution from $u_0$ has endpoint $T_*$ and agrees with $u$ before it. Fields are periodic functions on $\mathbb R^3$; pressure has zero spatial mean.
TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1.summary: The formal theorem proves the stated periodic singularity

TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2.text: For a smooth periodic divergence-free parent on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, let $X$ be its flow, $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$, and assume $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. The endpoint system $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+\nabla\phi$, $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, has a unique solution for each $L\in C_tC^{0,1/2}$. Both its velocity and $(\mathbb PK(t))^{-1}\mathbb P$ satisfy one uniform polynomial bound. The formal bound uses supremum bounds on $F^{-1},M,K,\Omega,D_aK,D_a\Omega$, instead of full coefficient Hölder norms. Smooth force sources give smooth solutions of the linearized Euler equation and $b(0)=c$. Uniqueness concerns $z,v,c$ and the pressure gradient, on the specified interval. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2.summary: Prove existence and estimates for the selected correction

TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6.text: Assume a smooth odd unit-periodic solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, with bands $2\mathsf D$ for velocity and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, residual bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$ and $0\le t_0<T$. The nonzero central seed solves $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, is transverse, has relative forward stability at most $\mathsf D$ and normalized coupling at least $\mathsf D^{-1}$, and satisfies $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. Fix a sufficiently small radius $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ and a depth-$P$ expansion, $P\ge2$. If $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, then at every order the transverse velocity, forcing and $\lambda$ times pressure have size $C_{n,p}\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$; means and mean sources have size $C_{n,p}\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/2-2(p-2)/3}$; $C_{p+1}$ has size $C_{n,p}\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-9/4-2(p-1)/3}$. The finite sums satisfy (5.37), and $\|R_P\|_{[m]}\le C_{m,P}\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$. Means use the whole interval, oscillations the active weighted norm. The same exponent works for all orders, levels and depths.
TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6.summary: The full hierarchy estimates hold with uniform parent powers

TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1.text: For each smooth radial Fourier cutoff and integer $a_0$, the theorem chooses $b\ge1$, an envelope exponent $a\ge a_0$ and fixed-order majorants. Every admissible threshold $\mathcal B$ above them permits construction for all sufficiently large $N$. It gives smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities on $[0,S_j]\times\mathbb R^3$, starting from $\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\varepsilon_1e_3)$, with $\|U_j\|_\infty,\|(D_aX_j)^{\pm1}\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ and $D^2\pi_j\le(\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1})I$. The central splitting has error $\le\lambda_j^{-1/4}$; at $t_{j+1}$, $\eta_j/\nu_j=\varepsilon_j$, $\pi\le\nu_j\le4\pi$ and $C^{-1}\lambda_j^{1/4}\le\sigma_j\le C\lambda_j^{1/4}L_{j+1}^2$, with $C=18e^3$. Also $t_j\to T_\infty\in(0,S_j)$ and $\|O_j\|_\infty,\|U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for $m\le q_j$. Each step equals its finite expansion and Fourier cutoff. The central seed is identified, but equality of central and transported covectors and first-wave initial directions and normalization are absent. Hölder bounds are pointwise in time, and the exact spatial norm definition is absent. The exponent can be chosen arbitrarily large; the assertion does not cover every sufficiently large exponent.
TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1.summary: Proves one common sequence with its actual localized steps

TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1.text:
On $[0,1]	imes\mathbb T^3$, let $K$ be symmetric and $\Omega$ skew-symmetric, continuous in time in $C^{0,1/2}$, spatially differentiable, with uniform value and first derivative bounds. Assume $K\ge\kappa I$, $\kappa>0$, and $\int(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)\ge\mu\int|z_t|^2$, $\mu>0$, for every $H^1_0$ path at each label. Every $L\in C_tC^{0,1/2}$ gives unique $z,v=z_t,c,
abla\phi$ solving $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+
abla\phi$, with divergence-free $z,c$ and zero endpoints. Moreover $\|v\|_0\le CQ^p\|L\|_0$, where $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv$ and $Q=2+\kappa^{-1}+\mu^{-1}+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1$; the subscripts give the uniform value and first derivative bounds. Smooth data give smooth $z,c,
abla\phi$. The paper's $C_tC^{1,1/2}$ assumption is stronger; scalar potentials remain undetermined up to time-dependent constants.
TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1.summary: Prove Theorem A.1 on the normalized time interval

TorusEuler.Paper.zeta.text: At physical time $t=t_0+\tau/r$, the formal vector is $\zeta=((E_1\cdot k)/\lambda,S(E_2\cdot k)/\lambda,(E_3\cdot k)/\lambda)$, where $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ and $S=\sigma/r$ use the positive activation strength and coupling of the preceding wave. In an orthonormal frame and for $\lambda\ne0$, this is exactly the wave-vector expansion (2.3). No new wave equation or initial frequency condition is imposed by this definition. It accepts $\lambda=0$, in which case all three divisions are assigned zero. The amplification theorems separately require $\lambda>0$ and physical times inside the compact set on which the frame assumptions hold.
TorusEuler.Paper.zeta.summary: Frequency and shear rescale the three moving-frame projections

TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef.text: For real $\varepsilon,\tau$, the formal vector is $\zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)=(\varepsilon\tau^2/2,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. This defines the reference coordinates in (2.4), and its initial value is $(0,0,1)$. The third component is identically one. The definition does not by itself state its differential equations or convergence of an actual wave to it. Those are separate calculations. Its norm is the Euclidean norm of these three coordinates; it is not the physical wave vector, whose second component also carries $S^{-1}$ in (2.3).
TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef.summary: The reference coordinates give the trajectory of the triangular limiting system

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn.text: For functions $k,\mathbf a$ and a prescribed spatial linear map $D(t)$ on a time set $J$, the formal condition requires $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ throughout $J$. The second equation is expressed as a linear operator applied to $\mathbf a$. Derivatives are relative to $J$, including one-sided derivatives when $J$ is an interval with endpoints. Transversality, nonzero vectors and the background Euler conditions are absent from this condition and must be imposed separately. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the displayed right-hand side is formally defined even when $k=0$.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn.summary: The wave vector and amplitude obey the prescribed linear evolution equations

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso.text:
Let a nonzero transverse preceding wave evolve over continuous trace-free $B$, with continuous $E_c$ and positive activation $\sigma,
u,\eta$. Set $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, $	au=r(t-t_0)$, $\delta=\|B_{12}/
u-1\|_\infty+\|B_{32}/\eta-1\|_\infty+\|B\|_\infty/r+\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$ on a compact set containing $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. Assume $T\ge2$, integer $C_0$ above an absolute threshold, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Launch $k'=-M^Tk$ at $\lambda E_3$, $\lambda>0$, $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. The formal statement bounds both Euclidean and summed coordinate errors from $\zeta_0=(\varepsilon	au^2/2,-\varepsilon	au,1)$ by $CT^p\delta\le1/2$. Here $\zeta=(k\cdot E_1,Sk\cdot E_2,k\cdot E_3)/\lambda$. For every transverse amplitude, $u=-S\mathbf a\cdot E_1$, $v=\mathbf a\cdot E_2$ satisfy $u'=-\varepsilon	au\sin2\varphi\,u+\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)v+(R(u,v))_1$, $v'=u+(R(u,v))_2$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$. One continuous $R$ works for all amplitudes, with maximum operator norm at most $CT^p\delta$. The absolute factor and integer exponent precede all data. The paper uses $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-u,v)$ and additionally bounds the relative wave-vector norm.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso.summary: One continuous error matrix controls every transverse amplitude in signed coordinates

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.eqOn_wave.text: Two solutions of WaveOn J D with the same initial wave vector and amplitude agree on J, provided J is order connected, contains t₀, and D is continuous there. The hypothesis hkn requires the second wave vector to stay nonzero. Linear ODE uniqueness first identifies the wave vectors, then their amplitude coefficients. No nonzero amplitude assumption is required.

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave.text: Let $J$ be a time interval on which relative derivatives are uniquely determined. Suppose $D$ is differentiable, $\operatorname{tr}D=0$, $D'+D^2$ is symmetric, and $k'=-D^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$, where $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$. For differentiable $F$ and any $P$ with $P'=F$, transverse data give an Euler velocity $u=Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$ and zero divergence. Nonzero perpendicular data at any $t_0\in J$ remain so throughout $J$, including earlier times. Unlike the paper, the formal statement requires neither a smooth odd periodic profile nor its normalization; the Euler identity also allows $k=0$, using zero for division by zero. The interval derivative includes one-sided endpoint derivatives.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave.summary: The prescribed wave and background give an exact incompressible Euler velocity

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.factor_eqOn.text: If two reference slopes agree on the nonnegative half-line, their exponential integral factors agree there as well. For a nonnegative evaluation time, the entire integration interval lies inside that half-line, so interval-integral congruence suffices. No differential equation or continuity hypothesis is used by this lemma; those enter when identifying the slopes in its callers.

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteComparison.text:

u,\eta$. Set $r=\sqrt{2\sigma

u-1\|_\infty+\|B_{32}/\eta-1\|_\infty+\|B\|_\infty/r+\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$, measured on a compact physical set containing $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. Assume $T\ge2$, sufficiently large integer $C_0$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$, $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Launch the new wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$ at $k=\lambda E_3$, $\lambda>0$, $\mathbf a=E_2-E_1/S$. Supply $Y(0)=1$, $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)-\varepsilon	au\sin2\varphi\,Y-Y^2$ on $[0,\infty)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$; put $a_{m ref}=e^{\int_0^	au Y}$. The formal statement gives $|\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{m ref})|\le\varepsilon$, $
u_+\ge\varepsilon
u/2$. For $	au\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, it gives $|
u_+/
u-1|\le\varepsilon$ and $|(\eta_+/
u_+)/\cos\varphi-1|\le1/2$. The couplings are $
u_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$, $\eta_+=E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ with $E_{1,+}=k/|k|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_{3,+}=E_{1,+}	imes E_{2,+}$. Between $u\le v$ in $[0,T]$, invertible transverse transport has Euclidean operator norm at most $252eS|\mathbf a(v)|/|\mathbf a(u)|$. Existence of $Y$ is an input. The paper assumes smoother backgrounds.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteComparison.summary: Growing initial data give amplitude, coupling and transverse-transport bounds

u$, $	au=r(t-t_0)$, $\delta=\|B_{12}/
u-1\|_\infty+\|B_{32}/\eta-1\|_\infty+\|B\|_\infty/r+\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$ on a compact physical set containing $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. Assume $T\ge2$, sufficiently large integer $C_0$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$, $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Launch the new wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$ at $k=\lambda E_3$, $\lambda>0$, $\mathbf a=E_2-E_1/S$. Supply $Y(0)=1$, $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)-\varepsilon	au\sin2\varphi\,Y-Y^2$ for $	au\ge0$, with $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$. If $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le T$, the formal statement gives $	au_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, $Y(	au_m)=0$, and $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$. Some crossing $\eta_+/

u_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$, $\eta_+=E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$, $E_{1,+}=k/|k|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_{3,+}=E_{1,+}	imes E_{2,+}$. For $0\le	au\le1$, $|\mathbf a|\le e^{3-1/\sqrt\varepsilon}A$. Crossing uniqueness is not asserted.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn.summary: A successor crossing occurs after the reference peak with controlled strength

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteWindowNorma.text: For a valid amplification window, positive carrier, sufficiently large C₀, both smallness conditions, prescribed growing-wave initial data, wave equations and Riccati hypotheses, this theorem adds transverse transport to normalizedComparison. For $u\in[0,T]$ and $v\in[u,T]$, it produces a continuous linear equivalence between the corresponding perpendicular planes, with norm at most $252eS\|A(v)\|/\|A(u)\|$. The action agrees with every transverse amplitude solution. It also retains the logarithmic and coupling bounds.

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva.text: Let nonzero perpendicular paths $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $k'=-B^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ on a time set $J$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. Put $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$ and $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$. The formal statement gives orthonormality and $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$, $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. Derivatives are relative to $J$. These are (2.2), with no regularity assumption on $B$ beyond the supplied wave derivatives and no symmetry assumption on $B'+B^2$. All normalizations and the logarithm have nonzero positive denominators or arguments under the stated hypotheses.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva.summary: The preceding wave frame and logarithmic strength satisfy the four identities

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.norm_three_le.text: The Euclidean norm of the three-vector with coordinates u, v, and z is bounded by $|u|+|v|+|z|$. The WithLp.toLp 2 wrapper selects the Euclidean norm, unlike the maximum norm on a plain product type. This elementary inequality converts the coordinatewise wave-vector error into the vector error used by the older additive-comparison wrapper.

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.normalizedCompari.text: There is an absolute threshold $N\ge240$. For $C_0\ge N$, a valid amplification window, positive carrier scale, both smallness conditions, the supplied wave equations and prescribed initial data, this theorem identifies that wave with the constructed growing wave. The supplied Y must solve the Riccati equation on the nonnegative half-line with $Y(0)=1$. It gives nonzero transverse data, logarithmic norm comparison, a positive first coupling and late-time coupling-ratio control. ODE uniqueness transfers the estimates to the supplied functions.

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.normalized_inputs.text: Given a physical amplification window with $T\ge2$, threshold $C_0\ge240$, admissible clock hclock, both smallness assumptions, supplied wave equations hWave and initial equalities hk₀ and ha₀, the rescaled functions have the required normalized initial data and satisfy WaveOn on $[0,T]$. The proof uses clock_zero to identify the initial frame and applies the chain rule to both wave equations. This bridge does not itself derive amplitude or coupling estimates.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.normalized_inputs.summary: Moving the initial data to normalized time

TorusEuler.PaperAffine.referenceModel.text: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, put $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement constructs $Y,e$ on $[0,\infty)$ satisfying $Y(0)=1$, $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,Y-Y^2$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi/4$, with $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$ and $|Y|\le1$. It gives exactly one zero $\tau_m$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$, $Y>0$ before it and $Y<0$ afterwards. Moreover $\int_0^{\tau_m}Y\ge1/\sqrt\varepsilon-1$, so $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ reaches a maximum at $\tau_m$ with that logarithmic gain. The derivative at zero is from the right. This constructs one solution; it does not assert uniqueness among all solutions or the amplitude representation with a common deviation in (2.14), both included in the full numbered lemma.
TorusEuler.PaperAffine.referenceModel.summary: One Riccati solution has the prescribed deviation and a unique amplitude peak

TorusEuler.PaperFirstWaveConclusion.text: For a first central wave over $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$ on $[0,T]$, set $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$ and $\nu=(\kappa/|\kappa|)\cdot B_\rho(\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|)$. The formal condition requires $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse amplitude solution, every $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $0\le t'\le t\le T$. It also requires $\nu(t)\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$ throughout the interval and $\lambda^{1/4}/2\le|\kappa(0)||\mathbf a(0)|\le\lambda^{1/4}$. This is a description of the conclusions, not a proof or a new wave construction. The estimates are proved when $0<\rho\le1$, $\lambda>0$ and $T\|B_\rho\|\le1/8$.
TorusEuler.PaperFirstWaveConclusion.summary: Collects precisely the three conclusions needed for the first wave

TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement.text: For specified approximate velocities $U_j$, a time $T$ and fields $u,p$, the formal condition requires a smooth odd periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ and smooth odd divergence-free initial data. It requires $U_j(0)\to u(0)$ in every spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm, and $U_j\to u$ in those norms uniformly on $[0,S]$ for every $S<T$. It also requires a continuous velocity on the closed slab and uniform velocity convergence through $T$. Every maximal solution from $u(0)$ must have lifespan at least $T$ and agree before $T$. These conditions strengthen the introduction’s $C^m$ convergence claim. The spatial norm sums the supremum and one-half Hölder seminorm of derivatives through order $m$.
TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement.summary: The limit agrees with every maximal solution from its data

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.text: On $[0,T]$, a solution here consists of a continuous curve $v$ of weakly divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ fields and a fixed divergence-free field $c$, satisfying $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Since $Jv(0)=0$, its displacement has both zero endpoint values. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the supremum and seminorm. This is the projected form of (4.9); it does not yet supply a scalar pressure or prove existence. All asserted equations concern the designated interval, despite the functions being defined for every real time. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.summary: Encode the velocity and its time-independent solenoidal part

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c.text: Suppose a continuous divergence-free half-Hölder velocity $v$ satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, $K(0)=I$ and $L(0)=0$. Then $c=v(0)$, since the primitive vanishes at zero and the Leray projection fixes $v(0)$. These are the initial conditions used in §4.3 for a source obtained by integrating a force. The additional identification $c=b(0)$ uses the actual flow normalization $X_{0,0}=I$ and $D_aX_{0,0}=I$; it is not part of this algebraic conclusion. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c.summary: Identify the constant removed by the time projection

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.text: On a positive slab, any integrated solution yields a mixed field representing its velocity, fixed by the mixed projection and solving the projected equation. Continuous coefficients and source, exact path-action identities `hKmix` and `hΩmix`, and the source representation `hf` are required. This transfers a candidate solution into the uniqueness domain of the mixed inverse.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.summary: An integrated solution has a mixed representative

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.text: Let $T\ge0$, and let divergence-free $z,v,c$ be half-Hölder fields with continuous $v$, $z_t=v$ on $[0,T]$, and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Suppose $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$, where $G$ is the gradient of a differentiable periodic potential at each time. Then the same $v,c$ solve the projected endpoint equation and $z=Jv$ throughout the interval. This is a conversion of an already supplied solution, not an existence theorem for a prescribed source. Periodicity is essential for the Leray projection to remove the gradient. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.summary: Preserve the displacement when removing its pressure gradient

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.text: Let $K,\Omega,L$ be time-continuous half-Hölder fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$. Suppose continuous divergence-free $v$ and constant $c$ satisfy $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ and $Jv(T)=0$. Then there is a periodic potential $\phi(t,\cdot)$ of zero spatial mean whose gradient $G$ is continuous in time in $C^{0,1/2}$ and satisfies $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G$. Mean zero is integration over the unit torus. This recovers the pressure gradient in (4.9). The conclusion does not assert time differentiability of the scalar potential. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e.summary: Choose a periodic potential with zero spatial mean

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.o.text: Packages a continuous solenoidal velocity and constant as an integrated solution when the terminal primitive vanishes and the original equation holds with a periodic continuously differentiable potential. The represented gradient `Gφ` is annihilated by the spatial projection. Thus the original pressure formulation supplies the exact projected field required by the inverse’s uniqueness theorem.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.o.summary: A periodic pressure solution satisfies the projected equation

TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p.text: Suppose two integrated equations on $[0,T]$ use the same coefficients and source, their velocities agree on this interval, and their time-independent fields agree. If their remaining terms are $G_1$ and $G_2$, so that $Kv-J(\Omega v)+L=c+G_i$, then $G_1=G_2$ throughout $[0,T]$. This is the final algebraic step in pressure-gradient uniqueness for Theorems 4.2 and A.1. It assumes velocity uniqueness rather than proving it, and does not identify scalar potentials without a normalization. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p.summary: Subtract two integrated equations with identical velocities

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.text: On $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, supply smooth matrix fields $F,M$, an inverse $G$ with $GF=FG=I$, and a continuous time derivative $M_t$. Require $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $\langle-(M_t+M^2)w,w\rangle\le|w|^2$ for every $w$. In §4 these are $F=D_aX$, $G=F^{-1}$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. The formal data themselves need not arise from any velocity or volume-preserving flow. They isolate the identities needed by the endpoint inverse; positivity of $T$ and bounds such as $D\ge1$ are imposed by theorems using them.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.summary: Record the deformation equations and coercivity assumptions

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_coeffi.text: A physical parent on a positive closed slab has finite nonnegative bounds for its kinetic and vorticity coefficients and their first spatial derivatives. The proof uses joint smoothness, spatial periodicity, and compactness after passage to the torus. The constants depend on the supplied parent and duration; this is not a uniform estimate over all parents.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_coeffi.summary: The smooth parent has finite coefficient bounds

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_coeffi.text: For a physical parent with $0<T\le1$, $D\ge1$, and $L\ge0$, constructs the Hölder and path-space representations of its kinetic and vorticity coefficients. The parent provides inverse deformation, derivative identities, and the Hessian upper bound. Spatial ellipticity comes from the inverse-deformation bound; mixed coercivity comes from the displacement energy with both endpoint traces.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_coeffi.summary: Build both coefficient representations from the parent

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr.text: Let $T>0$ and suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, with inverse $G$, bounds $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. For a smooth periodic label force $f_{\mathrm{lab}}(t,a)$, there is a smooth curve $L:[0,T]\to C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ whose values are $L(t,a)=-\int_0^tF(s,a)^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}(s,a)\,ds$. In Theorem 4.2 one first sets $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$. This construction does not itself perform that composition or solve the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr.summary: Integrate a smooth force already written in particle labels

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.kinetic.text:
The kinetic coefficient in physical label coordinates.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.kinetic.summary: The kinetic coefficient of the physical parent

TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.vorticity.text:
The vorticity coefficient in physical label coordinates.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.vorticity.summary: The vorticity coefficient of the physical parent

TorusEuler.PaperMeanPhysicalCoefficients.text: Packages Hölder time curves for the kinetic and vorticity coefficients, their mixed path operators, and exact evaluation and almost-everywhere action identities. It also records spatial and zero-time-mean coercivity with the physical constants determined by `D` and `L`. These fields are obligations on the record: the structure is not itself an existence theorem, and all regularity claims are restricted to the closed slab.
TorusEuler.PaperMeanPhysicalCoefficients.summary: Represent the kinetic and vorticity coefficients

TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.text: Packages the inequalities needed to use the same step coefficient `Γ` and exponent in the oscillation, residual, central-gradient, pressure and flow estimates. It requires `Γ ≥ 1` and several explicit bounds built from the supplied costs and depth. This is a proposition of numerical compatibility, not a choice of `Γ`; the later existence theorem proves such a budget from its parameter hypotheses.
TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.summary: One numerical budget for all physical estimates

TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.hiera.text: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$ and suppose the common step coefficient has been chosen to dominate all the specified costs, including $\Gamma_P\ge1$ and an exponent $b\ge6r$. If $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, then $(\mathsf D^r)^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. This is the precise implication supplied by the formal statement behind the sentence after (5.43). The hierarchy uses loss $\mathsf D^r$ and hence its sixth power here. The assertion is a numerical consequence of the coefficient choice; it does not independently prove any hierarchy estimate or select the frequency.
TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.hiera.summary: The common coefficient dominates the sixth power of the hierarchy loss

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.text: Fix smooth periodic coefficient fields $F,G,M$ with $G=F^{-1}$, $F_t=MF$ and the upper-curvature bound for the endpoint problem. A smooth mean solution consists of periodic fields $v,z,B,\mathsf q$ on $[0,T]$ satisfying $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f\circ X$. All smoothness is joint in time and label, including derivatives within the closed interval. The physical trajectory displacement is $\xi=Fz$, and the Eulerian correction is $b=B\circ X^{-1}$. Thus $z$ and $B$ are not themselves Eulerian displacement and velocity. This definition does not impose a mean-zero normalization on the scalar pressure.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.summary: The label displacement has zero values at both endpoints

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler.text:
Let $u$ be a smooth periodic divergence-free parent on $[0,T]$, $T>0$, with flow $X$. Suppose a smooth periodic label solution has $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$, and $B_t+MB+F^{-T}
abla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$, with $F=D_aX$, $M=(
abla u)\circ X$. Its coefficient data also carry the inverse, gradient and $H^\#\le I$ bounds. Then $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ and $q=\mathsf q\circ X^{-1}$ are smooth periodic fields, $\operatorname{div}b=0$, and $b_t+u\cdot
abla b+b\cdot
abla u+
abla q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}\circ X^{-1}$. Recovering the paper's $f$ requires $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler.summary: Push a smooth label solution through the actual flow

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist.text: Let $T>0$. Suppose smooth periodic matrix fields $F,M$ satisfy $F_t=MF$, have a bounded inverse, and satisfy the gradient and upper displacement-Hessian bounds used by the mean inverse. Let a smooth periodic label solution satisfy $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$ and $B_t+MB+F^{-T}\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$, with $B=Fv$. For a smooth half-Hölder source equal to $-J(F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}})$, this solution satisfies $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$ for some time-independent solenoidal $c$, with exactly the same label velocity. The coefficient representatives must equal $F^TF$ and $F^T(M^T-M)F$. This is a compatibility result for an existing solution. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist.summary: Identify its velocity with the projected endpoint solution

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.kinet.text: For a smooth mean solution at a slab time, differentiating $Kv$ gives $\Omega v+F^*f-\nabla q$. The proof combines the physical label momentum equation with the deformation ODE and the inverse identity. The derivative is `HasDerivWithinAt` on the closed interval, so endpoints are included without claiming differentiability of an arbitrary external extension.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.kinet.summary: Differentiate the kinetic momentum along a label

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_.text: Let $0<T\le1$ and suppose the smooth periodic parent coefficients satisfy $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, $\|G\|\le D$ with $D\ge1$, $\|M\|\le L$ with $L\ge0$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as quadratic forms. For the same smooth periodic forcing, take two smooth mean solutions with label displacements zero at both $0$ and $T$. The formal statement proves equality of their pulled-back physical means $B=Fz_t$ for every time in $[0,T]$. Hence their initial corrections agree. It compares existing solutions on the same interval; it does not establish existence or identify scalar pressures, whose additive time-dependent constants remain free.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_.summary: Two smooth mean solutions have the same pulled-back velocity

TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron.text: Suppose smooth periodic $F,M$ obey $F_t=MF$, $G=F^{-1}$, the inverse and gradient bounds, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ on $[0,T]$, $T>0$. Let a smooth periodic mean solution have $B=Fv$, zero endpoint displacement, divergence-free $v$, and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\mathrm{lab}}$. Then $Kv_t+\nabla_a\mathsf q=F^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}-2F^TMFv$, with $K=F^TF$. Taking $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$ gives (4.11), since $2F^TMF=2F^TF_t$. The equation holds at each time, using derivatives from within the closed interval at its endpoints.
TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron.summary: Write the differentiated equation in the label velocity

TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin.text: For a field $u$ and terminal time $T$, this condition requires a local $C^m$ limit for each of $u(t)$ and its time derivative, for every integer $m\ge0$ and compact $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. A local limit means a $C^m$ field on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and uniform convergence on $K$ of every spatial derivative through order $m$ as $t\uparrow T$ within $[0,T)$. The lattice is the set of representatives of the torus origin. The time derivative is defined relative to the half-open lifespan. Positivity of $T$ and the Euler equations are imposed elsewhere. This condition states the two limits of Proposition 8.4 without supplying existence or a smooth continuation.
TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin.summary: Define both local terminal limits without asserting time extension

TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime.text: For prescribed $T,u,p$, this condition requires a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$, with $0<T<\infty$ and mean-zero pressure, admitting no longer smooth Euler solution whose velocity agrees there. It also requires $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$. These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals; spatial norms are essential suprema over the unit cell, and the gradient uses its operator norm. The condition does not itself identify $T$ with a limit of activation times or prove its existence. Those identifications are made when all Section 8 conclusions are established for one construction.
TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime.summary: Require maximal Euler evolution and divergence of both time integrals

TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl.text: For a given field $u$ and real time $T$, this condition records a single finite bound for the essential supremum of $|u(t,x)|$ over $x\in[-1/2,1/2]^3$, valid for every $0\le t<T$. It also records $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T$ within that interval: every prescribed threshold is exceeded at all sufficiently late times. In the periodic Euler application the cell represents $\mathbb T^3$ and $T=T_\infty>0$. The condition alone supplies neither positivity of $T$, periodicity, nor the Euler equations. Unlike the enlarged formal Proposition 8.2 conclusions, it contains no quantitative lower bound indexed by activation intervals.
TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl.summary: Specify a uniform velocity bound and full central vorticity blow-up

TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions.text: For a given scheduled construction, this condition records smooth odd divergence-free periodic velocities $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]$, starting from the stationary sine shear. Residuals are bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, Fourier support by $2\lambda_j^5$, and pressure Hessians above by $\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1}$ times the identity. It records the central gradient as the preceding gradient plus a switched rank-one wave and an error bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1/4}$. Crossing times have the prescribed coupling ratios and shear bounds and tend to a finite positive $T<S_j$. Oscillations are supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of lattice points and bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$; the remaining increments are small in spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ for $m\le q_j$. This specifies conclusions for a construction; it does not assert existence.
TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions.summary: One sequence satisfies support, error, crossing and lifetime bounds

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.text: The formal object is a real function $\widetilde\chi$ that is smooth on $[0,T]$, takes values in $[0,1]$ there, and vanishes at times $t<t_0$ within that interval. It encodes the cutoff in (3.7). The function is defined at all real times, but no restriction is imposed outside $[0,T]$, and no condition says that it eventually reaches one. For $0<t_0<T$, smoothness and vanishing to the left give flatness at activation. The first wave is treated separately by choosing $t_0=0$ and the constant function one.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.summary: The cutoff is constrained only on the construction interval

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.abs_le_one.text: At every time in the slab, the absolute value of a `PaperWaveCutoff` is at most one. Its bundled range already gives both nonnegativity and an upper bound by one, so this theorem is a convenient consequence. It does not prove that the cutoff ever reaches one or has a nonzero derivative.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.abs_le_one.summary: The cutoff has absolute value at most one

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative.text: Defines the cutoff derivative using `derivWithin` on $[0,T]$. This is the time domain on which the cutoff has bundled smoothness. It therefore includes a consistent endpoint derivative when $T>0$, rather than requiring any arbitrary continuation outside the slab to be differentiable.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative.summary: The activation derivative on the closed slab

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz.text: For a smooth cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ on $[0,T]$, define the real supremum $\sup_{t\in[t_0,T]}|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}(t)|\gamma(t)$. The derivative is taken within $[0,T]$, including its one-sided values at the endpoints. If $0\le t_0\le T$, $T>0$, and $\gamma$ is continuous and nonnegative, compactness makes this a finite nonnegative number, equal to the quantity $\|\widetilde\chi\,{}^{\prime}\gamma\|_\infty$ in (5.48). The definition alone does not assume those properties of $\gamma$; with signed weights it is a supremum of the displayed product, not its absolute value. The formal real supremum has a default value when the set is empty or unbounded, so boundedness is established before using it as a norm.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz.summary: Take the activation supremum on the active time interval

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz.text: For $T>0$ and $0\le t_0\le T$, a continuous nonnegative weight `γ` makes `derivativeSize γ` nonnegative and bounds every $|\chi^{\prime}(t)|\gamma(t)$ on the active interval. Compactness supplies boundedness and the interval is nonempty. These conditions make the real supremum a genuine maximum-type bound instead of relying on a default value.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz.summary: The activation supremum bounds every weighted derivative

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_fi.text: The within-time derivative of the first-wave cutoff is identically zero for every real `T` and evaluation time. That cutoff is the constant function one, so the total derivative convention gives zero even for a degenerate slab. This is the scalar reason that the first wave has no activation residual.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_fi.summary: The first wave has no activation derivative

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_sm.text: For $T>0$, the cutoff’s within-time derivative is infinitely smooth on $[0,T]$. Smoothness of the cutoff is bundled, and the nondegenerate interval supplies unique differentiation. The conclusion is restricted to the closed slab; it does not assert that the chosen total derivative function is smooth across its exterior endpoints.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_sm.summary: Smoothness of the within-time cutoff derivative

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_ze.text: For a nondegenerate slab and a time strictly earlier than `t₀`, the cutoff’s selected within derivative is zero. The proof combines local vanishing of the cutoff with uniqueness of derivatives on $[0,T]$. It does not assert that the derivative vanishes during the activation transition or at arbitrary exterior times.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivative_ze.summary: The cutoff derivative vanishes before activation

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first.text: For the first wave the formal construction chooses activation time zero and $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$ for every real $t$. This satisfies the cutoff conditions on $[0,T]$: smoothness, range in $[0,1]$ and vanishing before activation within that interval, because there are no such times in $[0,T]$. Therefore the leading wave and its curl correction are not attenuated. The cutoff derivative vanishes, so this choice contributes no activation residual in (3.8). The formula specifies the first-wave cutoff; it does not assert the same choice for later activation times.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first.summary: Its time cutoff is identically one

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.hasDerivWithi.text: At a time belonging to the slab, the cutoff has within derivative equal to its defined `derivative`. Smoothness provides differentiability, and the total derivative operator selects a valid derivative. This statement does not require a separate positive-duration binder because it asserts derivative existence, not uniqueness or an ambient extension.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.hasDerivWithi.summary: The cutoff derivative is its actual within derivative

TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.hasDerivWithi.text: If a function is zero at every slab time before `t₀`, its within-slab derivative is zero at any time strictly before `t₀`. The theorem states `HasDerivWithinAt`, using local equality with zero. Strict inequality is essential: it does not by itself identify the derivative exactly at the activation time.
TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.hasDerivWithi.summary: A field vanishing before activation has zero derivative there

TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.text: For a real normed-space-valued field $f$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, this condition requires $\|D_a^j f(t,a)\|\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ at every nonnegative integer order $j$ and every point. The same natural-number slope $p$ and offset $c$ apply at every order. Derivatives are multilinear maps with operator norm, including order zero. The definition asserts these inequalities but imposes no smoothness condition independently; the coefficient theorems provide smoothness and the bounds together. Proposition 5.1 uses such polynomial bounds before inserting the radius weights, and coordinate derivative sums are recovered up to order-dependent constants.
TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.summary: A fixed exponent slope controls successive label derivatives

TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_.text: All $C_j$ are nonnegative, $\mathsf D\ge1$ and $\ell_*\ge0$; the norms use multilinear derivatives, not a separately normalized coordinate sum. If $\lVert D_a^j f\rVert\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$, the weighted derivative sum is at most $(\sum_{j\le n}C_j)\mathsf D^c$. Thus the remaining exponent is independent of $n$. This is the final summation step behind (5.8); the polynomial derivative bound is an input to it.
TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_.summary: Radius weights remove the order-dependent parent power

TorusEuler.PeriodicComplexL2.text: This is the $L^2$ space of complex Euclidean three-vectors with respect to normalized torus Haar measure. Elements are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. The Euclidean coefficient norm is used so that orthogonal Fourier-mode projections produce a contractive Hilbert-space Leray operator.
TorusEuler.PeriodicComplexL2.summary: Square integrable complex vector fields on the torus

TorusEuler.PeriodicVelocityJetSpace.text: The space is the closure of the range of actual smooth periodic jet tuples inside the finite product of bounded continuous functions. Taking the closure yields a Banach space while preserving approximation by compatible tuples. It is a restricted subspace, not the full space of arbitrary bounded derivatives.
TorusEuler.PeriodicVelocityJetSpace.summary: Compatible periodic jets form a complete space

TorusEuler.PhaseJetBound.text:
A uniform bound for all Fréchet derivative norms up to the indicated order.

Default-value audit (b5): This predicate bounds iteratedFDeriv but does not include ContDiff. Even with the zeroth bound, higher derivatives may take default values outside their classical domain; every use as a smooth jet estimate must also establish regularity.
TorusEuler.PhaseJetBound.summary: Uniform bounds through a finite Fréchet derivative order

TorusEuler.PhaseJetBound.mono_order.text: A uniform `PhaseJetBound` through order `n` immediately supplies the same constant through any order `m≤n`. This is restriction of a family of derivative bounds; it introduces no new regularity or scaling estimate. It is used when successive directional differentiations consume the available derivative order.
TorusEuler.PhaseJetBound.mono_order.summary: A derivative bound remains valid at lower order

TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveApproximationBoun.text: Records full-depth velocity size, residual decay at the next frequency, oscillation size, mean bounds through the scheduled order, and an upper quadratic-form bound for the pressure-Hessian increment. The last field compares the approximate pressure to the parent pressure; it is not a two-sided Hessian norm estimate. These are hypotheses used to close the numerical induction after truncation.
TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveApproximationBoun.summary: Eulerian estimates required before the Fourier cutoff

TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveApproximationBoun.text: Packages separately supplied full-depth velocity, residual, oscillation, mean, and pressure-Hessian estimates into `PhysicalWaveApproximationBounds`. Frequency recurrence identifies the indexed induction scales, and the slice-potential identity transfers the pressure estimate to the cutoff representation. The theorem does not derive these five analytic bounds; it ensures they describe the same actual approximation.
TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveApproximationBoun.summary: Collect the measured estimates for the actual approximation

TorusEuler.Pressure.text:
A pressure field is a total real function of time and spatial position. It has the type ℝ → Vec3 → ℝ. This is the scalar potential p in the Euler equation; its gradient, not its value, enters momentum. The mean-zero gauge and spatial periodicity are requirements of IsEulerSolution, not of this abbreviation.

Default-value audit (b4): No derivative or integral occurs in the abbreviation. An arbitrary pressure function need not be differentiable or integrable. The later solution structure supplies the regularity that makes its gradient and mean meaningful.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a completely unrestricted scalar function type. Smoothness, periodicity, the PDE and mean-zero normalization are separate obligations.

TorusEuler.PressureInput.text: This local abbreviation gives the nine-coordinate complex pressure tensor type a shorter name in the convolution estimates. It does not impose reality, symmetry, spatial regularity or periodicity. Those properties belong to the supplied tensor field and the hypotheses of later lemmas identifying the dyadic operator with physical pressure.
TorusEuler.PressureInput.summary: The dyadic pressure accepts complex tensor coordinates

TorusEuler.RealNormedTorusFourierBand.text:
Fourier support of a real normed-space-valued field, measured by its continuous dual. This definition also applies when the target space is incomplete.

Default-value audit (b5): The input is already a continuous torus field. Testing all continuous real linear functionals gives the band condition without assuming a complete target space; it is a support predicate, not an estimate.
TorusEuler.RealNormedTorusFourierBand.summary: A Fourier band defined through the continuous dual

TorusEuler.RealNormedTorusFourierBand.co.text: A continuous function into any real normed space has an infinitely smooth Euclidean lift when `RealNormedTorusFourierBand R g` holds. The proof uses its finite expansion in scalar Fourier functions with fixed vector coefficients. Smoothness is obtained from band limitation, without imposing a Banach-space completion or additional derivative assumptions.

TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand.text: For a continuous real vector field on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, frequency support at most $\Lambda$ means that its complex Fourier coefficient at every $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ with Euclidean length $|\xi|>\Lambda$ is zero. The Fourier convention is $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. Frequencies on the boundary are permitted, and the condition does not remove the zero mode. This is the definition introduced in §5.1. The parent hypotheses use radii $2\mathsf D$ and $4\mathsf D$ for velocity and residual; the next truncated stage uses $2\Lambda$ and $4\Lambda$. The condition alone says nothing about time regularity or incompressibility.
TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand.summary: Specify precisely which spatial Fourier coefficients must vanish

TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand.add.text: Two continuous real vector fields supported in the same Euclidean frequency band have their sum in that band. Complexification and Fourier coefficients both preserve addition. The radius `r` is unrestricted; the conclusion follows from the supplied support predicates even when the band would be degenerate.

TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand.endpoint.text: Applying the concrete spatial Leray projection to a half Hölder field does not enlarge its Fourier band. The hypothesis `hf` bounds the support of the continuous representative. At every excluded frequency the projection acts by a linear multiplier on a zero coefficient, so the output coefficient remains zero.
TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand.endpoint.summary: Projection preserves the parent Fourier band

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_fst_le.text: The absolute value of the first coordinate of a real pair is at most its norm. The norm here is the standard product norm, namely the maximum of the two coordinate absolute values. This helper extracts a component estimate from a normalized-state comparison; it does not use a Euclidean inner-product norm.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_fst_le.summary: The first component is bounded by the pair norm

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_log_ra.text: If $a,b\ge m>0$ and $|a-b|\le\delta$, then $|\log(a/b)|\le\delta/m$. The proof applies $\log x\le x-1$ in both directions. The positive lower bound prevents totalized division or the value of the logarithm at zero from entering the argument; nonnegativity of $\delta$ follows from the assumed error bound.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_log_ra.summary: Positive lower bounds control logarithmic changes

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_snd_le.text: The absolute value of the second coordinate is bounded by the standard norm on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$. This is the maximum norm, so the proof is simply the second entry being no larger than their maximum. It extracts the deviation-coordinate estimate from bounds on normalized states.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.abs_snd_le.summary: The second component is bounded by the pair norm

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.continuous.text: If $Y$ satisfies the Riccati equation within $[0,T]$, its reconstructed deviation is continuous on that interval. The proof first obtains its derivative from the change of variables and then extracts continuity. No initial-value condition or positivity of $\varepsilon$ is needed for this regularity conclusion; those enter the invariant-strip estimate separately.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.continuous.summary: A supplied Riccati solution has continuous deviation

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.continuous.text: The algebraic factor $s=(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$ is continuous on the entire real line for every fixed $\varepsilon$. The proof uses its previously established derivative at every time. This supplies the coefficient continuity needed by the kernel and triangular propagator calculations without imposing the physical positive-parameter range.

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exists_pos.text: For a positive continuous amplitude on a nonempty compact interval $[0,T]$ and a prescribed positive height `Ustar`, there exist a maximizing time and a positive scalar that makes its maximum exactly that height. The scalar is `Ustar / A a`, whose denominator is positive. The conclusion is existence, without uniqueness or a selected peak time.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exists_pos.summary: Scaling a positive amplitude to a prescribed maximum

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exists_pos.text: Assume the norm of a vector-valued path has an attained greatest value `peak>0` on `J`, and the target `Ustar` is positive. The theorem supplies a positive scalar $c$ with $c\,\mathrm{peak}=U_*$ and proves that the scaled path attains exactly that maximum. It does not assume compactness or continuity; attainment is already in `hpeak`.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exists_pos.summary: A positive constant sets the prescribed amplitude peak

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exp_integr.text: The polynomial smallness budget bounds the arbitrary-start exponential amplification factor uniformly on the normalized slab.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.exp_integr.summary: The normalized growth error has a uniform exponential bound

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growingFac.text: If a continuous rate is nonnegative before $p$ and nonpositive after $p$ in $[0,T]$, its exponential integral attains a maximum at $p$. The hypotheses constrain only the open intervals on either side, and `hp` places the candidate in the closed interval. The conclusion does not assert that the maximizer or the zero of the rate is unique.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growingFac.summary: A sign change of the rate gives an amplitude maximum

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_am.text: Assuming the global reference Riccati solution, nonvanishing continuous physical amplitude, its logarithmic comparison, late wave-coordinate bounds and continuous ratio comparison, the theorem supplies the reference turning time, an attained physical peak, and a crossing after that turn. Every crossing in the specified bracket has normalized strength $\|a(\tau)\|\,\|k(\tau)\|/(\mathrm{scale}\cdot\mathrm{peak})$ between explicit multiples $e^{-1}/4$ and $18e^3$ of $(\varepsilon\,\mathrm{next})^{-1/2}$. It also gives the early gain bound. The assumptions include $2\varepsilon\le1$ and $0<\mathrm{next}\le\varepsilon/32$.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_am.summary: A late crossing has controlled strength and early gain

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_bu.text: A sufficiently large fixed coefficient and exponent in the finite-smallness hypothesis absorb both the normalized matrix-error contribution and the geometric norm correction. The result gives their explicit sum at most epsilon.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_bu.summary: The logarithmic amplitude budget fits finite smallness

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_co.text: If the normalized state is within $\delta\le1/2$ of $(1,0)$ in the product maximum norm, then $|h-1|\le\delta$, $|l|\le\delta$ and $h\ge1/2$. The estimate is pointwise and needs no differential equation. In applications the comparison theorem supplies `hclose`, which then prevents the physical second amplitude component from vanishing.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.growing_co.summary: Closeness gives a positive normalized amplitude

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: Under the Riccati equation, the kernel satisfies $K'=-(2Y+damping)K$ within $[0,T]$. Differentiating its clock factor and diagonal decay makes the coefficients combine in this form. Initial-value and positivity assumptions are unnecessary for this identity; they are introduced later to obtain the kernel's uniform bounds.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.summary: The differential equation for the selected kernel

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: For a Riccati path on $[0,T]$, the within-interval derivative of the selected kernel integral is the kernel itself. Continuity of the kernel comes from its differential equation, allowing the fundamental theorem of calculus. The statement includes both interval endpoints and does not yet assert bounds for the integral.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.summary: The accumulated kernel differentiates back to the kernel

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: For a supplied Riccati path, the diagonal factor used in the kernel has within-interval derivative $-2s(1+e)$ times itself. The deviation here is reconstructed from $Y$. The theorem requires the differential equation on $[0,T]$ and a time in that interval, but neither an initial value for $Y$ nor a sign restriction on $\varepsilon$.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.summary: The decay equation for the selected kernel factor

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: If $g,h$ are positive on a set $J$, $F$ is nonnegative there, and $\phi\ge0$, then the logarithmic derivative of the packaged amplitude is $g'/g+h'/h+\phi F'/[2(1+\phi F)]$. The supplied derivative hypotheses are within $J$ at `t`, and `ht` puts that point in the positivity domain. No wave or Riccati equation is assumed.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.summary: Separating the three contributions to the logarithmic rate

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: With positive $\varepsilon$, $Y(0)=1$, and the Riccati equation, the logarithm of the selected second amplitude has derivative $Y-K/(1-I)$. Here $K$ is the kernel and $I$ its integral. The denominator is at least one half under these assumptions. This correction distinguishes the alternate seed's rate from the paper's canonical reference rate $Y$.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.summary: The logarithmic rate of the alternate seed

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.hasDerivWi.text: For a continuous scalar function on $[0,T]$, its integral from zero has derivative equal to the integrand within that closed interval. Membership `ht` provides both the nonnegative time and the upper bound. This private calculus helper is used to differentiate the growth factor and the selected-seed kernel.

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated.text: For $0\le a\le t\le T$, $T\ge2$, $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, nonnegative uniform raw error `η`, and continuous $|Y|\le1$, the weighted perturbation integral lies between zero and $4T^3\eta$. Its integrand is nonnegative, so removing the initial interval $[0,a]$ cannot increase the budget already proved from time zero.
TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated.summary: The same error budget bounds every forward subinterval

TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated.text: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$, $0\le t\le T$, and $\eta\ge0$. Suppose $Y$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ and $|Y|\le1$ there. With $\cos\varphi(\tau)=(1+\varepsilon^2\tau^4/4)^{-1/2}$, the formal statement proves $0\le\int_0^t(1+|Y|)^2\eta/\cos\varphi\le4T^3\eta$.
