The reciprocal squared norm is the only potentially singular scalar factor. The statement is algebraic in the supplied fields and does not assume the wave-vector transport equation.
TorusEuler.contDiffOn_transverseCoeffici.summary: Nonvanishing wave vectors give smooth transverse operators

TorusEuler.contDiffOn_truncatedParentSli.text: For a nondegenerate closed time interval and a jointly smooth family of torus lifts, proves joint time-space smoothness of the finite pressure family on that slab. Each Fourier coefficient varies smoothly in time and only finitely many modes occur. The radius is fixed; a band hypothesis on the input is unnecessary for this regularity result.
TorusEuler.contDiffOn_truncatedParentSli.summary: The normalized pressure is jointly smooth on the slab

TorusEuler.contDiffOn_truncatedParent_fo.text: For a jointly smooth velocity on a nondegenerate closed slab, integration of each complexified Fourier integrand over the centered cell produces a smooth time curve. The theorem concerns this integral even without a periodicity assumption. Periodicity is needed separately to identify it with the Fourier coefficient of a descended torus field.
TorusEuler.contDiffOn_truncatedParent_fo.summary: Fourier coefficients are smooth through the time endpoints

TorusEuler.contDiffOn_tsum_of_jet_majora.text: A family of globally smooth maps has a smooth sum on an open set when every derivative order admits a uniform summable majorant there. Each derivative of the sum equals the sum of the derivatives. Completeness of the target is assumed, and the proof constructs compatible Taylor data from uniform convergence of finite partial sums.
TorusEuler.contDiffOn_tsum_of_jet_majora.summary: Summable derivative majorants justify a smooth infinite sum

TorusEuler.contDiffOn_union_of_matching_.text: A function smooth on two closed sets is smooth on their union when both sets admit unique differentiation and every iterated within derivative agrees on their intersection. The proof glues the two Taylor series. This supplies the general mechanism for joining the active wave to its zero extension at the activation time.
TorusEuler.contDiffOn_union_of_matching_.summary: Matching all derivatives glues smooth closed pieces

TorusEuler.contDiff_adjoint_field.text: A smooth field of linear operators remains smooth after taking adjoints pointwise. The adjoint is a continuous linear equivalence over the real numbers. This supplies the regularity of $F^T$ and $M^T$ before forming the kinetic coefficient and the antisymmetric part used in the vorticity coefficient.

TorusEuler.contDiff_and_iteratedFDeriv_p.text: A jointly smooth integrand on a fixed compact phase interval has a smooth parameter integral, with every parameter derivative obtained inside the integral.
TorusEuler.contDiff_and_iteratedFDeriv_p.summary: Parameter derivatives pass through the phase integral

TorusEuler.contDiff_bilinear.text: For a continuous bilinear map `B`, the field $x\mapsto B(f(x),g(x))$ is $C^m$ when both input fields are $C^m$. The statement gives regularity only, without a size estimate. It supplies the differentiability prerequisite for the later quantitative Leibniz bounds on momentum tensors.
TorusEuler.contDiff_bilinear.summary: A continuous bilinear product preserves finite smoothness

TorusEuler.contDiff_complexPressureTenso.text: For a smooth tensor input with global bounds on every jet, the complex dyadic pressure sum is smooth and each derivative equals the sum of block derivatives. Summable half-moment majorants hold at every order. The proof applies the general smooth-series theorem on all Euclidean space and thereby removes the raw infinite-sum ambiguity.
TorusEuler.contDiff_complexPressureTenso.summary: The full dyadic pressure series is smoothly differentiable

TorusEuler.contDiff_cross3_of_contDiff.text: The pointwise cross product of two smooth vector fields on time and label space is smooth. The proof expands each component into products and differences of scalar coordinate functions. This is the elementary regularity step for the numerator of the localized vector potential.

TorusEuler.contDiff_curl.text: If a vector potential is $C^{m+1}$, its curl is $C^m$. The curl is obtained by composing the derivative with a fixed continuous linear extraction map. This statement gives the exact regularity cost; for an infinitely smooth potential the resulting completed wave remains infinitely smooth.
TorusEuler.contDiff_curl.summary: Taking a curl uses one spatial derivative

TorusEuler.contDiff_currySlab_of_contDif.text: When the parameter domain is the whole normed space and the slab has positive duration, joint smoothness implies smooth dependence on the parameter as a map into uniform continuous paths. This supplies the strong path-space hypotheses required by the parameterized ODE theorem. It does not claim a smooth time extension outside the slab.
TorusEuler.contDiff_currySlab_of_contDif.summary: Jointly smooth slab data give globally smooth parameter dependence

TorusEuler.contDiff_cutoff_smul_of_contD.text: If $\chi$ is globally $C^m$, its topological support lies in `offOrigin`, and $f$ is $C^m$ on that open set, then $\chi f$ is globally $C^m$. Outside the support the product agrees locally with zero. Thus no regularity or particular value of $f$ on the singular lattice is required.
TorusEuler.contDiff_cutoff_smul_of_contD.summary: A cutoff removes arbitrary behavior on the lattice

TorusEuler.contDiff_deriv_waveSwitch.text: The derivative of the time switch is smooth on the real line for arbitrary `t₀` and `r`. This uses the smoothness of the chosen switch and differentiation of a smooth real function. A nonnegative rate is unnecessary for this regularity statement, although it is needed for the subsequent vanishing-before-activation result.

TorusEuler.contDiff_divergence.text: If a Euclidean vector field is smooth of all orders, so is its divergence. The statement uses Lean’s `∞` differentiability order and obtains the result by differentiating the field once and summing its diagonal components. This permits divergence itself to serve as a smooth test potential in the converse weak-solenoidal argument.
TorusEuler.contDiff_divergence.summary: Smooth vector fields have smooth divergence

TorusEuler.contDiff_dyadicEuclideanMulti.text: A dyadic Euclidean kernel is smooth everywhere because inverse Fourier transform preserves the Schwartz class and positive scalar dilation preserves smoothness. Multiplication by the volume factor changes no regularity. This supplies the smooth summands required for the subsequent termwise differentiation arguments.
TorusEuler.contDiff_dyadicEuclideanMulti.summary: Each rescaled Euclidean kernel is globally smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_dyadicPeriodicMultip.text: At a fixed dyadic grade, the periodized kernel is globally smooth, and each derivative is the sum of translated Euclidean derivatives. Around any point, polynomial decay supplies a summable lattice majorant on a bounded neighborhood. Completeness of the target ensures that the norm-convergent series defines a genuine smooth function.
TorusEuler.contDiff_dyadicPeriodicMultip.summary: One periodic block is smooth and differentiates termwise

TorusEuler.contDiff_endpointFiniteFourie.text: Every pressure constructed from a finite set of modes is smooth as a real function of Euclidean space. Each Fourier character is smooth, and a finite sum followed by real-part extraction preserves smoothness. No decay, summability, or projection hypothesis is needed because the series is finite.
TorusEuler.contDiff_endpointFiniteFourie.summary: Finite Fourier pressures are smooth in space

TorusEuler.contDiff_endpointMeanSlice.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field to one time in the closed slab gives a globally smooth function of the spatial variable. The result is polymorphic in the normed target space and requires no spatial periodicity. It supplies the slice regularity used to compare derivative-word norms of the recovered mean.

TorusEuler.contDiff_endpointParityPart.text: If a spatial field is `ContDiff` at order `m`, then its reflection average has that same order of regularity for any real sign. The proof uses composition with negation and linear combinations. The order may be finite or infinite; no stronger differentiability is obtained by averaging.
TorusEuler.contDiff_endpointParityPart.summary: Reflection averaging preserves any stated spatial regularity

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstLabelPressureCo.text: Multiplies the smooth raw coefficient by the smooth radial envelope to obtain smoothness of the localized coefficient at each fixed time. Nonzero frequency and positive radius are explicit assumptions. This is the regularity needed by the pressure product rule; the separate support restriction for its sign is not needed for smoothness.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstLabelPressureCo.summary: The localized first pressure coefficient is smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveInverseDefo.text: The explicit inverse deformation is infinitely differentiable as a function of time and label. The proof combines the smooth material-gradient field with multiplication by time and subtraction from the identity. No inverse-function theorem or determinant lower bound is needed for this explicit polynomial-in-time formula.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveInverseDefo.summary: The inverse shear deformation is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveLocalizedPo.text: With nonzero frequency, $r>0$, a strict support collar $2r<1/2$ and $0<h\le1$, the first localized potential is jointly smooth for all real times and spatial positions. The proof combines the smooth inverse-curl coefficient, the smooth primitive, collar periodization and the explicit inverse shear flow.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveLocalizedPo.summary: The periodic first potential is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveLocalizedPo.text: Fixing a time in the jointly smooth first-wave potential gives a smooth spatial vector potential. The assumptions remain nonzero frequency, positive radius, a strict cell collar and $0<h\le1$. This slice result supplies the twice differentiable potential needed for the divergence-of-curl identity.

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveLocalizedVe.text: Under the same nonzero-frequency, positive-radius, strict-collar and profile-width assumptions, the completed first-wave velocity is jointly smooth. It is the spatial curl of the jointly smooth localized potential. This theorem establishes regularity of the constructed field, without asserting that this single wave by itself solves the unforced Euler equation.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveLocalizedVe.summary: The completed first velocity is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveMaterialGra.text: The label-dependent material gradient is infinitely differentiable for every shear parameter `s`. It is a smooth cosine factor times a fixed bounded linear map. This coefficient regularity is used when embedding the first-wave hierarchy data into the smooth time-label-phase profile space.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveMaterialGra.summary: The material shear coefficient is smooth in labels

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePotentialCo.text: For nonzero frequency and any jointly smooth vector field `U`, the coefficient $-|\kappa|^{-2}(\kappa\times U)$ is jointly smooth. The explicit identity $|\kappa|^2=\lambda^2(1+z^2)$ rules out a zero denominator at every point. The statement is more general than the particular first seed subsequently substituted for `U`.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePotentialCo.summary: The inverse curl coefficient is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePotentialPr.text: At a fixed time, the first potential profile is smooth jointly in its label and independent phase. Nonzero frequency controls the inverse-square covector, while positive radius and $0<h\le1$ provide smooth envelope and primitive. A cell collar is unnecessary here because this statement precedes periodization.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePotentialPr.summary: The first potential is smooth in label and phase

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePressureWit.text: The explicit primary pressure is jointly smooth when `freq ≠ 0` and `0 < h ≤ 1`. Nonzero frequency makes the transported covector nonzero everywhere, so its squared norm can be divided into a smooth coefficient. Smoothness of the phase primitive then gives the full pressure regularity.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWavePressureWit.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveSmoothSeed.text: For arbitrary fixed shear parameter and amplitude scale, the explicit seed is smooth jointly in time and label on the entire Euclidean product. Positivity of $1+z^2$ justifies the rational operations, and arctangent is smooth everywhere. No separate argument is needed at labels where the local shear vanishes.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveSmoothSeed.summary: The explicit first seed is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveSmoothSeed_.text: The unit-scale seed is jointly smooth in shear ratio, time, and label. Its rational coefficients have denominators built from $1+z^2$, which never vanish, and its third component uses the smooth arctangent. This is a global smoothness statement; compact restrictions on ratio and time enter only when bounds are extracted.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveSmoothSeed_.summary: The unit seed depends smoothly on all parameters

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveSweep.text: The accumulated shear is an infinitely differentiable function of the real time and Euclidean label. Its only nonconstant spatial input is the cosine of the label’s second coordinate. This global smoothness statement is independent of the finite time window later used to normalize and estimate the first wave.

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveTransported.text: For fixed shear parameter and frequency, the first-wave covector varies smoothly with time and label. The proof uses its two-component formula and the smooth accumulated shear. The conclusion remains true at zero frequency, when the field is identically zero; smooth inverse-square constructions still require nonzero frequency.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveTransported.summary: The transported first covector is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveVelocityWit.text: Under `0 < h ≤ 1`, the primary velocity before localization is infinitely differentiable jointly in time, label, and phase. The smooth seed depends on time and label, while the scalar wave profile depends on phase. Multiplication preserves smoothness, independently of any frequency or support choices.
TorusEuler.contDiff_firstWaveVelocityWit.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_first_wave_raw_press.text: For nonzero `freq`, the first-wave pressure coefficient formed from the explicit seed and material gradient is smooth in the label at any fixed time. The proof rewrites it using the normalized coefficient, whose denominator never vanishes. This checks regularity of the coefficient before its phase primitive and envelope are inserted.
TorusEuler.contDiff_first_wave_raw_press.summary: The raw pressure coefficient is spatially smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_fourierMode.text: Each integer-frequency Fourier mode is infinitely differentiable as a function of the real Euclidean label. The proof writes it as a complex exponential composed with a continuous real linear phase. This concerns ambient derivatives on the lift, where later periodic differential operators are defined.
TorusEuler.contDiff_fourierMode.summary: Fourier characters are smooth on the Euclidean lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_gradient_truncatedPa.text: Turns all-order smoothness of a real scalar function into all-order smoothness of its gradient. The gradient is the derivative transported through the Euclidean duality isomorphism. This justifies using ordinary divergence and Leray identities on the pressure-gradient term in the finite-band projection argument.

TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyHigherPress.text: If the coframe adjoint, strain, longitudinal projection, pressure, force and velocity are smooth, their reconstructed gradient profile is smooth in label and phase. Smoothness of the projection is an explicit premise, so possible singular behavior at a zero covector is not being disregarded. The pressure contribution uses one derivative of a smooth function.
TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyHigherPress.summary: The reconstructed pressure gradient is smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyLongitudina.text: A smooth covector field that never vanishes gives a smooth field of longitudinal projection operators. Nonvanishing controls the inverse squared norm in the projection formula.
TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyLongitudina.summary: The longitudinal projection varies smoothly off zero

TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyRelayPotent.text: A smooth covector field that never vanishes gives a smooth map of potential coefficients. The coefficient is minus the cross-product operator divided by the squared covector norm. Smooth inversion therefore requires the explicit nonvanishing hypothesis. This theorem supplies regularity of the actual wave potential before its scaled derivative budget is estimated.
TorusEuler.contDiff_hierarchyRelayPotent.summary: The wave-potential coefficient is smooth on nonzero covectors

TorusEuler.contDiff_iteratedPhaseDerivat.text: For every nonnegative order `j`, a jointly smooth profile remains jointly smooth after taking `j` derivatives in phase. The statement preserves dependence on the parameter as well as on phase. It enables the subsequent mixed-derivative construction and the exchanges of those derivatives with phase averages and primitives.
TorusEuler.contDiff_iteratedPhaseDerivat.summary: Repeated phase differentiation retains joint smoothness

TorusEuler.contDiff_joint_curl.text: Taking curl in the three-dimensional spatial variable preserves smooth dependence on an arbitrary normed parameter. The full spatial derivative varies smoothly by the preceding lemma, and curl is a continuous linear function of that derivative. This gives smooth velocity from the localized vector potential.

TorusEuler.contDiff_joint_fderiv_right.text: The spatial derivative of a jointly smooth function remains jointly smooth in its parameter and spatial arguments. The theorem is formulated for general normed parameter, source and target spaces. It obtains the slice derivative by composing the full derivative with the spatial inclusion, avoiding any unsupported interchange of derivatives.

TorusEuler.contDiff_joint_periodizeCente.text: A smooth parameter-dependent profile multiplied by a radial envelope has a smooth centered periodic extension when $r>0$ and $2r<1/2$. The strict collar keeps the support away from the cell walls. The proof replaces the discontinuous centered representative by a smooth periodic proxy wherever the envelope can be nonzero.
TorusEuler.contDiff_joint_periodizeCente.summary: A collar makes periodic extension jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_latticeDetector.text: The sum of squared coordinate sines is infinitely differentiable on all of Euclidean space. The proof composes each continuous linear coordinate projection with multiplication by $\pi$, sine and squaring, then sums the three smooth functions. No exclusion of the lattice is needed for this auxiliary detector.
TorusEuler.contDiff_latticeDetector.summary: The lattice detector is smooth everywhere

TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_finiteFourierSu.text: A finite sum of Fourier characters with coefficients in a complex normed vector space is infinitely differentiable on Euclidean labels. The coefficients are arbitrary because the sum is finite. No convergence theorem, coefficient decay, or infinite-series differentiation is needed for this smoothness statement.
TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_finiteFourierSu.summary: Finite Fourier synthesis is smooth on the lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_momentumTensorF.text: The smooth lift of the actual tensor Fourier cutoff.
TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_momentumTensorF.summary: The tensor Fourier cutoff has a smooth lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_of_realFourierS.text: A real function belonging to `realFourierSpace R` has an infinitely smooth lift along `toUnitTorus`. Membership in the finite span is the essential hypothesis. The proof proceeds through the span operations and smooth Fourier characters; it does not claim that an arbitrary torus function becomes smooth merely by being lifted.

TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_realVectorFouri.text: The truncated field has a smooth spatial lift.
TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_realVectorFouri.summary: A finite Fourier cutoff has a smooth lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_smoothFourierCu.text: For any real symbol `ψ`, scale `Λ`, and torus function `g`, the implemented cutoff has an infinitely differentiable Euclidean lift. This conclusion follows from finite synthesis alone. It does not assume the input is smooth or that the symbol meets the support conditions needed for the intended multiplier formula.
TorusEuler.contDiff_lift_smoothFourierCu.summary: The finite Fourier cutoff always gives a smooth lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_listSum.text: A finite list sum of smooth functions is smooth. The hypothesis `hf` supplies smoothness for every indexed function, and induction uses closure of smooth maps under addition. This general helper permits differentiation of the list of terms generated by the ordered Leibniz formula.

TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransported.text: Fix a time, a differentiability order $m$, and a map $A$. Suppose $A$ and the evaluated label field $a\mapsto f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ are $C^m$. Assume $0<\delta\le1/2$ and that this field vanishes whenever some coordinate satisfies $|a_i|>1/2-\delta$. Extending it periodically from the centered cell and composing with $A$ gives a $C^m$ field; the result includes $m=\infty$. The formal result imposes no lattice condition on $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$. The zero collar is the reason arbitrary phases can be extended without seams; periodicity of the resulting Eulerian field additionally requires the inverse map to commute with integer translations.
TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransported.summary: A boundary collar prevents seams when the evaluated wave is periodized

TorusEuler.contDiff_meanPressure_slice.text: A field with `ContDiffOn` regularity of order `n` on the closed slab has ordinary `ContDiff` regularity of the same order in space at each slab time. The target may be any normed real space. This permits the purely spatial Poisson calculation to be applied to the time-dependent mean equation.
TorusEuler.contDiff_meanPressure_slice.summary: Restrict joint regularity to a time slice

TorusEuler.contDiff_nearPressureCutoffTe.text: A smooth cutoff whose topological support lies off the lattice turns the quadratic tensor of an off-origin smooth velocity into a globally smooth field. The proof applies the cutoff smoothing lemma at every finite order. No value or regularity of the original velocity on the lattice enters the conclusion.
TorusEuler.contDiff_nearPressureCutoffTe.summary: The near tensor is smooth across the excluded lattice

TorusEuler.contDiff_normalizedFirstWaveP.text: The normalized scalar pressure coefficient is globally smooth as a function of the pair `(t,a)`. The shear rate is a cosine, the sweep is smooth, and the denominator is strictly positive. The result supplies joint regularity before compactness is used to obtain constants independent of time and label.
TorusEuler.contDiff_normalizedFirstWaveP.summary: The normalized pressure is smooth in time and label

TorusEuler.contDiff_of_smooth_derivative.text: If `hf` gives the derivative of a scalar function at every real point and `hdf` makes that derivative infinitely smooth, then the original function is infinitely smooth. This general calculus lemma is used twice, first for the wave profile and then for its pressure primitive.
TorusEuler.contDiff_of_smooth_derivative.summary: A function with a smooth prescribed derivative is smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_one_crossAdvection.text: If both vector fields are twice continuously differentiable, the map sending `x` to the derivative of `F` applied to `G x` is once continuously differentiable. This regularity level permits a further divergence calculation. The theorem supplies differentiability of a product term without assuming the fields solve an equation.
TorusEuler.contDiff_one_crossAdvection.summary: Two derivatives make cross advection differentiable

TorusEuler.contDiff_operatorLiftConvolut.text: An integrable operator-valued kernel convolved with a smooth input whose every spatial jet has a global bound gives a smooth output. The theorem identifies each output derivative with the integral of the kernel applied to that input derivative at $x-y$. Completeness of the output space supports the Bochner integrals; domination uses the next input-jet bound.
TorusEuler.contDiff_operatorLiftConvolut.summary: Bounded smooth inputs may be differentiated under convolution

TorusEuler.contDiff_parameter_jet.text: For a jointly smooth function of a parameter and phase, its iterated Fréchet derivative in the parameter variable remains jointly smooth in both variables. The order `k` is arbitrary. This supplies the regularity needed to differentiate parameter-dependent phase integrals repeatedly, with phase held fixed during each parameter derivative.

TorusEuler.contDiff_periodicWaveBump.text: For an admissible width $0<h\le1$, the periodic bump is infinitely differentiable on the real line. At every point it agrees locally with a fixed smooth translated copy. Thus the floor function appearing in its definition causes no loss of regularity in the narrow-bump regime.
TorusEuler.contDiff_periodicWaveBump.summary: The repeated bump is smooth at the cell seams

TorusEuler.contDiff_periodizeCentered.text: If a globally $C^m$ profile vanishes whenever any coordinate lies in a collar of the centered-cell boundary, its centered periodization is $C^m$. The collar width must lie in $(0,1/2]$. Near seams the periodized field is locally zero; elsewhere it is a translate of the original profile.
TorusEuler.contDiff_periodizeCentered.summary: A profile vanishing near cell faces periodizes smoothly

TorusEuler.contDiff_phaseAnchoredPrimiti.text: The primitive obtained by integrating a jointly smooth profile from phase zero to the variable phase endpoint is jointly smooth in the parameter and phase. The target is complete, and the parameter space has the section's properness assumptions. This is the unnormalized primitive; subtracting its phase mean is a later operation.
TorusEuler.contDiff_phaseAnchoredPrimiti.summary: The anchored phase integral is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_phaseDerivative.text: Joint smoothness in parameter and phase implies joint smoothness of the first derivative in phase. This helper takes a spatially parameterized profile and treats phase differentiation as a component of the full derivative. It prepares repeated phase differentiation before the parameter derivatives defining a mixed derivative are taken.

TorusEuler.contDiff_phaseOperatorWord.text: A smooth function differentiated along any finite word of smooth direction fields remains smooth. This permits subsequent derivative manipulations without treating the words as independent formal variables.
TorusEuler.contDiff_phaseOperatorWord.summary: Smooth directions preserve smoothness of derivative words

TorusEuler.contDiff_phasePrimitive_word.text: A globally smooth profile depending on a proper normed label space and a real phase has a globally smooth normalized phase primitive. The target space is complete for parameter integration. The proof rescales the variable integration interval and subtracts its average; phase periodicity is not needed for this smoothness assertion.
TorusEuler.contDiff_phasePrimitive_word.summary: The normalized primitive is jointly smooth in label and phase

TorusEuler.contDiff_pressureNearBlock.text: Each dyadic pressure block is smooth when the input is smooth and each input jet has a global bound. The result applies differentiation under an integrable operator kernel using the previously proved kernel integrability. Periodicity is not required here; it is one later way to obtain the global bounds.
TorusEuler.contDiff_pressureNearBlock.summary: A pressure block preserves bounded smooth inputs

TorusEuler.contDiff_pressureTensorDyadic.text: A smooth periodic complex tensor field has a smooth real pressure lift. Periodicity converts compact-cell bounds into bounds for every spatial jet on the whole lift, enabling smooth convergence of the dyadic series. Composition with real part then gives the real-valued conclusion; no divergence or symmetry of the tensor is required.
TorusEuler.contDiff_pressureTensorDyadic.summary: Smooth periodic tensors give smooth real pressure

TorusEuler.contDiff_pressure_of_contDiff.text: If `hD` identifies `g` as the gradient of `p` at every point and `g` is smooth, then `p` is smooth in space. The gradient identity first gives differentiability and identifies the Fréchet derivative via inner-product duality. This result is spatial; it does not alone establish smooth dependence on an external time parameter.
TorusEuler.contDiff_pressure_of_contDiff.summary: A smooth gradient gives a smooth spatial pressure

TorusEuler.contDiff_radialEnvelope.text: For positive radius, the radial cutoff is smooth everywhere. Near the origin it is identically one, avoiding the lack of smoothness of the norm at zero; away from zero ordinary composition applies.

TorusEuler.contDiff_rawFirstWavePressure.text: For a nonzero carrier frequency, proves smoothness in the spatial labels of the first pressure coefficient before multiplication by the radial envelope. The explicit stationary formula has denominator $(1+\mathrm{sweep}^2)^2$, which is everywhere positive. The result is for each fixed time and does not supply a uniform derivative bound.
TorusEuler.contDiff_rawFirstWavePressure.summary: The uncut first pressure coefficient is smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_scalarizedFourierMod.text: For any lattice frequency, complex amplitude, and bounded real-linear functional, the Euclidean lift of the scalarized Fourier wave is smooth of all orders. Smoothness comes from the exponential Fourier mode and linearity of `L`. This prepares the classical integration-by-parts argument for its weak solenoidal membership.
TorusEuler.contDiff_scalarizedFourierMod.summary: A scalarized torus wave has a smooth lift

TorusEuler.contDiff_scaledPhaseCoefficie.text: A smooth label-dependent coefficient remains smooth after evaluation at the scaled label component of a label-phase pair. The scalar `ℓ` is arbitrary, including zero. This is a regularity statement about composition with a linear map; it does not impose an inverse-Jacobian interpretation or provide a quantitative derivative bound.
TorusEuler.contDiff_scaledPhaseCoefficie.summary: Rescaling a smooth coefficient preserves smoothness

TorusEuler.contDiff_scaledPhaseDirection.text: If the label coefficient field `B` is smooth, each induced label-phase direction is smooth for any fixed scales, wave vector, and spatial coordinate index. The conclusion follows by composing with fixed continuous linear maps. Nonzero scales are unnecessary for smoothness of the resulting total expression.

TorusEuler.contDiff_slabPath_eval.text: A $C^n$ map into continuous slab paths remains $C^n$ in the parameter after evaluation at a fixed slab time. The proof composes with the bounded linear evaluation map. This conclusion concerns parameter derivatives at that fixed time, not time derivatives or joint smoothness of the evaluated family.
TorusEuler.contDiff_slabPath_eval.summary: Evaluation preserves parameter smoothness at each time

TorusEuler.contDiff_slabSlice.text: A jointly smooth family on $[l,r]$ times a full parameter space gives a smooth parameter function at each time in the interval. Composing with the constant-time inclusion proves the claim. The helper permits spatial or label derivatives of coefficients and solutions while retaining within-time derivative conventions at the endpoints.
TorusEuler.contDiff_slabSlice.summary: Parameter slices of a smooth slab family are smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_slice_of_contDiffOn_.text: A jointly smooth field on a closed time slab is smooth in all spatial variables at every time belonging to that interval. The proof composes with the fixed-time inclusion. No strict inequality between the slab endpoints is required for this restriction; the conclusion concerns only a slice already inside the specified domain.
TorusEuler.contDiff_slice_of_contDiffOn_.summary: Restrict closed slab smoothness to a spatial slice

TorusEuler.contDiff_slice_on_closedSlab.text: A time slice of a jointly smooth closed-slab family is spatially smooth.
TorusEuler.contDiff_slice_on_closedSlab.summary: Every closed-slab time slice is spatially smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_spatialSlice.text: A jointly smooth field on the product slab remains smooth as a function of space after fixing any time in the slab. The conclusion is `ContDiff` of all orders on the full spatial space. It is stronger than pointwise differentiability but makes no assertion outside the supplied time interval.
TorusEuler.contDiff_spatialSlice.summary: Every time slice retains all spatial derivatives

TorusEuler.contDiff_stationaryShearFlow_.text: The inverse stationary-shear map, obtained by replacing time with its negative, is globally smooth in time and position. The proof expands the explicit sine shear. This provides the regular composition map taking the centered periodic label potential to the Eulerian first-wave potential.

TorusEuler.contDiff_terminalBorelAtom.text: The Borel atom is infinitely smooth for every degree and every real scale. Composition with a fixed linear rescaling and multiplication by a scalar prove this even at zero scale. This theorem concerns regularity alone; the endpoint derivative identities require a strictly positive scale and cannot be inferred from smoothness here.

TorusEuler.contDiff_terminalBorelBase.text: The normalized monomial times the fixed bump is infinitely smooth for every natural degree. The proof uses smoothness of polynomial powers, division by a constant and multiplication by the bump. This establishes the regularity needed for global derivative bounds of each later rescaled atom.

TorusEuler.contDiff_terminalMeanCoeffici.text: If a coefficient field is jointly smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, then at any time in the interval its spatial slice is smooth everywhere. This is composition with the map $x\mapsto(t,x)$. The helper supplies ordinary spatial differentiability when constructing Hölder and Lipschitz caps for the actual mean coefficients.
TorusEuler.contDiff_terminalMeanCoeffici.summary: A smooth coefficient has smooth fixed-time spatial slices

TorusEuler.contDiff_truncatedParentSlice.text: Proves all-order spatial smoothness of the slice pressure for every real cutoff radius and continuous torus input. The proof uses smoothness of a finite trigonometric sum and then negation. No smoothness or band assumption on the original input is needed for the synthesized pressure itself.

TorusEuler.contDiff_velocitySlice.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the closed slab is smooth in space at any fixed time `t` belonging to that slab. Composition with $x\mapsto(t,x)$ removes the time variable. The statement concerns spatial smoothness on all of $\mathbb R^3$ and does not assert an extension in time beyond the slab.

TorusEuler.contDiff_waveBump.text: The concrete bump formed by composing the smooth transition with $1-64s^2$ is infinitely differentiable. The polynomial inner function is globally smooth. This establishes the regularity input for scaling, periodization, and uniform derivative bounds in the construction of the phase profile.
TorusEuler.contDiff_waveBump.summary: The chosen compact bump is infinitely smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_wavePressurePrimitiv.text: For an admissible positive width h ≤ 1, the selected pressure primitive is smooth on the phase line. Periodicity and zero phase mean are recorded by separate theorems.
TorusEuler.contDiff_wavePressurePrimitiv.summary: The normalized pressure primitive is smooth

TorusEuler.contDiff_waveProfile.text: For 0 < h ≤ 1, the chosen periodic wave profile is smooth on the real phase line. The width restrictions are the same ones needed by the profile construction and its uniform bounds.
TorusEuler.contDiff_waveProfile.summary: The velocity profile is smooth at admissible widths

TorusEuler.contDiff_waveSlope.text: Under the admissible scale assumptions, the periodic bump is smooth, and subtracting its phase mean and dividing by a constant preserves smoothness. The result establishes infinite differentiability of the normalized slope as a phase function. Positivity of the denominator is proved separately for its quantitative use.

TorusEuler.contDiff_waveSwitch.text: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, equal to zero for arguments at most zero and one for arguments at least one. For any real activation time $t_0$ and rate $r$, the formal statement proves that $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$. In particular there is no loss of regularity at the activation time or at the end of the switching interval. This conclusion does not require $r>0$. That positivity is needed separately to interpret the transition as switching on as time increases.
TorusEuler.contDiff_waveSwitch.summary: The activation cutoff is smooth on the entire real line

TorusEuler.continuousFourierCoefficient.text: Package taking a fixed Fourier coefficient as a real continuous linear map from continuous torus fields to the value space. Its norm bound is one. The real-linear packaging matches the half-Hölder multiplier construction even though the integrand uses complex characters and the underlying coefficient operation also respects complex scalars.
TorusEuler.continuousFourierCoefficient.summary: Fourier coefficient extraction is a bounded linear map

TorusEuler.continuousFourierCoefficient_.text: Applying `continuousFourierCoefficient k` to a continuous field gives `mFourierCoeff g k` exactly. This identity connects the continuous-linear-map packaging to the standard Fourier notation. The package is used for continuity and summation, while the explicit coefficient expression is used for symbol calculations.
TorusEuler.continuousFourierCoefficient_.summary: The bounded coefficient map gives the usual Fourier coefficient

TorusEuler.continuousHalfHolder.text: Extract the underlying continuous torus field from a bundled half-Hölder field. This forgets the additional increment estimate but preserves all pointwise values. The function is used for Fourier coefficients and convolution kernels, which are first defined on continuous fields rather than directly on the half-Hölder Banach space.
TorusEuler.continuousHalfHolder.summary: Forget the half Hölder bound and retain the continuous field

TorusEuler.continuousHalfHolderEmbedding.text: Bundle extraction of the continuous field as a real continuous linear map from half-Hölder fields, with norm bound one. Addition and scalar multiplication preserve the underlying values, and the supremum norm is bounded by the full half-Hölder norm. This map is used before Fourier coefficient extraction in the separate mean contribution.
TorusEuler.continuousHalfHolderEmbedding.summary: The forgetful map to continuous fields is bounded linear

TorusEuler.continuousOn_aebound.text: Continuity of an operator field on $[0,T]$ supplies an almost-everywhere norm bound for the measure restricted to $(0,T]$. Compactness supplies the constant, and the restricted measure is supported inside the closed interval. No positivity of `T` is assumed here; an empty restricted interval makes the almost-everywhere assertion vacuous.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_aebound.summary: A continuous time coefficient is essentially bounded

TorusEuler.continuousOn_affineWaveAmplit.text: Continuous background and wave-vector curves give a continuous amplitude-operator curve on any set where the wave vector never vanishes. The nonzero hypothesis controls its reciprocal squared norm.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_affineWaveAmplit.summary: Continuity of the amplitude evolution operator

TorusEuler.continuousOn_currySlabWithin.text: Data jointly continuous on the compact time slab times the parameter set yield a map continuous within that parameter set into the uniform path space. This upgrades pointwise-in-time continuity using the compact time domain. The zero extension outside the parameter set does not enter the conclusion and need not be globally continuous.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_currySlabWithin.summary: Joint continuity gives uniform path continuity within the domain

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointFixedInv.text: Suppose $S(t)$ is a family of bounded linear isomorphisms of a Banach space and $t\mapsto S(t)$ is continuous in operator norm on a specified set of times. Then $t\mapsto S(t)^{-1}$ is continuous in the same norm. The interval may be closed. In Appendix A.2 this applies to $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ on solenoidal $C^{0,1/2}$ fields. Existence of the isomorphisms and their uniform bounds are premises, obtained separately from ellipticity and Lemma A.2.

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointForceSli.text: Restricting a jointly continuous velocity on the closed slab to a fixed spatial point gives a continuous time curve on $[0,T]$. The inclusion map sends each admissible time into the product slab. This supplies the elementary continuity hypothesis needed to differentiate the primitive of the pulled-back force.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointForceSli.summary: A continuous force has continuous time slices

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointKinetic.text: Continuity of the deformation field `F` on the slab implies continuity of $F^*F$. The proof combines continuity of adjoint with composition of continuous linear maps. No inverse deformation is needed for this regularity statement; positivity bounds are supplied separately when the kinetic coefficient enters the endpoint equation.

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointPrimitiv.text: An interval-integrable velocity on a nonnegative-length slab has a primitive continuous on the entire closed interval. This constructs a pointwise displacement path from integrable data without claiming the velocity is continuous. The endpoint values belong to that continuous path and are not merely values of an arbitrary $L^2$ representative.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointPrimitiv.summary: The primitive is continuous through both endpoints

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointSkew.text: If the deformation `F` and gradient coefficient `M` are continuous on the closed time interval, then $F^*(M^*-M)F$ is continuous there. The proof composes continuous adjoint, subtraction and operator multiplication. It supplies the coefficient regularity needed to define multiplication on temporal $L^2$, without assuming that these coefficients arise from Euler flow.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointSkew.summary: Continuity of the pulled-back vorticity coefficient

TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointVorticit.text: Continuous deformation and gradient fields on the slab give a continuous pulled-back vorticity coefficient $F^*(M^*-M)F$. All dependence is through continuous operator algebra. This provides the measurable, bounded coefficient required by the weak product operator, while leaving the flow identities and Hessian upper bound to the coercivity theorem.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointVorticit.summary: Continuity of the space-time vorticity coefficient

TorusEuler.continuousOn_farPressureCutof.text: If cutoff and velocity are continuous on a set `S`, their far quadratic tensor is continuous there. Continuity of the bounded bilinear tensor map and scalar multiplication gives the result. On the compact far source set this supplies the integrability required by the actual kernel pressure estimates.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_farPressureCutof.summary: Continuous cutoff and velocity give a continuous far density

TorusEuler.continuousOn_fixedTransverseG.text: If the physical gradient `M`, forward coordinate lift `J` and coordinate reader `R` are continuous on a time set, their generator $-2R M J$ is continuous there. The target coordinate space may be any real normed space. This supplies the continuous coefficient needed for the fixed-plane linear ODE; inverse or projection identities are not needed for this continuity statement.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_fixedTransverseG.summary: The coordinate generator varies continuously in time

TorusEuler.continuousOn_freezingCompress.text: Assume `B` is continuous on `I` and each supplied equivalence `e t` has underlying map equal to the compression of `B t`. Then the inverse equivalences vary continuously in operator norm on `I`. The hypotheses already supply invertibility; this theorem establishes continuity and is used to recover a continuous velocity from a weak solution.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_freezingCompress.summary: Continuous coefficients give continuous fixed time inverses

TorusEuler.continuousOn_iteratedFDeriv_d.text: Every actual derivative of the full periodic kernel is continuous on `offOrigin`. This follows from the established smoothness on that open set. The private lemma is used to obtain measurable kernels and uniform bounds on compact sets of separated target and source differences.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_iteratedFDeriv_d.summary: Kernel derivatives are continuous on the punctured lift

TorusEuler.continuousOn_oscillatoryTrans.text: A continuous wave vector that is nonzero throughout the chosen time set gives a continuous family of transverse projection operators. The reciprocal squared norm is continuous only under the nonvanishing condition. This provides the coefficient regularity needed to solve the forced transverse ODE on a closed interval.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_oscillatoryTrans.summary: A nonvanishing wave vector gives continuous projections

TorusEuler.continuousOn_paperMeanIntegra.text: Continuous coefficient curves `K`, `Ω`, source `src`, and solenoidal velocity `g` give continuity of the integrated momentum on the closed slab. The primitive term is treated in the Banach Hölder space, using continuity of coefficient multiplication. This establishes regularity of the expression before it is projected or identified with a pressure gradient.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_paperMeanIntegra.summary: The integrated momentum is continuous in time

TorusEuler.continuousOn_periodicProjecte.text: For a smooth periodic time family, continuity of its completed jet tuple through order two implies time continuity of the signed quadratic momentum at each fixed point. This follows by continuity of the bounded bilinear extension and the bounded zeroth evaluation map. The conclusion is on the supplied closed time slab.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_periodicProjecte.summary: Continuity of two spatial orders controls the momentum value

TorusEuler.continuousOn_periodicVelocity.text: For a family of smooth periodic fields, joint continuity of every actual spatial derivative on the closed slab implies continuity of its finite completed jet tuples in the uniform norm. Periodicity reduces the spatial supremum to a compact fundamental cell. Compact uniform continuity then gives a single time modulus valid at all spatial points.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_periodicVelocity.summary: Joint spatial jet continuity gives uniform time continuity

TorusEuler.continuousOn_phaseAnchoredInt.text: If `f` is jointly continuous on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R$ with $a\le b$, its anchored phase integral is continuous on the same set. Time is clamped to the closed slab to build a continuous extension. This auxiliary extension does not assert any differentiability beyond the slab.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_phaseAnchoredInt.summary: Phase integration preserves continuity on a closed time slab

TorusEuler.continuousOn_ringInverse_of_u.text: On a set `U`, assume `A` is operator-norm continuous, every `A x` is a unit, and its inverse norm is bounded uniformly by `M`. The inverse family is then continuous on `U`. The resolvent estimate supplies the comparison at nearby parameters; no continuity of arbitrarily chosen solution representatives is asserted.

TorusEuler.continuousOn_slabVolterra_inh.text: The real-time function obtained by applying the clamped coefficient path to the clamped vector path is continuous everywhere. Although the declaration name contains `continuousOn`, its conclusion is global `Continuous`. This follows directly from continuity of the two extensions and continuous evaluation of an operator on a vector.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_slabVolterra_inh.summary: The extended Volterra integrand is globally continuous

TorusEuler.continuousOn_spatial_jet_of_c.text: For a jointly smooth field on a nondegenerate closed time slab, every spatial iterated derivative is jointly continuous on that slab. The proof restricts the joint Taylor series to purely spatial directions and uses uniqueness of within-slab derivatives. No periodicity assumption is needed for this local continuity statement; periodicity enters the later uniform bounds.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_spatial_jet_of_c.summary: Spatial jets are jointly continuous through the time endpoints

TorusEuler.continuousOn_weightedGenerato.text: If the original generator, weight and specified weight derivative are continuous on `I`, and the weight is strictly positive there, the transformed generator is continuous. Only continuity and positivity are used in this lemma; `dg` is not yet required to be an actual derivative. The result prepares the weighted linear-ODE existence and comparison arguments.
TorusEuler.continuousOn_weightedGenerato.summary: A positive differentiable weight gives a continuous generator

TorusEuler.continuousRealHalfHolder.text: This private definition forgets the quantitative half Hölder bound and retains the underlying continuous real vector field on the torus. Evaluation is unchanged. The conversion allows the Fourier band predicate, which is formulated for continuous maps, to be applied to inputs and outputs of the bounded Leray projection.
TorusEuler.continuousRealHalfHolder.summary: The continuous representative of a half Hölder field

TorusEuler.continuous_and_norm_sub_le_en.text: Let $w$ be a spatially half-Hölder field with values in $L^2([0,T];E)$. Its primitive $Jw(t)$ is continuous in the spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norm and satisfies $\|Jw(t)-Jw(s)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le|t-s|^{1/2}\|w\|_{C^{0,1/2}(L^2)}$ for $s,t\in[0,T]$. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of supremum and seminorm. The formal statement allows an arbitrary metric label space, including the unit torus. Applied to $w=\Omega v$, this makes the right side of (A.9) continuous before continuity of $v$ has been recovered. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
TorusEuler.continuous_and_norm_sub_le_en.summary: Control integration in the spatial half-Hölder norm

TorusEuler.continuous_appendixCutoffKern.text: For fixed symbol, scale and evaluation point `x`, the cutoff kernel is continuous in the integration variable. The sum contains only finitely many Fourier characters, and the symbol values are fixed coefficients. Consequently the theorem needs no regularity assumption on `ψ` and makes no uniform bound in the scale.

TorusEuler.continuous_coordinateHessian.text: For a complex scalar field of class $C^2$ on Euclidean space, each coordinate Hessian entry is continuous. Differentiation and evaluation in the fixed direction $e_j$ first give a $C^1$ scalar field, whose derivative evaluated at $e_i$ is continuous. These hypotheses justify the compact-cell Hessian integrals.
TorusEuler.continuous_coordinateHessian.summary: Twice continuous differentiability makes each mixed partial continuous

TorusEuler.continuous_curlOfDerivative.text: The map taking a three-dimensional derivative matrix to its curl vector is continuous. Each component is a difference of two matrix entries, so continuity follows from continuous coordinate evaluation. The maximality proof applies this to a hypothetical smooth extension to contradict the unbounded vorticity already established at the origin.
TorusEuler.continuous_curlOfDerivative.summary: Curl depends continuously on the velocity derivative

TorusEuler.continuous_divergence_of_cont.text: For `hv : ContDiff ℝ 1 v`, divergence is a continuous scalar function. The proof expresses divergence as the finite sum of diagonal coordinate derivatives of `v`. This supplies integrability on the compact fundamental cell for the periodic integration-by-parts argument; no divergence-free assumption is needed.
TorusEuler.continuous_divergence_of_cont.summary: A continuously differentiable field has continuous divergence

TorusEuler.continuous_endpointL2Energy.text: For nonnegative duration and continuous coefficient curves, the endpoint energy is a continuous real-valued function of the temporal $L^2$ velocity. Its two pieces are the squared norm of multiplication by `F` and an inner product involving the skew multiplier and primitive. This continuity lets a coercive estimate extend from smooth paths by density.
TorusEuler.continuous_endpointL2Energy.summary: The endpoint energy varies continuously with velocity

TorusEuler.continuous_endpointMixedPrimi.text: If `post` is a bounded linear operation turning primitive evaluation into an operator between spatial normed spaces, applying it to a fixed mixed-space element yields a continuous time path. The theorem abstracts the function-space bookkeeping. It assumes the bounded postcomposition map instead of constructing the particular Hölder-space map used in Appendix A.
TorusEuler.continuous_endpointMixedPrimi.summary: Bounded postcomposition gives a continuous spatial time path

TorusEuler.continuous_endpointPrimitiveE.text: For any real terminal parameter `T`, the primitive-evaluation family is continuous on the subtype of times in $[0,T]$. The previous operator-norm half-Hölder estimate proves this directly. If `T<0`, the subtype is empty, so continuity is vacuous; applications to endpoint recovery use a positive interval.
TorusEuler.continuous_endpointPrimitiveE.summary: Primitive evaluation varies continuously across the whole slab

TorusEuler.continuous_endpointSpatialSeg.text: Evaluation of a half-Hölder field along $a+\operatorname{toUnitTorus}(sh\,u)$ is continuous in the real segment parameter `s`. The result works in any real normed target space and imposes no condition on `h` or `u`. It ensures that segment averages used to recover derivatives are ordinary integrable continuous functions.
TorusEuler.continuous_endpointSpatialSeg.summary: Evaluating a Hölder field along a segment is continuous

TorusEuler.continuous_endpointTimeCoeffi.text: The uniform spatial half-Hölder coefficient estimate implies continuity of the label-to-time-operator map in operator norm. The proof squeezes the norm difference by $M\sqrt{d(a,b)}$. This conclusion is continuity in the spatial label; the construction does not require or establish operator dependence on a varying terminal time.
TorusEuler.continuous_endpointTimeCoeffi.summary: The path operator family is continuous in the label

TorusEuler.continuous_extendSlabPath.text: The clamped real-time extension of a continuous slab path is continuous on all of $\mathbb R$. It is the composition of the path with the continuous interval projection. Nonnegative duration is required to define that projection; smoothness outside or across the endpoints is not part of this result.

TorusEuler.continuous_finiteFourierSum.text: A finite sum of torus Fourier characters with fixed amplitudes is continuous in any complex normed target. Each term is a continuous scalar character multiplying a constant vector, and finite addition preserves continuity. This supplies the continuous-map packaging used in Fourier uniqueness arguments for spectral cutoffs.

TorusEuler.continuous_iteratedFDeriv_sla.text: For a $C^n$ path-valued map and $m\le n$, its evaluated order-$m$ parameter derivative is jointly continuous in slab time, parameter and all direction arguments. Evaluation commutes with differentiation because it is continuous linear. This supplies continuity of parameter jets, without claiming differentiation in the time variable.
TorusEuler.continuous_iteratedFDeriv_sla.summary: Evaluated parameter jets vary continuously with time and directions

TorusEuler.continuous_parentFiniteFourie.text: A finite sum of torus characters multiplied by arbitrary vector coefficients is continuous. The coefficient space is a complex normed space; no decay condition is needed because `s` is finite. This supplies the continuity hypotheses needed when products of parent Fourier expansions are integrated term by term.

TorusEuler.continuous_phaseAnchoredInteg.text: Joint continuity of `f(t,s)` implies continuity of the integral from zero to the variable phase endpoint. The proof rescales that interval to $[0,1]$ and uses continuity of a parameter integral. The target is a real normed space; no periodicity or zero-mean assumption is needed.
TorusEuler.continuous_phaseAnchoredInteg.summary: The anchored phase integral depends continuously on its parameters

TorusEuler.continuous_pressure_slice.text: If `h : IsEulerSolution T U p` and `r ∈ Ico 0 T`, then the spatial pressure function `p r` is smooth to every order. This follows by composing joint smoothness with the fixed-time inclusion. Despite the short name mentioning continuity, the declaration’s conclusion is full spatial smoothness.
TorusEuler.continuous_pressure_slice.summary: Every preterminal pressure slice is smooth

TorusEuler.continuous_realBanachFourierC.text: For an integrable field on the torus, the real convolution cutoff is continuous in its evaluation point. The kernel is jointly continuous on a compact product, giving an integrable dominating function proportional to the input norm. The proof uses dominated continuity, and the declaration does not require the surrounding completeness assumption.
TorusEuler.continuous_realBanachFourierC.summary: Continuity of the real convolution output

TorusEuler.continuous_realVectorFourierC.text: The real vector cutoff of any torus function is continuous because its output is a finite Fourier sum followed by a continuous real-part map. No measurability or integrability hypothesis is asserted for the input. This regularity of the reconstructed output must be distinguished from a classical integral interpretation of its coefficients.

TorusEuler.continuous_segmentEval.text: Evaluating a `HalfHolder` field along the torus segment $a+[(sh)u]$ gives a continuous function of the real parameter $s$. This holds for every displacement $h$ and direction $u$, with no differentiability assumption on the field. Continuity follows from its bundled Hölder regularity and the continuous quotient map to the torus.
TorusEuler.continuous_segmentEval.summary: Half Hölder fields vary continuously along label segments

TorusEuler.continuous_toUnitTorus.text: The map from Euclidean three-space to the product unit torus is continuous because every coordinate map to the additive circle is continuous. This structural fact supplies measurability and continuity for lifted or translated torus fields inside convolution integrals. It does not assert differentiability of the quotient map as a Euclidean-valued function.
TorusEuler.continuous_toUnitTorus.summary: The Euclidean to torus quotient map is continuous

TorusEuler.continuous_torusDirection.text: Evaluating a half-Hölder derivative field `df` along the path $a+\operatorname{toUnitTorus}(shu)$ is continuous as a function of `s`. The argument composes the continuous value field with the Lipschitz quotient map and a linear path. This continuity permits the fundamental theorem of calculus along each directional segment.
TorusEuler.continuous_torusDirection.summary: A derivative field stays continuous along a translated line

TorusEuler.continuous_wavePotential_prof.text: For a continuous phase profile $V$ and fixed vector $\kappa$, proves continuity of $-\|\kappa\|^{-2}(\kappa\times V(s))$. The wave vector may be zero because the scalar coefficient is constant in phase and Lean defines its inverse there. Nonzero $\kappa$ is required later for curl inversion, not for this continuity statement.
TorusEuler.continuous_wavePotential_prof.summary: The potential integrand is continuous in phase

TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne.text: Let $\mathbf a,\kappa\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $D$ be the linear map $v\mapsto(\kappa\cdot v)\mathbf a$, the convention for $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$. Forming the coordinate curl from this derivative matrix gives $\kappa\times\mathbf a$, with the usual orientation of the coordinate basis. No differentiability assertion about a velocity is needed for this algebraic identity; no orthogonality or nonzero-vector assumptions are required. When $D$ is a contribution to $\nabla U_j(t,0)$, the identity gives exactly the contribution to vorticity used in Proposition 8.2. It fixes both the tensor order and the cross-product sign.
TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne.summary: The gradient contribution has vorticity equal to the covector cross amplitude

TorusEuler.coordinateDirection.text:
The Eulerian coordinate directions in the lift.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.

TorusEuler.coordinateHessian.text: The coordinate Hessian entry first differentiates in direction $e_j$, then differentiates that scalar function in direction $e_i$. The scalar field may be complex, with both derivatives taken over the real spatial domain. Later $C^2$ hypotheses ensure these expressions are the classical mixed partial derivatives used by periodic integration by parts.
TorusEuler.coordinateHessian.summary: Differentiate a scalar field in two coordinate directions

TorusEuler.coordinateL2.text: For a fixed coordinate `i : Fin 3`, project a complex vector-valued spatial L² field to scalar L². The map is complex-linear and continuous because the Euclidean coordinate projection is bounded. It is used to reduce vector Fourier density to the scalar Fourier density theorem.
TorusEuler.coordinateL2.summary: Extract one coordinate of a complex spatial field

TorusEuler.coordinate_hessian_ofReal.text: For a real $C^2$ field, either taking two coordinate derivatives before complexification or after complexification gives the same result. The proof applies the first-derivative conversion twice. This allows the complex Fourier integration-by-parts formulas to be used for the real pressure potential.
TorusEuler.coordinate_hessian_ofReal.summary: Complexification commutes with the coordinate Hessian

TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain.text: For a real number $L$, the formal definition is $\varepsilon=1/L^2$. With the positive gains of §1.5, this gives $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$ and makes large prescribed gains correspond to small positive coupling ratios. The formula is nevertheless defined for every real input: negative inputs give the same value as their absolute values, and at $L=0$ the value is zero because division by zero is assigned zero. Thus positivity of the ratio cannot be concluded without $L\ne0$. This definition alone neither chooses the gains nor proves the smallness needed in Proposition 2.8.
TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain.summary: Positive gains determine inverse-square coupling ratios

TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain_step.text: Let $L>0$ and $L_+\ge640L$, and set $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$. The formal statement gives $\varepsilon_+=(L/L_+)^2\varepsilon\le\varepsilon/32$, together with $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}=LL_+\le L_+^2$. For step $j$, take $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$; then these are the ratio estimate (7.9) and the following comparison of crossing times. Both gains and both ratios are positive under the hypotheses, so inverse squares and the negative half-power have their ordinary meanings. The statement assumes the gain separation; it does not prove it from the frequency recurrence.
TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain_step.summary: Relates consecutive gains, coupling ratios and the crossing horizon

TorusEuler.cross3.text:
Define the standard Euclidean cross product by transporting the coordinate cross product to the Euclidean-space type. It fixes the orientation of the third moving-frame vector and of curl-based constructions.

Default-value audit (b5): The coordinate cross product is bilinear and total, including zero and parallel vectors. It gives a unit third frame vector only when the first two vectors satisfy the separate normalization and perpendicularity assumptions.
TorusEuler.cross3.summary: The oriented cross product in three dimensions

TorusEuler.cross3Left.text:
This continuous linear map sends v to κ × v in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The construction transfers the coordinate cross product through the Euclidean-space equivalence.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.

TorusEuler.cross3Left_apply.text: Applying the bounded linear cross-product map to v gives the ordinary vector cross product κ × v. This identifies the operator packaging used in the divergence completion.
TorusEuler.cross3Left_apply.summary: The linear cross-product map has the expected value

TorusEuler.cross3_cross3.text: In three-dimensional Euclidean space, expands $\kappa\times(u\times v)$ as $\langle\kappa,v\rangle u-\langle u,\kappa\rangle v$. The formula is unconditional and fixes the sign convention used by the wave potential. The proof transfers the coordinate cross-product identity through the Euclidean-space wrapper; no nonzero or orthogonality hypothesis enters.

TorusEuler.cross3_frameDerivative.text: Assuming perpendicular unit axes $u,v$, simplifies the cross-product derivative formed from $u\prime=-\nu v-\gamma(u\times v)$ and $v\prime=\nu u-\eta(u\times v)$ to $\gamma u+\eta v$. This is a pointwise algebraic identity in arbitrary real rates. It does not itself assume differentiable paths; the preceding product-rule theorem supplies those derivatives.
TorusEuler.cross3_frameDerivative.summary: The third axis follows from the first two

TorusEuler.cross3_neg_inv_norm_sq_smul.text: For nonzero $\kappa$ and a transverse vector $v$, proves that applying $\kappa\times$ to $-\|\kappa\|^{-2}(\kappa\times v)$ returns $v$. The transverse hypothesis removes the longitudinal term in the triple product, while `hκ` justifies cancellation of the squared norm. This is the algebraic inversion used before integrating the wave potential in phase.

TorusEuler.cross3_neg_left.text: The cross product changes sign when its first argument is negated. This algebraic identity holds for arbitrary three-dimensional vectors and needs no transversality or nonvanishing assumption. It is used when differentiating the transported covector, whose evolution has a minus sign.
TorusEuler.cross3_neg_left.summary: Negating the covector negates the cross product

TorusEuler.cross3_self_smul.text: The cross product of `k` with any scalar multiple of `k` vanishes. This includes the zero vector and zero scalar. In the potential time derivative, the pressure contribution lies in the covector direction and is removed by this identity, so no pressure derivative enters the final source.
TorusEuler.cross3_self_smul.summary: A vector has zero cross product with its multiples

TorusEuler.cross3_smul_smul.text: The cross product of two scaled vectors equals the product of the scalars times the original cross product. This private bilinearity identity is used to express a preceding wave’s curl in its normalized moving frame. It has no nonzero or orthogonality assumptions, because the algebraic identity holds for all vectors.
TorusEuler.cross3_smul_smul.summary: Scaling both vectors scales their cross product

TorusEuler.cross3_sub_right.text: For a fixed first vector, taking a cross product is linear in the second vector and therefore preserves subtraction. The identity is unconditional. It separates the forcing, strain, and longitudinal-pressure pieces of the transverse velocity equation during the time differentiation of the curl potential.
TorusEuler.cross3_sub_right.summary: The cross product distributes over a difference

TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf.text: Suppose $\mu,c,L>0$, $L_+\ge640L$, $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$ and $L_+\ge2/c$. Define $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$, $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$ and $\tau=\mu^{-1/8}L_+^3$. The formal theorem proves $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}/r\le\tau$. With $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$, the left side is the physical duration corresponding to the upper end of the crossing bracket, while $\tau=\tau_j$. This places any crossing already known to lie in that bracket before $t_j+\tau_j$. The theorem neither constructs a crossing nor states the intermediate bound by a constant times $\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^2$.
TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf.summary: Bounds the physical crossing horizon by the endpoint half-length

TorusEuler.crossingHorizon_eq_of_gains.text: For positive `L` and $640L\le L_{next}$, the abstract crossing horizon at the two inverse-square gain ratios equals $2LL_{next}$. These assumptions select the appropriate horizon branch and justify the reciprocal-square-root simplification. The theorem is an exact scalar identity, preceding any choice of a physical crossing.
TorusEuler.crossingHorizon_eq_of_gains.summary: The crossing horizon is twice the product of gains

TorusEuler.curl.text:
The vorticity of v at x is curlOfDerivative applied to fderiv ℝ v x. On a differentiable field this is the usual three-dimensional curl with the orientation used in the paper. The bare definition imposes no regularity on v; the smoothness of an Euler solution is supplied by its surrounding predicate.

Default-value audit (b4): A nondifferentiable v has default derivative zero at the offending point, and hence curl v x = 0 there. This can make an isolated curl equation misleading. The main witness requires smoothness on the physical slab, and IsEulerSolution.contDiff_velocity_slice exposes the guard. Its terminal curl limit uses actual smooth slices before T; no derivative at T is assumed.
TorusEuler.curl.summary: Vorticity from the spatial velocity derivative

TorusEuler.curlDerivativeLinear.text: This private real linear map sends a vector-valued derivative matrix to its coordinate curl vector. Additivity and scalar compatibility are supplied by earlier calculations. Since the spaces are finite dimensional, it can subsequently be viewed as continuous and composed with the derivative of a potential.
TorusEuler.curlDerivativeLinear.summary: Curl extraction as a linear map on derivatives

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.text: For monotone activation times and a gain sequence tending to infinity, eventual positive-frequency, normalized-delay, rate, and central-curl bounds force the curl integral on $[0,T)$ to be infinite. The velocity slices must be spatially continuously differentiable. Each eligible interval already carries mass proportional to its gain; the proof does not sum disjoint intervals or require activation times to converge to `T`.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.summary: Unbounded interval mass forces the total curl integral to diverge

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.text: The direct interval-mass conclusion remains valid when the central curl lower bound contains the errors $B\mu_j^{1/32}+B$, provided the frequency sequence and gain sequence both tend to infinity. Activation times are monotone, relevant intervals lie in $[0,T)$, and spatial slices are continuously differentiable. The errors are absorbed into half the positive leading coefficient before applying the exact-bound theorem.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.summary: Lower-order curl errors preserve divergence of the integral

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_induct.text: With diverging frequencies, monotone activation times below `T`, continuously differentiable spatial slices, and eventual strength and coupling bounds, actual growing crossings from `activation (j + 2)` to `activation (j + 3)` supply the normalized delays needed for integral divergence. The curl lower bound uses `freq (j + 1)` with lower-order errors. These crossings and intervalwise curl bounds are hypotheses; neither an Euler equation nor convergence of activation times is required.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_induct.summary: Actual scheduled crossings force the terminal curl integral to diverge

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_lower_bound_on_i.text: If every slice on $[0,T)$ is spatially continuously differentiable and its central curl is at least $m\ge0$ on $[a,b)$, with $a\ge0$ and $b\le T$, the total curl integral is at least $m(b-a)$. The statement does not require $a\le b$; in the reversed case the extended-nonnegative lower bound is zero.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_lower_bound_on_i.summary: A central curl lower bound forces interval integral mass

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative.text:
Given an actual continuous linear map D : Vec3 →L[ℝ] Vec3, take its three columns D e₀, D e₁, D e₂. The output is ((D e₁)₂−(D e₂)₁, (D e₂)₀−(D e₀)₂, (D e₀)₁−(D e₁)₀) in zero-based indexing. When D=Dv this is (∂₂v₃−∂₃v₂, ∂₃v₁−∂₁v₃, ∂₁v₂−∂₂v₁) in the paper’s indexing. This operation only reads the antisymmetric part; it does not itself differentiate a field.

Default-value audit (b4): Finite linear algebra only: subtraction, application to three basis vectors and a Euclidean wrapper. There is no denominator or derivative computation. If the caller obtained D from fderiv of a nondifferentiable function, the zero-default risk belongs to that caller, especially curl.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative.summary: The antisymmetric derivative entries giving curl

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivativeCLM.text:
Curl as a bounded linear function of the velocity gradient.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.curlOfDerivativeCLM.summary: Curl as a bounded linear map of the gradient

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative_add.text: The vector obtained by taking the antisymmetric coordinate combinations of a derivative matrix is additive in that matrix. This is a finite-coordinate linear identity. It permits the curl of the transported profile derivative to split into its label contribution and its rank-one phase contribution.

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative_smul.text: The algebraic curl of cD is c times the algebraic curl of D. No differentiability hypothesis is needed because D is already supplied as a continuous linear map.

TorusEuler.curl_planeWave.text: If `hF` gives the scalar profile derivative at $k\cdot x$, the curl of $F(k\cdot y)a$ at `x` is that derivative times $k\times a$. The wave vector and amplitude are constant here. The explicit derivative hypothesis prevents relying on totalized differentiation of an arbitrary profile.
TorusEuler.curl_planeWave.summary: The plane wave curl follows the frequency cross amplitude

TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile.text:
At a fixed $(t,x)$, suppose the inverse label map $A(t,\cdot)$ is differentiable with derivative $G$, and the potential $Q(t,a,s)$ is jointly differentiable in $(a,s)$ at $a=A(t,x)$ and $s=k_*\cdot a$. The formal statement gives $
abla_x	imes Q^
atural=(\mathbf d	imes Q)^
atural+\kappa	imes(\partial_sQ)^
atural$, where $\kappa=G^Tk_*$ and $\mathbf d=G^T
abla_a$. This is the curl version of (3.1). It is a local chain rule: neither a trajectory equation nor periodicity, support, transversality or nonvanishing of the covector is assumed.
TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile.summary: The physical curl separates label and phase derivatives

TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.text: Assume `hA` differentiates the inverse label, `hκ` identifies its transported covector, `hk` excludes zero covector, and `htrans` gives phasewise transversality. With phase continuity `hV` and joint potential differentiability `hQ`, the transported potential curl equals the evaluated oscillation plus its slow label curl. Periodicity is not required for this local identity.
TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.summary: The potential curl recovers the wave plus its slow correction

TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.text:
Fix a time and spatial point, and suppose the inverse label map $A$ is differentiable there. Require $\kappa(A(x))=(D_xA)^Tk_*
e0$, continuity of $V(A(x),s)$ in phase and $\kappa\cdot V=0$ at every phase. If $Q[V]$ is jointly differentiable in label and phase, the formal statement proves $
abla_x	imes Q[V]^
atural=V^
atural+C[V]^
atural$, with $C[V]$ the curl at fixed phase. This is the first identity of (3.6) after physical evaluation. Periodicity and zero phase mean are unnecessary for this local identity, although they ensure that the potential used in the paper is a periodic profile. The longitudinal identity is a separate result.
TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.summary: The fast curl recovers the transverse profile exactly

TorusEuler.currySlab.text: Jointly continuous data on a closed slab define, for every parameter, a continuous time path obtained by fixing that parameter. The continuity proof is stored with the path. This definition only constructs the path-valued function; its continuity or smoothness in the parameter is proved by subsequent results.
TorusEuler.currySlab.summary: View joint data as parameterized time paths

TorusEuler.currySlabWithin.text: For a parameter belonging to `S`, this constructs its continuous time path from joint continuity on the slab times `S`. For parameters outside `S`, it returns the zero path. The later continuity and smoothness statements are within `S`, so the arbitrary total extension does not supply behavior across its boundary.
TorusEuler.currySlabWithin.summary: Restrict parameterized time paths to their valid domain

TorusEuler.currySlabWithin_apply.text: If `hp : p ∈ S`, evaluation of the restricted curried path at a slab time gives the original value $X(t,p)$. The membership hypothesis selects the nondefault branch of the definition. There is no corresponding equality outside `S`, where the constructed path has deliberately been set to zero.
TorusEuler.currySlabWithin_apply.summary: Inside the parameter domain the path is exact

TorusEuler.cutoffHolderConstant_nonneg.text: For any Schwartz kernel and natural order `m`, the uniform Hölder tail constant is nonnegative. The proof unfolds its absolute-moment formula and uses positivity of the constituent norms and integrals. This sign is needed when multiplying the analytic cutoff estimate by upper bounds for the differentiated input fields.

TorusEuler.cutoffHolderTailConstant.text: Defines the loss-`k` tail constant as the absolute kernel moment, with an additional one when `k=0`.
