The conclusion therefore follows inside the intended projection domain, rather than from the lift’s zero fallback for inadmissible inputs.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_gradi.summary: The lifted Leray projection removes smooth periodic gradients

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_holde.text: The periodic Leray Hölder bound used in the estimate of (5.58).
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_holde.summary: The order-one Hölder bound for the Leray projection

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_pullb.text: On the lift of a torus half-Hölder field, the projection is its actual torus Leray projection.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_pullb.summary: The lifted projection agrees with the torus projection

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_slice.text: The within time derivative of a jointly smooth periodic divergence-free velocity on a nondegenerate closed slab is fixed by the actual periodic Leray projection. The proof differentiates its pairing with gradients of test potentials. Smoothness and periodicity put the derivative in the valid half Hölder domain, including at both time endpoints.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_slice.summary: The time derivative of a solenoidal field is projected identically

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_smul_.text: The periodic Leray lift of a real scalar multiple of a smooth periodic field equals the same multiple of its projection. The proof represents the field in the torus half Hölder space and uses the concrete bounded projection there. This domain restriction prevents the raw lift’s fallback branch from obscuring linearity.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_smul_.summary: Projection commutes with real scaling on smooth fields

TorusEuler.periodicLeray_translate.text: The strong spatial Leray projection commutes with every torus translation on half-Hölder vector fields. The proof uses its exact complex Fourier coefficient law, where translation contributes a scalar phase that commutes with each mode projection. This supplies the invariance needed to pass spatial derivatives through the projection.
TorusEuler.periodicLeray_translate.summary: The torus Leray operator commutes with translations

TorusEuler.periodicLongitudinalSpan.text: This submodule is the complex linear span of all longitudinal mode insertions. A span means finite algebraic linear combinations; it is not declared closed. Its orthogonal complement is nevertheless closed and supplies the solenoidal $L^2$ space used for the orthogonal Leray projection.
TorusEuler.periodicLongitudinalSpan.summary: Finite linear combinations of longitudinal Fourier modes

TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergence.text: The divergence of the tensor product of two bundled velocities is packaged as another smooth periodic velocity. Smoothness follows by differentiating their smooth tensor; periodicity follows because differentiation commutes with lattice translations. This object is defined before Leray projection and does not require either input to be divergence free.
TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergence.summary: Tensor divergence remains a smooth periodic field

TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergenceBil.text: The tensor divergence construction is bundled as an algebraic bilinear map on smooth periodic fields. Linearity in each slot uses the derivative rules for sums and scalar multiples of smooth tensors. No operator norm is asserted at this stage; a finite derivative estimate is supplied later on jet tuples.
TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergenceBil.summary: Tensor divergence is bilinear on smooth periodic velocities

TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergence_ap.text: Evaluating the constructed smooth periodic momentum divergence returns the contraction of the actual derivative of the pointwise tensor. This definitional equality connects the bundle to the expression used by the projected Euler equation. It remains a tensor divergence formula without a divergence-free premise on the inputs.
TorusEuler.periodicMomentumDivergence_ap.summary: The bundled divergence has the expected tensor formula

TorusEuler.periodicMomentumJetBound.text: This nonnegative scalar collects the operator norms of Leray projection, tensor divergence, and the momentum tensor, together with the finite product and Hölder comparison constants. It depends on the target order `m`. Its purpose is to prove boundedness of momentum from jets through `m+2` to jets through `m`.
TorusEuler.periodicMomentumJetBound.summary: An explicit constant for the finite jet momentum estimate

TorusEuler.periodicMomentumTensor_smooth.text: The pointwise tensor formed from two bundled smooth periodic velocities is smooth in space. The proof uses the continuous bilinear tensor map and smoothness of both inputs. Periodicity is not part of this theorem’s conclusion, although it is established in the following divergence construction.
TorusEuler.periodicMomentumTensor_smooth.summary: Two smooth velocities have a smooth momentum tensor

TorusEuler.periodicPoissonPressure_uniqu.text: Let $p,q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and $\mathbb Z^3$-periodic. If $\Delta p=\Delta q$ pointwise and both integrals over the centered unit cell vanish, then $p=q$. The difference is a periodic harmonic function and hence constant, and its zero mean removes the additive constant. This is a spatial uniqueness theorem; it can be applied independently at each time. Proposition 5.11 uses it to identify the constructed pressure with the normalized solution of $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)$. The theorem applies to any common Poisson source and asserts no existence or time regularity.
TorusEuler.periodicPoissonPressure_uniqu.summary: Equal periodic Laplacians and zero means determine the same pressure

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedEuler_of_sta.text: On a positive closed prefix, smooth periodic approximants with uniformly converging values and every spatial jet, a uniformly vanishing residual, and the actual stage evolution yield the integrated projected equation, its within derivative, and joint smoothness of the limit. Smooth spatial slices of the limit are also assumed. This theorem does not yet introduce pressure.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedEuler_of_sta.summary: Stage limits satisfy the actual projected evolution smoothly

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentum.text: The bilinear expression is $-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$ on the Euclidean lift, formed by differentiating the momentum tensor and applying the periodic Leray lift. The minus sign matches the evolution equation. This raw definition accepts arbitrary functions; agreement with an actual analytic projection requires its periodic Hölder domain.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentum.summary: The signed projected tensor divergence drives Euler evolution

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumBili.text: Composing tensor divergence with negative Leray projection gives a bilinear map on smooth periodic velocities. This package records that the output remains in the same smooth periodic submodule. Its later bounded extension uses finite jet norms; the present definition itself asserts algebraic bilinearity rather than a no-loss estimate.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumBili.summary: The smooth momentum operation is an algebraic bilinear map

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumBili.text: For smooth periodic inputs, forgetting the bundle on the algebraic momentum map yields exactly `periodicProjectedMomentum u v`. This is a definitional equality. It is the bridge from estimates proved for packaged smooth fields back to the explicit signed projected tensor divergence used in the limit equation.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumBili.summary: The bundled operation equals the raw momentum expression

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.text: The bounded bilinear momentum map extends from genuine smooth tuples to their closure, mapping two order `m+2` inputs to an order `m` output. Density and completeness justify the extension. On embedded smooth velocities it returns the actual signed projected tensor divergence, as the following agreement theorem proves.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.summary: Momentum extends to completed compatible derivative data

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.text: For smooth periodic inputs, each component of the extended momentum output equals the actual derivative of the signed projected tensor divergence. The index ranges through order `m`, while the two inputs are stored through `m+2`. This is the exact interpretation needed by the integrated jet bootstrap.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.summary: The extended map returns the actual momentum derivatives

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.text: On the completed tuples of two smooth periodic velocities, the extended momentum map equals the completed tuple of their smooth momentum field. The proof reduces the extensions to their agreement on the dense source. This rules out any change of the intended formula when completion is introduced.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.summary: Completion preserves the original smooth momentum calculation

TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray.text: Define the real spatial Leray operator as the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace annihilating all smooth gradient tests. Its codomain is the ambient real L² space, so ordinary operator composition is available. The later theorems identify this weak definition with the familiar Fourier-symbol projection.
TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray.summary: The real orthogonal projection onto solenoidal fields

TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray_realPart_eq.text: Projecting the real part of a complex spatial L² field equals taking the real part after the complex Leray projection. The proof characterizes orthogonal projection by range membership and orthogonality of the discarded part. The real/complex inner-product identity supplies the orthogonality transfer.
TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray_realPart_eq.summary: Taking real parts commutes with the Leray projection

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2.text: Apply the coordinatewise real-part map to complex vector-valued spatial L² fields. The result is a real continuous linear map between the corresponding Haar L² spaces. It is defined on equivalence classes using the bounded pointwise map; its representative formula is established separately and holds almost everywhere.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2.summary: Real parts of spatial square integrable fields

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_apply_ae.text: The L² representative of the real-part map agrees almost everywhere with taking the coordinatewise real part of the input representative. This is the compatibility provided by `compLpL`. It allows later inner-product calculations to use ordinary pointwise complex algebra while preserving the quotient-space meaning of the operators.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_apply_ae.summary: Real parts agree almost everywhere with pointwise evaluation

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_complexify.text: Complexify a real spatial L² field and then take its real part; the original L² field is recovered exactly. The equality is between equivalence classes and follows from almost-everywhere coordinate calculations. It supplies a left inverse for complexification, so no information is lost when passing to Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_complexify.summary: Taking real parts recovers an embedded real field

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_leray_mem_.text: The real part of the complex Leray projection of any spatial L² field belongs to the weak real solenoidal subspace. It is first proved on Fourier modes, whose projected amplitudes are transverse, then extended by density through each continuous gradient-testing functional. No smoothness of the original L² field is assumed.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_leray_mem_.summary: Projected complex fields have solenoidal real parts

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_mode_trans.text: For an amplitude `a` belonging to `transverseModeSpace k`, the real part of its vector Fourier mode lies in the weak real solenoidal space. The theorem translates the subspace membership into zero frequency contraction and identifies the representative with a real scalarized wave. It bridges the complex coefficient and real test-function definitions.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_mode_trans.summary: Real parts of transverse modes are weakly solenoidal

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_negI_apply.text: The real part of $-i$ times a complex spatial L² field agrees almost everywhere with its coordinatewise imaginary part. This formula expresses the imaginary projection using the already-defined real-part map. Its representative-level conclusion is enough to show later that a projected embedded real field has no imaginary component.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_negI_apply.summary: Multiplication by minus i reveals the imaginary part

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_negI_compl.text: Complexify a real spatial L² field, multiply it by $-i$, and take the real part: the result is zero. The statement is an L² equality and formalizes vanishing imaginary component of a real embedding. It is used to prove that the complex Leray projection preserves the embedded real subspace.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_negI_compl.summary: An embedded real field has zero imaginary part

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector.text:
Coordinatewise real part on the complex Euclidean spatial vector.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector.summary: Taking real parts of complex Euclidean vectors

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector_apply.text: The `i`th coordinate of `periodicRealPartVector v` is the real part of the `i`th complex coordinate of `v`. This pointwise identity identifies the bounded map with the usual real-part operation, despite the different Euclidean-space wrappers used for the real and complex vectors.

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector_comple.text: Complexification followed by real projection recovers the original vector.

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityHolderNorm_le.text: The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm of a smooth periodic velocity is at most $3(m+1)$ times the norm of its jet tuple through order `m+1`. Uniform value and derivative bounds yield the half Hölder increment estimate. This is one source of the finite derivative loss in the completed momentum construction.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityHolderNorm_le.summary: One extra uniform derivative controls the Hölder norm

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetComponent.text: This continuous linear map extracts a single bounded spatial jet from a completed compatible tuple. It first forgets the closed subspace membership and then projects onto the chosen finite coordinate. The coordinate index ensures that only an order stored in the tuple can be requested.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetComponent.summary: One derivative order is a bounded coordinate projection

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetInclusion.text: This linear isometry includes the range of smooth velocity jets in its topological closure. Norms are inherited from the same ambient tuple space, so preservation of norm is definitional. The map supplies the embedding along which the momentum operator will be extended by continuity.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetInclusion.summary: Smooth jet tuples sit densely in their closure

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.text: This function is the canonical completed jet tuple of a smooth periodic velocity. It is the evaluation of `periodicVelocityJetsLinear`, so all components still equal actual derivatives of the same field. The completed space is needed for integration and time regularity arguments, while these particular inputs remain smooth.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.summary: A smooth velocity enters the completed jet space

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetsLinear.text: This linear map first identifies a smooth periodic velocity with its exact finite jet tuple and then includes that tuple into the closure. It preserves the actual derivative values. The construction is algebraic at this stage; a norm on the original smooth velocity space is not being introduced.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJetsLinear.summary: The velocity map into completed compatible jets

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.text: For a smooth periodic input, evaluating any component of its completed jet tuple gives the corresponding actual iterated Fréchet derivative. The index `i : Fin (m + 1)` limits the order to the stored range. Completion has changed the ambient space, not the value of an embedded smooth tuple.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.summary: Completed smooth tuples still evaluate to actual derivatives

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.text: The scaled bump is evaluated after subtracting the nearest integer, implemented by $\lfloor s+1/2\rfloor$. The formula is one-periodic for all scales. Smoothness and evenness across the cell seams are proved under $0<h\le1$, where the bump vanishes well before those seams.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.summary: Repeating the scaled bump in each unit phase cell

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eq_on_cell.text: For $0<h\le1$ and phase in the closed interval $[-1/2,1/2]$, the periodic bump equals the original bump evaluated at $s/h$. The equality includes both boundary points because the bump vanishes there. It allows the phase mean to be estimated directly from the scaled support.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eq_on_cell.summary: The periodic bump matches the scaled bump on the closed cell

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eq_translate.text: For $0<h\le1$, if phase `s` lies within distance $3/4$ of an integer `z`, the periodic bump equals the bump scaled around that integer. If the nearest integer differs, both candidate bumps vanish. This overlap agreement removes the apparent discontinuity introduced by the floor function.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eq_translate.summary: A nearby bump copy agrees with the periodic definition

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_even.text: Under $0<h\le1$, reversing phase leaves the periodic bump unchanged. The proof compares copies centered at opposite integers and uses evenness of the original bump. The collar where copies vanish handles half-cell boundary choices, where the nearest-integer representative itself is not odd.

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eventuallyEq.text: Under $0<h\le1$, the periodic bump agrees near any phase with one fixed translated and scaled copy of the original bump. The integer center is chosen from the floor value at that phase. This local identity is stronger than a pointwise formula and allows all derivative orders to transfer.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_eventuallyEq.summary: Every phase has a smooth local bump formula

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_le_one.text: The periodic bump has value at most one at every scale and phase. This follows from the range of the smooth transition and remains true even outside the intended width range. Together with its support length, the bound controls the mean removed in the phase-profile construction.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_le_one.summary: The periodic bump is bounded above by one

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_nonneg.text: The periodic bump is nonnegative for every real scale and phase because the underlying smooth transition is nonnegative. This value bound does not rely on admissible scale or smoothness across seams. It enters the lower estimate for the normalized mean-free slope.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump_nonneg.summary: The periodic bump is everywhere nonnegative

TorusEuler.periodic_comp_hierarchyProfil.text: If a period direction `d` is negated by the joint reflection and `f` is periodic with period `d`, then composing `f` with reflection is still periodic with that period. The proof uses invariance under subtracting a period. This applies to both pure phase periods and twisted lattice shifts.

TorusEuler.periodic_coordinateWord.text: Starting from a spatially periodic field, any finite word of coordinate derivative operations remains periodic. Induction applies periodicity of the Fréchet derivative at each step and then evaluates a coordinate direction. No regularity is assumed, so this alone does not prove that the derivative word has the analytic meaning or bounds required later.
TorusEuler.periodic_coordinateWord.summary: Every coordinate derivative word is periodic

TorusEuler.periodic_firstWavePressureWit.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, the unwrapped pressure has period one in phase. Its coefficient is independent of phase, while the pressure primitive is periodic. The theorem does not require nonzero frequency because it proves periodicity of the total expression, rather than smoothness of its coefficient in the labels.
TorusEuler.periodic_firstWavePressureWit.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure has unit phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_firstWaveVelocityWit.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, the unwrapped primary velocity is periodic in its phase variable with period one. Time and label are fixed, so the smooth seed is a constant vector in this assertion. Periodicity is inherited solely from the scalar wave profile.
TorusEuler.periodic_firstWaveVelocityWit.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity has unit phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_holderLift.text: The lift of a half-Hölder torus field is invariant under integer lattice translations. This follows from the quotient map alone and needs no differentiability assumption. It is the periodicity input used when the derivatives of a lifted field are descended back to torus Hölder fields.

TorusEuler.periodic_iteratedDeriv_phase.text: If a function is periodic with period `τ`, every iterated derivative has the same period. No smoothness hypothesis is present in this declaration because Lean's derivative is a total function and translation preserves its definition. In applications to smooth profiles, these total derivatives agree with the ordinary analytic derivatives.

TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.text: If each vector field is spatially periodic and odd and the sequence converges pointwise, its limit has both symmetries. The proof compares limits at translated points and at $x$ and $-x$. No smoothness or uniform convergence is assumed here; these are purely closed symmetry identities in a normed target.
TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.summary: Periodicity and oddness survive pointwise convergence

TorusEuler.periodic_periodicWaveBump.text: Adding one to the phase leaves the periodic bump unchanged because the nearest-integer floor also increases by one. The theorem holds for every real scale, even degenerate scales. It is an algebraic periodicity statement; smoothness at the wrapping points requires the separate admissible-scale hypotheses.

TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.text: If a profile is one-periodic, subtracting its phase mean gives another one-periodic profile. This proof only uses that the subtracted mean is constant in the phase; continuity and integrability are not hypotheses. It does not assert that the resulting profile has zero mean, which is proved separately under the appropriate integration assumptions.
TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.summary: Subtracting the mean preserves the phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive.text: Let $f$ be a continuous period-one function with values in a real normed space and with $\int_0^1f(s)\,ds=0$. Form $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$ and subtract the average of $J$ over $[0,1]$. The formal statement proves that this normalized primitive has period one. This is the compatibility needed for $\partial_s^{-1}$ in (3.5). The zero mean of $f$ removes the drift of $J$ between periods; subtracting an additive constant alone would not do so. This result establishes periodicity; derivative and size properties of the primitive are proved separately.
TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive.summary: Zero mean prevents a primitive from drifting between periods

TorusEuler.periodic_sliceTimeDerivWithin.text: If every time slice on the closed interval is spatially periodic, its total within-interval time derivative is spatially periodic at each interval time. This follows from equality of the translated curves on the differentiation set. The lemma assumes neither differentiability nor distinct endpoints; later results supply actual derivative witnesses and interval nondegeneracy.
TorusEuler.periodic_sliceTimeDerivWithin.summary: The total time derivative retains spatial periodicity

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.text: For continuous one-periodic $V$ with zero phase mean, proves one-periodicity of `wavePotential κ V`. The proof transfers the mean through the fixed cross-product operator and uses the periodic primitive theorem. It does not require $\kappa\ne0$ or transversality; these conditions enter the separate fast-curl recovery theorem.
TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.summary: The wave potential has the prescribed phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv.text: For every $0<h\le1$, the formal statement proves $P_h(s+1)=P_h(s)$ for all real $s$. The chosen $P_h$ is the integral of the constructed $F_h$ with the integral's phase mean subtracted. Continuity, period one and zero phase mean of $F_h$ make that primitive periodic. This is the pressure-profile periodicity required in Lemma 3.1 and (3.3). The theorem concerns the phase variable alone; it does not assert spatial periodicity of a pressure evaluated at an arbitrary real plane phase. That requires the lattice condition or localization and periodic extension.
TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv.summary: The normalized primitive repeats after one phase cycle

TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile.text: For each $0<h\le1$, the constructed profile satisfies $F_h(s+1)=F_h(s)$ at every real phase. Its definition integrates the normalized periodized bump slope from zero, and the zero integral of that slope over one period eliminates any additive drift. This is the periodicity asserted in Lemma 3.1. The theorem does not use a lattice condition on a spatial wave vector: it concerns only the one-dimensional phase function. Oddness, derivative bounds and the normalized pressure primitive are separate properties of the same family.
TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile.summary: The mean-free slope integrates to a period-one function

TorusEuler.periodic_waveSlope.text: The normalized slope is one-periodic for every real scale because its phase dependence comes only from the periodic bump. Subtracting a fixed mean and dividing by a fixed scalar do not change the period. This includes degenerate scales, although the intended normalization requires the later positive-width hypotheses.
TorusEuler.periodic_waveSlope.summary: Subtracting the mean preserves slope periodicity

TorusEuler.periodic_zeroMean_of_phase_li.text: For phase-independent continuous operators, a jointly continuous forced ODE solution starting from zero inherits period one and zero phase mean from its forcing. The proof applies uniqueness to the phase-shift difference and to the averaged solution. It allows nonnegative duration and concludes these properties at a specified time of the closed slab.
TorusEuler.periodic_zeroMean_of_phase_li.summary: Zero-start dynamics preserve periodicity and zero phase mean

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.text:
Extend a label profile periodically using its values on the centered cell.

Default-value audit (b5): Periodicity is automatic, but continuity across cell faces is not. The construction uses profiles vanishing near the boundary before claiming smooth periodic extension.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension from the centered cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.text: The periodic extension agrees on the whole closed cell when the profile vanishes near its boundary.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.summary: The periodic extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.text: If a profile transforms under reflection by a map `L` fixing zero and vanishes on the negative cell walls, its centered periodic extension obeys the same reflection law. No continuity is assumed. The wall hypothesis handles points where negation does not commute with the half-open centered representative; away from those walls the representatives are exact negatives.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.summary: Periodic extension preserves reflection when cell walls vanish

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.text:
The label coordinate directions and the separate phase direction.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.summary: Three label directions and one phase direction

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateValue.text: Select one scalar coordinate of a label-phase pair: a spatial component for an index in `Fin 3`, or the phase component for the `Unit` index. The sum type provides exactly four coordinate choices. This is the bookkeeping needed to compare mixed coordinate derivative bounds with a Fréchet operator norm.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateValue.summary: Coordinates on labels and the independent phase

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.text: Assign the envelope scale `ℓ` to each label-coordinate direction and the profile width `h` to the phase direction. Products of these weights encode the mixed derivative factors in the finite profile norm. The definition records scaling alone; positivity and smallness are separate assumptions in estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.summary: Each derivative receives its own geometric scale

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.text:
A coordinate derivative, with a direction field allowed to vary with the base point.

Default-value audit (b5): A raw fderiv value is zero at nondifferentiability points. Smoothness is supplied separately in the word-calculus theorems; a numerical bound for this expression alone is not a differentiability theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.summary: Differentiation along a possibly varying direction field

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.text: For smooth coefficient field `D` and profile `f`, bounds through orders `n` and `n+1` give a bound $2^nCM$ through order `n` for the derivative of `f` in direction `D`. The nonnegative constants are explicit. Time weights can stay inside `M` because every derivative here acts only on the profile domain.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.summary: One directional derivative obeys the weighted product bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.text: Two smooth functions with jets through order `N` bounded by nonnegative constants `A` and `B` have a bilinear product bounded by $2^N\cdot A\cdot B$, provided the bilinear operator has norm at most one. The same bound covers every derivative order below `N`. This is the explicit finite Leibniz factor used for coframes, amplitudes, and potential coefficients.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.summary: A bilinear product has a finite Leibniz bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_clm_application.text: Specializes the bilinear product estimate to evaluation of a continuously varying linear map on a vector field. If both inputs are smooth and their jets through order `N` are bounded by nonnegative `A` and `B`, the resulting vector field has bound $2^N\cdot A\cdot B$. The evaluation operator has norm at most one, so no additional constant is needed.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_clm_application.summary: Applying a varying linear map preserves finite jet control

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_contractio.text: If a smooth function has a phase-jet bound through order `N`, precomposing it with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves that bound. The proof bounds the multilinear derivative after inserting the linear map in every argument. This embeds label-only coefficients in label-and-phase space without an extra derivative cost.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_contractio.summary: A linear contraction cannot increase a jet budget

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.text: Postcomposing a smooth function with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves its finite Fréchet-jet bound. The order and the numerical bound are unchanged.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.summary: A linear contraction preserves a finite derivative bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_const_smul.text: Multiplying a smooth function by a real constant `c` multiplies any finite phase-jet budget by $\lVert c\rVert$. The scalar may be zero or negative; the norm absorbs its sign. This helper applies time switches at a fixed time without introducing time derivatives, since the jet variable consists only of labels and phase.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_const_smul.summary: A fixed scalar multiplies the jet budget by its norm

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_constant_of_nor.text: If $\|c\|\le A$, the constant field with value $c$ has `PhaseJetBound n A` for every finite order $n$. The zeroth derivative uses the given norm bound; all positive parameter derivatives vanish. This turns the scalar time derivatives of a switching function into spatially constant factors in the leading-wave product estimate.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_constant_of_nor.summary: A constant field satisfies every parameter derivative bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: For a positive frequency and a smooth nonvanishing covector, assumes finite jet bounds for the normalized covector, strain, and normalized reciprocal squared norm. Their product gives smoothness and an explicit bound $2\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BQ}\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BK}\cdot \mathrm{BM}$ for the normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient. All three budgets are nonnegative; no frequency-independent estimate follows until their sizes are supplied.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Normalized pressure coefficients inherit three product budgets

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: Assumes a positive frequency and radius, $D \ge  1$, radius smallness $\ell\cdot D^{16} \le  1$, and prescribed raw jets of strain, normalized covector, and reciprocal squared norm. The normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient after label scaling is smooth and has finite jet budget $2\cdot 2^{2\cdot N}\cdot C^3\cdot D^7$. The exponent seven is independent of the derivative order; the prefactor is not.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Scaled pressure coefficients cost seven parent powers

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_add.text: If two smooth profiles satisfy `PhaseJetBound n` with constants `A` and `B`, their sum satisfies the same bound with constant `A + B`. The bound includes all derivative orders through `n`. This elementary calculus step is used to combine the slow and projected parts of the reconstructed pressure gradient.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_add.summary: Add bounds for derivatives of pressure profiles

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_clmApp.text: Smooth operator and vector profiles with nonnegative bounds `A` and `B` through order `n` give a bound $2^nAB$ for their pointwise application. The factor counts the product-rule contributions. This is the finite-order estimate for the coframe and projection factors in the reconstructed pressure gradient.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_clmApp.summary: Control an operator coefficient acting on a vector profile

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_smul.text: Multiplying a smooth profile by a constant scalar multiplies its `PhaseJetBound` by the scalar norm. The scalar is spatially and phase independent in this theorem, so no product derivatives appear. This accounts for numerical factors such as the factor two in the transverse pressure equation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_smul.summary: A scalar multiplies all pressure derivative bounds

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_sub.text: For two smooth profiles with derivative bounds through order `n`, their difference has the sum of the two bounding constants as its bound. The estimate uses the triangle inequality for iterated derivatives. It is applied to the force minus twice the strain correction in the transverse pressure formula.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_pressure_sub.summary: Subtract profiles while adding their derivative bounds

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhaseOnly.text: A smooth scalar function with bounds $h^j\|f^{(j)}\|\le C$ through order `n` gives a `PhaseJetBound n C` for the function $(a,s)\mapsto f(hs)$. The spatial coordinate is ignored, and the positive scale `h` is the phase derivative factor. The result lifts one-variable derivative estimates into the mixed label and phase norm used by the hierarchy.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhaseOnly.summary: Scalar phase derivatives control the rescaled product jet

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.text: For positive frequency, nonnegative radius, $D \ge  1$, and $\ell\cdot D^{16} \le  1$, assumes raw jet bounds for the normalized covector and reciprocal squared norm through order `N`. The scaled potential coefficient is smooth and has jet bound $2^N\cdot C^2\cdot D^6/\mathrm{freq}$. The covector must be smooth and nonvanishing; the bound isolates an inverse frequency before the later slow curl costs a label derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.summary: Scaled potential jets retain an inverse frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.text: For a smooth profile and positive envelope radius, a second-order bound on the rescaled profile gives a first-order bound $3\ell^{-1}M$ on its label divergence. One derivative is spent to form divergence and three coordinates contribute the constant. The result tracks the envelope cost separately from phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.summary: Label divergence costs one envelope reciprocal

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.text: The combined divergence identity `hdiv` replaces the large phase derivative of $\langle k,c\rangle$ by label divergence. With positive scales, smooth one-periodic data, a second-order oscillation bound, and a first-order mean bound, the longitudinal first-order bound is $(2+h)3\ell^{-1}M_{\rm osc}+\|k\|M_{\rm mean}$. The full wave-number factor applies only to the mean.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.summary: Divergence cancellation controls the longitudinal phase velocity

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.text: For a smooth, one-periodic, zero-mean profile and nonzero phase scale, a scaled jet bound through order `n` gives a bound $2\cdot B$ for its normalized phase primitive through the same order. Derivatives may involve both label and evaluation phase. The proof translates the integrand and applies a mixed-jet integral estimate; the nonzero phase scale permits division in that translation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.summary: A normalized periodic primitive preserves the jet order

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile of zero mean at every label, an order-one bound on its rescaled profile gives an order-one bound $(2+h)M$ for the rescaled normalized primitive. The phase width is positive and `hprim` supplies differentiability. Label integration costs at most two, while phase differentiation recovers the input with a factor `h`.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.summary: The phase primitive gains one phase-width factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.text: For a positive label radius and smooth potential and inverse coframe, assumes potential jets through order $n+1$ and radius-weighted coframe jets through `n`. The scaled slow curl is smooth and has budget $\lVert \mathrm{curlOfDerivativeCLM}\rVert \cdot \ell^{-1}\cdot 2^n\cdot \mathrm{BP}\cdot \mathrm{BG}$. The extra derivative and inverse radius are explicit, so a two-jet activation estimate requires three potential jets.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.summary: A slow curl uses one extra potential derivative

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.text: For a smooth periodic zero-mean profile, smooth potential coefficients, and nonzero phase scale, bounds the exact wave potential from profile and coefficient budgets through the same order `n`. The resulting budget is $2\cdot 2^n\cdot \mathrm{BK}\cdot \mathrm{BV}$, and joint smoothness is also proved. One finite Leibniz factor comes from applying the coefficient; the factor two comes from the normalized primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.summary: The actual wave potential inherits a product jet bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_smul_localized.text: For smooth scalar and vector functions on label-phase space, nonnegative jet bounds `A` and `B` through order `n` imply a bound $2^nAB$ for their scalar product. The binomial product rule supplies the factor $2^n$. This general estimate combines a slowly varying envelope-amplitude factor with the rapidly varying scalar phase profile.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_smul_localized.summary: Multiplying profiles combines their finite jet bounds

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.text: For every level from two through `P`, assume the profile is differentiable to order `n` and satisfies the stated jet bound. The finite sum then has the sum of those constants as a jet bound. An empty higher-level range gives the zero profile, so the lemma also covers shallow truncations.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.summary: Sum the higher pressure profiles at fixed derivative order

TorusEuler.phaseMean.text: For a real normed-space-valued phase function, the formal definition is $\langle f\rangle_s=\int_0^1 f(s)\,ds$. Because the phase period is one, no further normalizing factor appears. Time and particle label are held fixed, so this is distinct from a spatial average over $\mathbb T^3$. For the smooth periodic profiles used in §1.3, it is the ordinary phase mean separating mean and oscillatory forcing. The formal integral is assigned zero when its integrability conditions fail; such a value does not certify a mathematical average. Continuity on the period ensures the intended integral in the applications.
TorusEuler.phaseMean.summary: The average holds time and particle label fixed

TorusEuler.phaseMean_add.text: The phase mean of the sum of two continuous profiles is the sum of their phase means. Continuity supplies the integrability required by the interval integral.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_add_phase.text: For a one-periodic profile, translating the phase by any real number preserves its integral over one unit interval. The statement imposes no continuity hypothesis and concerns Lean’s interval-integral expression. It is used to identify the zero-mean normalization after moving the phase origin in derivative estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_add_phase.summary: A phase translation leaves the period average unchanged

TorusEuler.phaseMean_comp_clm.text: For a continuous phase profile `V` and a fixed continuous linear map `A`, averaging `A(V)` over one period gives `A` applied to the average of `V`. This only uses integrability supplied by continuity on the integration interval. Periodicity is not required for the averaging identity.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_comp_clm.summary: A fixed linear map commutes with phase averaging

TorusEuler.phaseMean_congr_unit.text: Two profiles that agree on the closed unit interval have equal phase averages. This is an interval-integral congruence, with no continuity or periodicity hypothesis. It is used to compare an actual profile with a clamped continuous-path representative that may have unrelated values outside that interval.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_congr_unit.summary: Only the values on one interval determine the average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.text: The average of a constant over a phase interval of length one is the same constant. This fixes the normalization of the phase average.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.summary: A constant profile equals its phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.text: A real scalar factor may be moved outside the unit-period phase mean. The scalar is constant in the phase variable.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.summary: A constant scalar passes through the phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.text: If f has a continuous derivative df everywhere and period one, the phase mean of df vanishes. The proof is the fundamental theorem of calculus with matching endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.summary: A periodic derivative has zero phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.text: Assume periodic completion and profile, a continuous phase derivative of the profile, and `hslave` identifying the completion's longitudinal component with the negative primitive of `divV`. Phase integration by parts converts the mean of $(C\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ into the mean of $\mathrm{divV}\,Y$. Periodicity cancels the boundary term; the slaving identity supplies the sign.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.summary: Integration by parts removes the fast derivative

TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile, the phase average of every positive-order derivative is zero. The fundamental theorem of calculus reduces that average to equal endpoint values of a periodic lower derivative. The theorem supplies the mean-zero condition needed when the normalized primitive is applied after phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.summary: Positive phase derivatives have zero mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_map.text: For a continuous profile and continuous linear map `L`, taking the phase average after applying `L` equals applying `L` to the phase average. Completeness ensures the relevant Bochner integrals behave as intended. This permits coordinate or multilinear evaluation to pass through the averaged profile.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_map.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with taking the phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.text: The phase average of $(B\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ vanishes when $Y$ is periodic with continuous derivative. Here $B$ and $\kappa$ do not depend on the phase variable. The statement uses the integral of a derivative over one period, and does not require either constant vector to vanish or be transverse.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.summary: A constant phase coefficient has zero derivative mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_periodicWaveBump_le.text: For $0<h\le1$, the phase mean of the periodic bump is at most $h/4$. The proof shifts integration to the centered cell and restricts it to the support interval of length $h/4$, where the bump is at most one. This supplies a positive lower bound for slope normalization.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_periodicWaveBump_le.summary: The bump mean is at most one quarter of its width

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phaseOscillation.text: For a continuous profile in a complete real normed space, the average of $f-\operatorname{phaseMean}(f)$ over the unit period is zero. Linearity of the integral and the unit interval length give the cancellation. Periodicity is not required for this identity, because only values on the integration interval enter the mean.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.text: For continuous $f:\mathbb R\to E$ in a real Banach space, define $F(s)=\int_0^s f(\sigma)\,d\sigma-\int_0^1\int_0^r f(\sigma)\,d\sigma\,dr$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1F(s)\,ds=0$. The averaging interval has length one, so subtracting that constant removes the mean exactly. For the Banach and finite-dimensional targets used in Appendix D this is the usual integral normalization. The declaration does not require the input to be periodic or to have zero average; those assumptions enter the separate result that makes $F$ periodic. Recovery of $f$ by differentiation is also a separate assertion.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.summary: Subtracting the mean makes the phase primitive have zero average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.text: Shows that averaging a one-periodic phase function after replacing phase by its negative gives the original mean. Orientation reversal and periodicity move the integral back to one period. This preserves the normalization used to identify reflected pressure primitives; integrability is supplied in the smooth applications, rather than asserted by this theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.summary: Reflection leaves a periodic phase average unchanged

TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.text: For a scalar one-periodic weight $u$ and a vector one-periodic profile $v$, both differentiable with continuous displayed derivatives, proves $\langle u v\prime\rangle=-\langle u\prime v\rangle$. The two periodicity hypotheses cancel the boundary term over $[0,1]$. Completeness is required for the vector-valued integral; no spatial derivative or zero-mean hypothesis is included.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.summary: Move a phase derivative by integration by parts

TorusEuler.phaseMean_sub.text: The phase mean of the difference of two continuous profiles is the difference of their phase means. This is used when separating the mean from the oscillation.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_forActiva.text: For any one-periodic vector function, translation of the phase leaves its mean over one period unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and applies periodicity. No continuity hypothesis appears in this identity; it is used to preserve the zero-mean condition when the centered wrapping introduces a label-dependent phase translation.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_forActiva.summary: A phase translation preserves the periodic mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.text: For a one-periodic phase function, translating its phase argument by any real number leaves the phase mean unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and uses periodicity. No separate integrability hypothesis appears in this algebraic identity; analytic uses have smooth phase slices so that the integral has its usual meaning.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.summary: A periodic phase average is invariant under translation

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePotential.text: For continuous $V$, the potential defined by taking the mean-adjusted primitive of the cross-product integrand has zero phase mean. This property holds for every fixed $\kappa$, with no transverse, periodic, or zero-mean assumption on $V$. Those stronger assumptions are needed for its intended periodic inverse-curl interpretation, not for the normalization itself.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePotential_refle.text: If the input velocity is continuous, periodic, and zero mean, then the phase-reflected potential also has zero phase mean. The proof changes variables in the integral and uses periodicity to move the interval back to a unit period. This fixes the constant when identifying reflected normalized primitives.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePotential_refle.summary: Reflecting a periodic potential preserves its zero mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti.text: For the constructed family and $0<h\le1$, the formal statement proves $\int_0^1P_h(s)\,ds=0$. The primitive is defined by integrating $F_h$ and subtracting the resulting phase mean, which chooses one function from the primitives differing by constants. This is the normalization used in Lemma 3.1 and the pressure formula (3.3). It is an average in the independent phase coordinate. Multiplying by a label-dependent coefficient and evaluating at a transported phase does not preserve a spatial mean-zero condition automatically; no such assertion about the full Eulerian pressure is made here.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti.summary: The phase normalization fixes the additive constant of the primitive

TorusEuler.phaseMean_waveProfile.text: For an admissible positive width h ≤ 1, the selected wave profile has zero average over one phase period. This normalization makes the oscillatory profile compatible with the hierarchy.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_waveSlope.text: For an admissible width, the normalized slope has zero mean over one period. The numerator subtracts exactly the bump’s own mean, and division by a constant preserves zero mean. This is the condition that makes the integral based at zero a periodic wave profile rather than a function with linear drift.

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.text:
The first letter of an ordered word is the outermost derivative.

Default-value audit (b5): The empty word is the identity on functions. Nonempty words use totalized Fréchet derivatives; analytic word identities require the stated smoothness of fields and directions.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.summary: Ordered directional derivatives of a profile

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_add.text: For two smooth functions and a list of constant parameter directions, the iterated directional word applied to their sum equals the sum of the two word values. Induction on the list uses additivity of the Fréchet derivative at each step. Smoothness is required so that the derivative operation is additive on the intermediate functions.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_add.summary: Constant directional words distribute over a sum

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_append.text: The derivative indexed by a concatenation `v ++ w` equals applying the derivative word `v` to the function already differentiated by `w`. This follows from the recursive definition and has no smoothness hypothesis. It is a syntactic composition identity, not a claim that different derivative orders commute.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_append.summary: Concatenated words compose their derivative operators

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_append_rela.text: The derivative operator associated with `w ++ v` equals the operator for `w` applied to the operator for `v`. This follows directly from the recursive definition of an ordered derivative word. No smoothness is required for the identity, though later exchanges or estimates of such derivatives impose it.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_append_rela.summary: Appending words composes their derivative operators

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.text: Exact ordered Leibniz formula for a real continuous bilinear operator, including application of an operator-valued coefficient to a vector field.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.summary: The exact ordered Leibniz formula for bilinear products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.text: Finite-order sup and difference bounds for a product. The hypotheses need only hold for subwords of the specified derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.summary: Finite sup and difference bounds for differentiated products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.text: Subtracting $B(f,D_wg)$ from the full derivative $D_w(B(f,g))$ leaves precisely those Leibniz terms with a derivative on $f$. Smoothness of the direction fields and both factors is explicit. Each remaining second word is shorter than $w$, providing the lower-order terms in the derivative-lifting argument.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.summary: Remove the highest derivative of the solution

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.text: A time weight may be applied to the field before taking any label or phase derivative at fixed time.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.summary: A fixed time weight commutes with spatial differentiation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.text: Smooth directional derivatives in constant real directions are unchanged by a permutation of the ordered coordinate word.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.summary: Constant directional derivatives are invariant under permutation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.text: For a smooth function, an ordered word of constant directional derivatives is its iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on the same ordered directions. This identifies the word calculus with the usual finite derivative norms.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.summary: Constant derivative words equal evaluated Fréchet derivatives

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.text: For a globally smooth function and a list `w` of constant directions, the repeated directional derivative equals the iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on those directions in the same order. The list length sets the derivative order. This identity converts the coordinate-word representation of hierarchy norms into an operator-norm estimate.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.summary: Ordered constant derivatives equal Fréchet derivative evaluation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.text: For a smooth function, successive derivatives in constant directions equal evaluation of the iterated Fréchet derivative on that ordered list. This is the word-to-tensor identification used by the differentiated ODE estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.summary: Constant words evaluate the Fréchet derivative tensor

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_zero_of_.text: If one direction field is identically zero and its letter occurs anywhere in a word, the derivative word evaluates to the zero function. No differentiability assumption is required for this total-derivative identity. It removes all words containing the phase letter when the profile depends only on labels.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_zero_of_.summary: A zero direction annihilates the entire derivative word

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eventuallyE.text: If two functions agree on a neighborhood of a point, then their corresponding directional-word functions agree on some neighborhood there for any finite word. The directions may depend on position in this lemma. Induction uses locality of the Fréchet derivative, enabling derivative vanishing outside a closed support from local equality with zero.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eventuallyE.summary: Local equality survives repeated directional differentiation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_fst_of_cons.text: For a smooth label function pulled back along the first projection, a derivative word in constant label-phase directions equals the corresponding word in their label projections. The resulting function is again pulled back to label-phase space. This identifies how mixed words act on a profile that is genuinely independent of phase.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_fst_of_cons.summary: Project each mixed direction onto the label space

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.text: Each weighted label derivative introduces one factor of the label radius.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.summary: Each weighted label derivative contributes the radius

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.text: A list `w` of smooth directional operators maps an order-`N` profile bound to an order-`n` bound when `hn` ensures $n+|w|\le N$. Each step contributes at most $2^NC$. The resulting constant is $(2^NC)^{|w|}M$, and the order of the operators is preserved by the list.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.summary: A word of derivatives consumes its length in regularity

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.text: Parameter word derivatives of a linear solve satisfy the time derivative of the differentiated right-hand side, including at both slab endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.summary: Spatial derivative words satisfy the differentiated time equation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_map_letters.text: Mapping a word’s letters through `e` before applying the derivative-word operator is the same as replacing the direction family by its composition with `e`. This algebraic identity has no smoothness hypothesis. It is used when identifying the three label letters inside the four-letter mixed alphabet.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_map_letters.summary: Relabeling a word relabels its derivative directions

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.text: Replacing each smooth direction field $D_i$ by the constant scalar multiple $r_iD_i$ multiplies the word derivative by the product of its letter weights. The weights depend on the index, not on position. For coordinate directions this accounts for the factors $\ell^m h^j$ in the finite norm.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.summary: Coordinate weights multiply along the derivative word

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_zero.text: A word of constant directional derivatives applied to the zero function is zero, including the empty word. The proof proceeds by induction on the list. This is used for zero initial data and for localized solutions outside their support, where every derivative of the identically zero field vanishes.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_zero.summary: Every directional word annihilates the zero function

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.text: The formal definition gives $f^\circ(s)=f(s)-\int_0^1f(r)\,dr$. This is the decomposition used for $H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s$ in (1.12); it subtracts a vector independent of phase at each fixed time and label. For an integrable period-one profile, the result has zero phase average and remains periodic. Those conditions are not required merely to write the formula: if the integral is not defined in the usual sense, the formal integral has a default value. The paper's smooth profiles are integrable, so the intended mean and oscillatory split applies.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.summary: Subtract the phase mean at each fixed time and label

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.text: Let $c(a,s)\in\mathbb R^3$ be smooth and one-periodic in $s$. At the label considered, assume $\operatorname{div}_a c+k_*\cdot\partial_s c=0$ for every phase. Write $\bar c=\int_0^1c\,ds$ and $c_{\rm osc}=c-\bar c$. Then $\operatorname{div}_a\bar c=0$ and $k_*\cdot c_{\rm osc}=-\partial_s^{-1}\operatorname{div}_a c_{\rm osc}$, where $\partial_s^{-1}$ is the periodic primitive with zero phase mean. This is the identity used in Lemma 5.10 to estimate the longitudinal oscillation through label derivatives. The statement is spatial at one label and does not assume a time evolution, a small norm, or nonzero $k_*$.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.summary: Recover the oscillatory longitudinal component by a zero mean primitive

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_map.text: Applying a continuous linear map to a continuous profile commutes with subtracting its phase mean, at every phase `s`. The identity combines linearity with commutation of `L` and the integral. It allows scalar or coordinate bounds to be applied directly to the oscillatory part of a mixed derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_map.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with the oscillatory part

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive.text: For a phase function $f$, write $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$. The formal definition is $\partial_s^{-1}f=J-\int_0^1J(s)\,ds$. Thus its normalization is zero phase mean, not value zero at phase zero. For a continuous period-one $f$ with zero mean, it is the period-one primitive used in (3.5), with derivative $f$. A nonzero mean causes drift and cannot be removed by subtracting an additive constant. The formula is also assigned values for inputs lacking ordinary integrability, because the formal integral has a default zero value there; no primitive or periodicity claim follows in those cases.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive.summary: Integrate from zero and subtract the mean of that integral

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_add_phase.text: For a continuous, one-periodic, zero-mean profile, shifting the input phase shifts its normalized primitive by the same amount. The zero-mean assumption ensures that the primitive itself is periodic. Uniqueness of the zero-mean antiderivative then removes the otherwise possible additive constant.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_add_phase.summary: The normalized primitive commutes with phase translation

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_const_smul.text: Multiplying a scalar phase function by a fixed real scalar before taking its mean-corrected primitive is the same as multiplying the primitive afterward. The proof unfolds phase oscillation and uses linearity of the interval integral and phase mean. It is an algebraic helper in the normalized-pressure estimate, without smoothness or nonzero-scalar assumptions.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_const_smul.summary: Scalar multiplication commutes with the normalized phase primitive

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.text: Assuming `hderiv` gives a derivative $df$ of $f$ at every phase and `hdf` makes it continuous, proves $\operatorname{phasePrimitive}(df)=f-\operatorname{phaseMean}(f)$. The primitive starts at zero and then has its own mean removed. The identity does not require periodicity; periodicity is an additional condition when interpreting this operation as the inverse phase derivative.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.summary: A primitive recovers the profile without its mean

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_map.text: A continuous linear map passes through both the anchored phase integral and the mean subtraction that defines the normalized primitive. The profile is assumed continuous, so these integrals are well-defined in the complete target spaces. The conclusion is pointwise in phase and does not add periodicity hypotheses.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_map.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with the normalized primitive

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_translate_forA.text: For a continuous one-periodic function with zero phase mean, the normalized primitive of its phase translate evaluated at zero equals the original normalized primitive at the translating phase. The proof compares derivatives and uses the zero mean of the primitive. This formulation turns a moving evaluation phase into a parameter of the integrand.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_translate_forA.summary: The normalized primitive commutes with phase translation

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.text: The primitive of the potential time source for `freq • k` is exactly `freq⁻¹` times the primitive for `k`, with positive frequency. The statement is an equality of normalized phase integrals, not a derivative assertion. It combines the source’s algebraic homogeneity with linearity of the primitive.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.summary: Phase integration preserves the inverse-frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.text: Phase normalization determines the additive constant of a primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.summary: The phase mean fixes the primitive constant

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text:
Extend a profile by shifting its phase with its lattice translation.

Default-value audit (b5): The centered representative jumps across cell walls. This raw extension is periodic with the matching phase shift but need not be smooth; compact support away from the walls is used by the smooth-extension theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension with the matching phase shift

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The extension agrees with the profile on the entire closed cell.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If simultaneous label and phase reflection transforms a profile by a zero-preserving map `L`, and the profile vanishes on every negative cell wall, its twisted extension has the same reflection law. The wall condition handles the centered representative’s half-open boundary convention. The map `L` need not be linear for this algebraic result, only satisfy `L 0 = 0`.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Wall vanishing preserves reflection through the twisted extension

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: Evaluating the phase-twisted extension at label `A t x` and phase $\langle k,A(t,x)\rangle$ gives exactly the localized transported profile. The phase shift cancels the uncentered label contribution, leaving the graph phase at the centered representative. This is an identity for arbitrary maps, profiles and real covectors; it does not require smoothness, periodicity or an integer frequency.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted profile agrees with its transported phase evaluation

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If each original label slice has a specified phase period, the twisted periodized profile has that same phase period. The period need not equal one in this general statement.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Twisted periodization preserves a supplied phase period

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: When the positive envelope radius leaves a strict collar before the cell walls, the twisted extension equals the original enveloped profile at every point of the closed centered cell and every phase. This includes boundary points that have different centered representatives, since the envelope vanishes there. The equality does not require smoothness of the underlying profile.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees throughout the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The envelope confines the extension to the translates of its original support ball.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The periodized envelope stays near lattice points

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: For a positive envelope radius with $2\ell\le1/2$, multiplying a profile by the radial envelope preserves any simultaneous label-phase reflection represented by a continuous linear map `L`. The twisted extension inherits that same law. The weak radius inequality suffices because only zero values at the cell walls are needed; smooth gluing elsewhere uses a strict inequality.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The radial envelope preserves a linear reflection law

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The twisted periodization is invariant when labels and phase are shifted together by the lattice vector and its pairing with k. The identity is valid for the raw extension; smoothness across cell walls is a separate result.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The extension respects simultaneous lattice and phase shifts

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost.text: Assume $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, a nonnegative integer $a$, $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$. Then $\ell_*^{-1}+h^{-1}|k_*|\le2\mathsf D^{\max(a,1)}\lambda^{3/2}$. This is the scalar estimate behind the derivative cost in Lemma 5.7: a label derivative contributes $\ell_*^{-1}$ and a phase derivative contributes $h^{-1}|k_*|$. The derivative of the inverse flow contributes another factor separately. The formal inequality contains no profile, function norm or chain rule, so those analytic identifications must be supplied before applying it to a physical field.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost.summary: Combine the label scale and the carrier divided by phase width

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.text: If `RV` is exactly the depth tail plus `chiPrime` times the primary field, and both have the stated two-jet bounds, its first half-Hölder norm is bounded by $C_{step}\lambda^2(\lambda^{-2P/3}+S)$. The hypotheses control $|\chi^{\prime}|\gamma$ by `S` and absorb both numerical constants into `Cstep`. The final power is enlarged from $7/4$ to two.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.summary: Depth and activation errors combine in the residual norm

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.text: Supplied jets through order `m + 1` yield half-Hölder bounds for both oscillation and mean. With $\lambda\ge1$ and $0\le\gamma\le1$, the oscillation has exponent $3(m+1)/2-5/4$, while the mean retains $-5/2$. The theorem combines exponents and converts jets to norms; it assumes the preceding physical jet estimates.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.summary: Oscillation and mean retain their distinct Hölder frequency rates

TorusEuler.physicalMeanWordScalar_rearra.text: An exact polynomial identity rewrites the nested product from the mean estimate into an order-dependent factor times $R d^2 f$. It holds for arbitrary real arguments, without sign assumptions. The purpose is to identify the defined finite order constant before applying the separate inequality that bounds inverse and radius losses by a power of $D$.
TorusEuler.physicalMeanWordScalar_rearra.summary: Separate the scalar factors in the mean bound

TorusEuler.physicalMean_labels_periodic.text: For any time-dependent function on torus labels, its Euclidean evaluation through `toUnitTorus` is periodic at a fixed time. The codomain is arbitrary and no continuity is needed. This supplies periodicity of the deformation and gradient lifts when smooth coefficient representations are built for the physical mean inverse.
TorusEuler.physicalMean_labels_periodic.summary: Label evaluation gives a periodic physical lift

TorusEuler.physicalWave_next_frequency.text: Rewrites the frequency two stages ahead as the current scheduled child frequency raised to the next scheduled exponent. The proof uses the defining frequency recurrence twice. This identity aligns the cutoff error estimate, whose parameters are written as powers of the parent frequency, with the induction’s indexed next frequency.
TorusEuler.physicalWave_next_frequency.summary: Express the next frequency by two scheduled powers

TorusEuler.physicalWave_schedule.text: From an initial frequency at least two, obtains the same lower bound for the parent frequency, monotonicity from the current to the next derivative order, and $\max\{2,\mathrm{order}\}\le\mathrm{depth}$. The depth is six times the next frequency exponent. These inequalities justify using the cutoff tail at order two and at every order required by the induction.
TorusEuler.physicalWave_schedule.summary: The scheduled depth covers the requested derivative order

TorusEuler.physicalWave_slice_smooth.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field on `[0,T] × Vec3` to a slab time gives a smooth spatial field on all of `Vec3`. The theorem is polymorphic in the target normed space. It supplies differentiability and Hölder regularity inputs for the Fourier cutoff and central-gradient calculations.
TorusEuler.physicalWave_slice_smooth.summary: Smooth physical fields have smooth time slices

TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.text: Let $w(y)=F(k\cdot y)\mathbf a$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$. If $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$, the formal statement proves $(w\cdot\nabla)w(x)=0$. This is the self-advection cancellation used in §1.1 and Lemma 2.1. It is a spatial identity at a fixed point; no time equation, nonzero vector assumption or global profile regularity is needed. The statement gives the zero conclusion directly, while the paper also displays the intermediate expression $(k\cdot\mathbf a)FF'\mathbf a$.
TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.summary: A transverse plane wave has no self-advection at a differentiable phase

TorusEuler.potentialCrossLinear.text: Packages $v \mapsto  (x \mapsto  v \times  x)$ as a continuous linear map from vectors to continuous linear operators. Linearity follows from the cross product identities, and continuity follows from the estimate $\lVert v \times  x\rVert  \le  \lVert v\rVert \cdot \lVert x\rVert$. This representation lets iterated derivative estimates treat the potential coefficient through ordinary operator composition.
TorusEuler.potentialCrossLinear.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: If the newest covector is nonzero, its scale is positive, and its third scaled coordinate in the preceding frame is at least one half, a bound on its scaled length gives a lower bound for its normalized projection against the preceding curl. The formula uses the actual cross product, with its sign retained.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The newest direction detects a positive preceding curl component

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: Combining coordinate bounds, window length at most $CL^4$, logarithmic loss $L^8\le\mu^{1/8}$, and preceding strength at least $c\mu^{1/4}$ gives a signed curl projection of at least $c\mu^{1/8}/(6C^2)$. Nonzero perpendicular preceding data and positive frequency scales are explicit. The conclusion retains `c` as supplied; its positivity is not assumed here.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The projected preceding curl grows as a positive frequency power

TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o.text: Let $\mu\ge1$ and $r-l\le\mu^{-1/16}$. On $[l,r]$, assume nonzero transverse $\kappa,\mathbf a$ solve $\dot\kappa=-B^T\kappa$ and $\dot{\mathbf a}=-B\mathbf a+2\langle\kappa,B\mathbf a\rangle\kappa/|\kappa|^2$, with trace-free $B$ and $\|B\|\le\mu^{1/32}$. Then for every $t\in[l,r]$, $|\kappa(t)||\mathbf a(t)|\ge e^{-1}|\kappa(l)||\mathbf a(l)|$. Derivatives at the endpoints are taken within the closed interval. Nonvanishing makes the denominator and the logarithm of the strength legitimate. The formal statement makes the fixed loss explicit; it gives a lower bound, not conservation of strength. In Proposition 8.2 one takes $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ and $[l,r]=[t_j,t_{j+1}]$.
TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o.summary: A short interval limits the multiplicative loss of wave strength

TorusEuler.pressureAssemblyTensorEntry.text: This private complex linear functional selects entry $(i,j)$ from a pressure tensor. It makes coordinate extraction commute with tensor integrals and preserves smoothness of the selected spatial component. These facts allow the physical double-divergence equation to be compared with the Fourier pressure symbol component by component.
TorusEuler.pressureAssemblyTensorEntry.summary: Extract a tensor component for periodic integration by parts

TorusEuler.pressureConvolutionJetMap.text: This bounded real bilinear map applies a complex-linear operator to the output of a real multilinear spatial jet. Restricting scalars preserves the operator norm, and composition leaves the spatial arguments unchanged. It is the integrand map for differentiating the operator-valued convolution kernel against a smooth complex tensor field.
TorusEuler.pressureConvolutionJetMap.summary: An operator acts on the output of a spatial jet

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.text: For an integer frequency $k$ and a complex vector coefficient $a\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal definition multiplies the divergence coefficient $2\pi i\,k\cdot a$ by the inverse Laplacian coefficient $-1/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$. At nonzero $k$, this gives the scalar coefficient of $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}v$ in the paper’s Leray formula. At $k=0$, inversion of zero is defined to be zero, so the scalar correction vanishes and its mean is fixed. The contraction $k\cdot a$ is complex-linear in $a$, with no complex conjugation. The definition alone does not construct a spatial pressure or establish convergence of a Fourier series.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.summary: The inverse Laplacian fixes the scalar zero mode

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.text: For every complex vector coefficient $a\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal theorem states that the scalar pressure correction at frequency $k=0$ is zero. This follows from the Fourier definition of $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$, which assigns the inverse Laplacian the value zero on the constant mode. It is the normalization used for the scalar potential in $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. It does not set the velocity’s constant coefficient to zero: the Leray projection preserves constant divergence-free velocities.
