Nor does this single coefficient identity assert the full spatial projection formula or establish a solution of the Euler equations.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.summary: The Fourier coefficient at zero is exactly zero

TorusEuler.pressureGraph_spaceSlice.text: A jointly smooth field on the closed slab has a smooth spatial slice at every slab time. This private helper is used for physical graph fields before differentiating their pressures. The entire spatial domain is available, so the derivative is ordinary spatial differentiation even when the selected time is an endpoint.
TorusEuler.pressureGraph_spaceSlice.summary: The graph field has smooth spatial slices

TorusEuler.pressureGraph_timeSlice.text: At a fixed spatial point and a time in the closed slab, joint smoothness implies differentiability of the time slice within that interval. This makes the temporal derivative in the physical momentum identity well defined at both endpoints. The theorem does not extend the field to an open time neighborhood.
TorusEuler.pressureGraph_timeSlice.summary: The graph field has a within-slab time derivative

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.text: Defines the real angular operator $I-\mathbb P(\xi)$, which projects onto the frequency direction for nonzero $\xi$. Its value at zero is zero because the Leray symbol there is the identity. This is the angular part of $D^2\Delta^{-1}$; the definition alone does not identify any field as an actual pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.summary: The pressure projection onto the frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.text: Applying the angular pressure operator to $v$ gives $(\langle\xi,v\rangle/\|\xi\|^2)\xi$. The formula is valid also at zero under Lean’s total division convention, where both sides vanish. To interpret it as projection onto a one-dimensional direction one must additionally have $\xi\ne0$.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.summary: The pressure projection is the longitudinal component

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_lattic.text: At an integer frequency `k`, the entry obtained by applying the angular operator to coordinate vector `j` and reading coordinate `i` is $k_jk_i/|k|^2$. `frequencyNormSq` is the squared lattice norm. The formula includes the zero frequency through total division, giving zero there.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_lattic.summary: Read a matrix entry of the lattice pressure symbol

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.text: The angular pressure operator is even in its frequency argument: replacing $\xi$ by $-\xi$ leaves it unchanged. This includes zero. The identity is used to pair positive and negative Fourier modes when proving the real cosine and sine moment formula; it is not a regularity statement about the symbol.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.summary: Opposite frequencies have the same pressure projection

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.text: For `hc : 0 < c`, the angular pressure operator at $c\xi$ equals that at $\xi$. Thus the operator depends on the frequency direction, not its positive magnitude. The theorem includes $\xi=0$ but excludes a zero scaling factor, which would collapse a nonzero frequency to the distinguished zero mode.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.summary: Positive rescaling leaves the pressure projection unchanged

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.text: The angular pressure operator is zero at frequency zero. This is the intended Fourier convention for a Hessian, which cannot contain a nonzero constant Fourier mode when obtained by differentiating a periodic potential. The declaration is a symbol identity; the later Poisson comparison proves that the constructed multiplier has the corresponding physical meaning.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.summary: The pressure Hessian has zero constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier.text: This is the continuous linear operator $D^2\Delta^{-1}:C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)\to C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$. At a nonzero frequency $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ it multiplies the scalar Fourier coefficient by $\xi\otimes\xi/|\xi|^2$; its zero-frequency value is zero. Thus constants are discarded, as required when the inverse Laplacian is normalized on the torus. Both function spaces use finite half-Hölder norms. The declaration supplies boundedness and the chosen multiplier, not a Poisson equation for a particular pressure. To identify its output with $D^2q$, Lemma 5.9 uses the equation satisfied by the summed mean pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier.summary: Define the bounded multiplier and remove its zero Fourier mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.text: If a periodic $C^2$ potential has Laplacian represented by `f` and Hessian represented by the half-Hölder operator field `H`, then the multiplier output is exactly `H`. The theorem requires these representation hypotheses; it does not create the potential or assume an arbitrary source is a periodic Laplacian. Entrywise Fourier uniqueness proves the equality.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.summary: Identify the multiplier with the actual pressure Hessian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.text: The real Fourier moment of the Hessian output equals the corresponding scalar input moment multiplied by the angular pressure operator at that frequency. The complex parameter `c` encodes both cosine and sine tests. Evenness of the symbol allows the positive and negative modes to combine, establishing a real-valued identity without selecting a pressure potential.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.summary: The real multiplier acts on cosine and sine moments

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.text: At each real frequency, constructs a complex-linear map taking a scalar Fourier coefficient to that coefficient times the complexified angular pressure operator. The result is operator-valued, so its coordinate entries represent the Hessian entries. Boundedness of the resulting periodic operator and agreement with a Poisson solution are later theorems.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.summary: The complex symbol converts a scalar to a Hessian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_apply.text: Unfolds the complex symbol as scalar multiplication of the complexified angular projection. This identity is valid for every frequency and complex scalar. It exposes the exact action used in the Fourier coefficient calculations, without requiring the scalar to be real or the frequency to be nonzero.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.text: Each lattice-frequency matrix entry of the pressure symbol equals the two Fourier derivative factors times `inverseLaplacianMode` and the scalar input. The proof handles `k = 0` separately before cancelling the nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue. This fixes the sign and the $2\pi$ normalization of the intended operator at every frequency.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.summary: The symbol equals two derivatives and an inverse Laplacian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_neg.text: The scalar-to-operator symbol is unchanged when the real frequency is negated. This follows from evenness of the underlying real angular projection and is valid including at zero. It supports the comparison of conjugate Fourier modes needed to recover a real operator from real source data.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.text: Positive rescaling of the real frequency leaves the complex pressure symbol unchanged. The explicit hypothesis `hc` excludes scaling by zero; no restriction on the scalar input to the symbol is needed. This homogeneity is passed to the periodic half-Hölder Fourier multiplier construction.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.summary: The complex pressure symbol has degree zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.text: At the zero frequency, the complex scalar-to-operator symbol is the zero continuous linear map. This eliminates the constant mode before any Fourier reconstruction. It records a deliberate normalization for the Hessian multiplier rather than a statement that arbitrary sources have zero mean.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.summary: The complex pressure symbol vanishes at zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.text: Let the Hessian operator split into leading, geometric, higher and mean pieces. A signed leading upper bound at scale $\mathrm{freq}^{-1/4}$ and nonnegative norm bounds for the other three pieces at faster decays give a common signed upper bound with summed constants. The theorem never deduces a norm bound for the leading piece or the total Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.summary: Combine one signed contribution with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.pressureJet_periodic.text: Every iterated Fréchet derivative of a spatially periodic function is spatially periodic. Translation by a fixed lattice vector has identity derivative, so differentiating the equality of translated functions preserves each jet. The statement does not require smoothness: it is an identity of the totalized derivative expressions, with regularity supplied by callers.

TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock.text: The block at scale $2^j$ convolves the input tensor with the inverse Fourier kernel of the annular pressure symbol. This is a scalar complex field on the Euclidean lift. Its kernel is integrable and has zero mean; bounded smooth inputs later allow differentiation and a summable half-moment estimate.
TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock.summary: One dyadic pressure block acts by Euclidean convolution

TorusEuler.pressureNearBlockMass.text: This nonnegative real number integrates the operator-kernel norm weighted by $\sqrt{\|y\|}$. It records exactly the moment needed after replacing a bounded Lipschitz jet by its half Hölder difference bound. Scaling makes these moments decay geometrically with the dyadic index, so their series is finite.
TorusEuler.pressureNearBlockMass.summary: The half moment measures one dyadic pressure block

TorusEuler.pressureNearBlockMass_nonneg.text: The integrand defining the block mass is a product of a norm and the nonnegative square root of a norm, so its integral is nonnegative. This estimate needs no strict positivity. It is used when summing block bounds and constructing an everywhere positive denominator for the uniform convergence estimate.

TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock_integrableK.text: The inverse Fourier transform of the annular pressure symbol is a Schwartz kernel, hence integrable. Dilation by the positive factor $2^j$ preserves integrability with the dimensional normalization in `scaledMultiplierKernel`. This establishes a property of the kernel alone; input-dependent integrability is proved separately.
TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock_integrableK.summary: Every dyadic pressure kernel is integrable

TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock_meanZero.text: Every dyadic pressure kernel has integral zero because its compact Fourier symbol vanishes at frequency zero. The positive scale normalization preserves that integral identity. This cancellation permits subtracting the input jet at $x$ inside convolution and is the source of the extra decaying half-moment factor.
TorusEuler.pressureNearBlock_meanZero.summary: The annular pressure kernel has zero integral

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_complexLaplac.text: The complex Laplacian of a real $C^2$ pressure, viewed as complex-valued, equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real gradient. The proof compares each diagonal coordinate derivative and sums them. This prevents a sign or coordinate convention from being hidden in the transition to Fourier Poisson uniqueness.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_complexLaplac.summary: The complexified Laplacian is the real pressure divergence

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_complexTensor.text: For a $C^2$ real velocity, double divergence of its complex pressure tensor equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real momentum tensor divergence. The proof expands both coordinate sums and uses commutation of complex inclusion with mixed derivatives. No incompressibility is needed for this representation identity; it is used later to identify tensor divergence with advection.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_complexTensor.summary: The complex source equals real momentum double divergence

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_coordHessian_.text: For a real $C^2$ scalar field, its complex inclusion has coordinate second derivatives equal to the complex inclusion of the original mixed partials. The proof applies the first-derivative compatibility twice, using $C^2$ regularity to make the first coordinate derivative $C^1$. This transfers the real pressure equation to complex coordinates.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_coordHessian_.summary: Complex inclusion preserves the mixed coordinate derivatives

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_coord_divTens.text: For a $C^2$ field valued in `MomentumTensor`, component $i$ of its tensor divergence is the sum over $j$ of the derivative of component `(j,i)` in direction $e_j$. Coordinate projection commutes with differentiation by the chain rule. The explicit ordering matches the momentum tensor’s column representation.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_coord_divTens.summary: Tensor divergence is the sum of coordinate derivatives

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_fderiv_ofReal.text: At a point where a real scalar field is differentiable, the real Fréchet derivative of its complex inclusion evaluated on a vector is the complex inclusion of its real derivative. This is the chain rule for `Complex.ofRealCLM`. The differentiability premise rules out reading a totalized derivative as an unsupported classical derivative.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_fderiv_ofReal.summary: Complex inclusion commutes with a real spatial derivative

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_leray_fixed_d.text: If a smooth periodic vector field is fixed by the periodic Leray lift, its divergence vanishes everywhere. The proof descends the field to the bundled half Hölder space, interprets the fixed point as solenoidality, then uses the smooth gradient-pairing characterization. Smooth periodicity ensures the raw lift is operating on its valid analytic domain.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_leray_fixed_d.summary: A smooth periodic fixed point of Leray is divergence free

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_slice.text: A jointly smooth field on the half-open Euler slab has a smooth spatial slice at every time in that slab. The proof composes with the map $x\mapsto(t,x)$ and removes the unrestricted spatial domain from `ContDiffOn`. The time may be zero, since no ambient time differentiation is used here.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_slice.summary: Joint smoothness restricts to a smooth spatial slice

TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_timeDerivativ.text: For an Euler solution and a time in `Ico 0 T`, the spatial divergence of its within-time velocity derivative is zero. A nondegenerate closed prefix containing the time allows differentiating the Leray fixed-point relation, including at time zero. Joint smoothness and periodicity of the derivative then convert its fixed-point property to pointwise zero divergence.
TorusEuler.pressurePoisson_timeDerivativ.summary: The within-time derivative remains divergence free

TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.text: The fixed dyadic cutoff localizes the pressure symbol into a compactly supported smooth operator-valued symbol, packaged as a Schwartz map. The cutoff removes the singular frequency origin before the Schwartz construction. Its inverse Fourier transform is the building block for the actual periodic far pressure kernel.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.summary: The pressure symbol is localized to one smooth frequency annulus

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.text: The double divergence of a complex tensor field is $\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j a_{ij}$, expressed using the coordinate Hessian entries. It is the source with a minus sign in the normalized pressure Poisson equation. The definition fixes the coordinate order used in the Fourier symbol and in the real Euler comparison.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.summary: Contract both spatial derivatives of the tensor source

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.text: The real pressure lift is the real part of the complex dyadic pressure sum. For smooth periodic tensor fields it is smooth and agrees with the actual half Hölder pressure multiplier. Its identification with a prescribed pressure additionally requires the periodic Poisson equation and zero spatial mean.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.summary: Take the real pressure produced by the dyadic series

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.text: If a half Hölder torus tensor `q` pulls back pointwise to a smooth periodic lift `f`, their real pressures agree pointwise after lifting. Finite dyadic convolutions converge both to the block sum and to the bounded multiplier output. The representative premise `hq` is explicit; the theorem does not select an arbitrary torus representative.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.summary: The smooth dyadic construction equals the bounded torus multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.text: For a smooth periodic tensor and a $C^2$ periodic complex pressure solving its Poisson equation with zero mean, the real dyadic lift is exactly the real part of that pressure. Smoothness provides the tensor’s half Hölder torus representative, continuity provides the pressure representative, and Fourier uniqueness identifies them. The equation alone would leave an additive constant.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.summary: The dyadic pressure equals the normalized Poisson solution

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_sub.text: For two smooth periodic tensor inputs, the pressure lift of their difference equals the difference of their pressure lifts. The proof descends both to half Hölder torus fields, uses the multiplier agreement theorem and its linearity, then lifts back. These hypotheses ensure that raw infinite sums and integrals represent the genuine linear operator.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_sub.summary: Pressure subtraction follows from bounded multiplier linearity

TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.text: This bounded real operator composes the complex pressure tensor multiplier with pointwise real part. It accepts complex tensor fields but returns a real half Hölder field. For tensors built from real velocities, later Fourier Poisson uniqueness identifies this output with the actual normalized Euler pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.summary: The real pressure is the real part of the complex multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.text: This real continuous linear map converts a complex-linear tensor-to-scalar operator into a real-linear one by taking the real part of its output. The input tensor remains complex. This lets the periodized complex Fourier kernel produce real pressure values without changing the source coordinate convention.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.summary: Take the real scalar output of a complex tensor operator

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.text: Applying the converted tensor operator to a complex tensor returns the real part of the original complex result. This definitional identity is used to commute the real-output map with integrals and to compare real pressure with its complex Fourier representation. It asserts no symmetry of the input tensor.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.summary: The real output map is pointwise real part

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.text: The scalar operator sends a tensor to $-\sum_{i,j}\xi_i\xi_j A_{ij}/\|\xi\|^2$. It is the symbol of $-\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div}$ with zero constant mode. The negative sign is essential for the pressure Poisson equation, and the finite tensor coordinate functionals make the operator continuous.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.summary: The normalized pressure symbol contracts the tensor twice

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.text: Applying the pressure symbol equals the negative finite double sum of weighted tensor entries. This expands the bundled continuous linear operator into coordinates. The formula is valid at zero as well, where all weights vanish; nonzero-frequency inversion is justified in later Fourier-mode identities.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.summary: The symbol has the explicit double contraction formula

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: At a lattice frequency, applying the scalar pressure symbol equals negative inverse Laplacian mode times the double-divergence Fourier contraction. The formula holds at zero with the prescribed normalization. This gives the exact modal interpretation of the abstract angular symbol used to build the bounded multiplier.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure symbol solves the Fourier Poisson equation

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: The pressure symbol applied to a tensor equals the negative scalar pressure-correction mode of its single divergence. This aligns the tensor convention with the existing Leray decomposition. The sign means the projected tensor divergence is the unprojected divergence plus the gradient of this normalized pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure scalar has the opposite complement sign

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_neg.text: Changing the frequency vector to its negative leaves the pressure operator unchanged. Each weight contains two coordinate factors and a squared norm. This parity matches the real pressure operator and is distinct from a parity assumption on the tensor field to which the multiplier is applied.

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.text: Positive scaling of the frequency vector leaves the pressure symbol unchanged. The proof transfers the homogeneity of each angular weight through the finite sum of coordinate operators. This is the degree-zero homogeneity premise needed to identify the dyadically constructed multiplier with its claimed Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.summary: The pressure multiplier depends only on frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.text: The pressure symbol at frequency zero is the zero operator. This follows from the chosen coordinate quotient convention and is used to normalize pressure and remove any constant-mode term from the far-kernel formula. It does not invert the Laplacian at zero; it prescribes the missing mode.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.summary: The pressure symbol removes the constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight.text: The coordinate weight is $\xi_i\xi_j/\|\xi\|^2$. Away from zero it is a smooth function of direction and unchanged by positive dilation. At zero Lean’s division convention makes the weight zero. The pressure symbol sums these weights with a minus sign against the tensor entries.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight.summary: The angular weight of the pressure symbol

TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight_lattice.text: At an integer frequency, the complex pressure weight equals the product of the two Fourier derivative symbols and the inverse Laplacian mode. The proof treats zero separately and cancels the $2\pi i$ factors for nonzero frequency. This checks both the normalization convention and the signs of the Fourier calculation.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight_lattice.summary: Angular weights match derivative and inverse Laplacian factors

TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight_pos_smul.text: The pressure weight at `c • ξ` equals its value at `ξ` whenever `c > 0`. The two numerator and denominator powers of `c` cancel. This includes the zero frequency under the totalized convention, while positivity guarantees the cancellation factor is nonzero.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorWeight_pos_smul.summary: Positive scaling leaves the angular pressure weight unchanged

TorusEuler.pressureTraceCLM.text: Defines the trace of a real spatial operator by summing its three diagonal coordinate entries. Bundling this as a continuous linear map permits it to act on half-Hölder fields while preserving the function-space structure. The following lemmas identify it with the algebraic trace and bound its norm by three.

TorusEuler.pressureTraceCLM_apply.text: Identifies the bundled coordinate-sum map with `LinearMap.trace` of the underlying linear map. The proof uses the standard Euclidean basis. This allows the Hölder-space construction of the source to be compared with the matrix trace in the pressure Poisson equation without changing the trace convention.

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: Defines the scalar half-Hölder field $\operatorname{tr}(U^2)-\operatorname{tr}(V^2)$ from two operator-valued fields. The products are composition of operators, not entrywise multiplication. The definition is algebraic; it becomes the pressure source’s quadratic difference only when `U` and `V` are identified as the two velocity gradients.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Compare the traces of the two gradient squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: With `hD : D = U - V`, rewrites the trace-square difference as the trace of $DV+UD$. This exact identity is valid for noncommuting operator fields. It makes the small cutoff-gradient difference appear once in each term, which is the structure needed for the pressure error estimate.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Factor the square difference without commuting matrices

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At each label, the scalar field evaluates to the difference of the traces of the two operator squares. This exposes the definition’s actual order of composition and trace convention. No assumption that either input is a derivative is used, so the identity remains an algebraic one until the physical representations are supplied.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Evaluate the traces of the operator squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At a fixed label and with `D = U - V`, the trace-square difference equals $\operatorname{tr}(DV)+\operatorname{tr}(UD)$. This is the pointwise form of the field factorization. It neither commutes the operator factors nor identifies `D` as a derivative unless that interpretation is furnished externally.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Read the cutoff difference inside the trace

TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.text: The tensor field at $x$ has complex coordinates $v_i(x)v_j(x)$, using the bounded bilinear velocity tensor map on the diagonal. It is the source of the pressure double divergence. Reality and symmetry follow from the diagonal real input, while smoothness and periodicity are established separately from properties of $v$.
TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.summary: Form the quadratic velocity source for pressure

TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.text: If `g` is the actual continuous gradient of a scalar field $p$, then $p(x)-p(0)$ equals the integral of $\langle g(sx),x\rangle$ from zero to one. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus along the radial segment. Periodicity and mean normalization are unnecessary for this difference identity.
TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.summary: Recover pressure differences along radial lines

TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.text: The order-`m` cost multiplies $4^m$, the four-direction product constant, and the parent’s finite coefficient-order constant. The factors account respectively for conversion to scaled Fréchet jets, the product estimate, and the inverse-coframe norm. The following lemmas use this fixed-order coefficient when turning a profile seminorm into a pullback derivative bound.
TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.summary: The finite cost of applying the inverse coframe

TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost_nonneg.text: If every value of the parent coefficient-cost function is nonnegative, the coframe cost is nonnegative at each order. The proof combines positivity of $4^m$, the finite product constant, and the coefficient-order sum. This arithmetic helper justifies multiplying inequalities in the subsequent scaled-jet estimates; it does not bound the inverse coframe itself.
TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost_nonneg.summary: Nonnegative coefficient costs give a nonnegative product budget

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.text: The common coefficient adds the oscillatory and mean costs and a further $1+C(1)$ allowance for the cutoff tail after applying the inverse coframe. It packages the three contributions without taking another maximum. Under nonnegative coefficient and level costs it is at least one, as the next theorem proves.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.summary: One coefficient pays for both profiles and the added tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.text: The chosen exponent is six times the hierarchy loss exponent plus eight. It dominates the oscillatory exponent $2r+1$, the mean exponent $6r+1$, and the cutoff-coframe exponent eight. This permits one parent power in the final pullback-jet record while retaining different frequency decay rates for the oscillation and mean.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.summary: One parent exponent covers both profiles and the cutoff tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.text: The mean coefficient uses the first-order coframe cost, the number of retained levels, and the common level constant. Only one mean term is counted per level, unlike the two oscillatory contributions. Its first-order choice matches the mean field required by the corrected pullback-jet interface used in the deformation argument.
TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the mean cost

TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.text: The oscillatory coefficient is the second-order coframe cost times twice the number of retained levels and the common level constant. The factor two comes from summing both transverse oscillations and their completion corrections. The count is exactly the cardinality of the natural interval from one through the chosen depth.
TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the oscillatory cost

TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.text: The profile width lies in the range of Lemma 3.1. Its product with the normalized seed scale is the leading velocity scale in §5.
TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.summary: The profile width gives the required velocity scale

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertBilin.text: Pair the projected operator applied to its first argument with its second argument in the closed Hilbert subspace. The result is a bounded bilinear form on `H`. It is the form passed to Lax–Milgram after a positive coercivity estimate is supplied; symmetry is not imposed by this definition.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertBilin.summary: The bilinear form of the compressed operator

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertBilin_coerciv.text: If the ambient operator satisfies $c\|u\|^2\le\langle Au,u\rangle$ on the closed subspace with `hc : 0 < c`, then the associated compressed bilinear form is coercive. The inner-product identity removes the orthogonal projection. No self-adjointness or symmetry assumption is required by this coercivity conclusion.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertBilin_coerciv.summary: Ambient coercivity passes to the compressed form

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.text: For a closed Hilbert subspace and a bounded ambient operator coercive there with strictly positive constant, Lax–Milgram gives a continuous linear equivalence of the subspace. Its forward map is later identified with the compressed operator. This construction supplies an actual inverse on the constrained space, not an extension to arbitrary ambient vectors.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.summary: Positive coercivity makes the compressed operator invertible

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.text: Under the closedness and positive coercivity hypotheses, the continuous linear equivalence produced by Lax–Milgram agrees on every subspace vector with `projectedHilbertOperator`. This links the abstract existence theorem back to the concrete projected equation. The inverse introduced by the equivalence therefore solves that equation on `H`.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.summary: The equivalence acts as the original compressed operator

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.text: Restrict the input of `A` to the closed subspace `H`, apply the ambient operator, and orthogonally project the result back into `H`. Closedness provides completeness of the subspace. This defines the projected operator of the weak endpoint equation before coercivity is used to show that it is invertible.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.summary: Compressing an operator to a closed Hilbert subspace

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.text: Solving the compressed equation with right-hand side equal to the projection of `f` is equivalent to the ambient inner-product identity against every test vector in `H`. Closedness provides the orthogonal projection. This equivalence needs no coercivity, because it only translates two formulations of the same equation.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.summary: A projected equation equals testing against the subspace

TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_contDiff_sl.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field on a closed time slab to any time in that slab gives a smooth function of space. The proof composes with the map sending `x` to `(t,x)`. It uses no derivative in time and therefore does not require a strict inequality between the two interval endpoints.
TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_contDiff_sl.summary: A jointly smooth slab restricts to a smooth spatial slice

TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_hasDerivWit.text: Joint smoothness on a closed slab ensures that each fixed spatial value has the within time derivative returned by `derivWithin`. The theorem simply restricts the smooth field along a time line. It does not compute the derivative by an Euler formula; that identification comes from the projected momentum hypotheses.
TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_hasDerivWit.summary: A smooth slab supplies its within time derivative

TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.text: The supplied projection converts the unprojected truncated momentum identity into the projected residual formula, provided it removes the cutoff pressure term from this particular momentum expression. The projection is otherwise an arbitrary map; no general linearity or gradient-annihilation theorem is assumed implicitly. The hypotheses retain the exact momentum representatives and incompressibility required by the preceding algebraic identity.
TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.summary: Apply a compatible projection to truncated momentum

TorusEuler.projectedPressure_slice.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the half open preterminal slab has smooth spatial slices at every time belonging to that slab. The proof restricts the joint function to a fixed time. This private lemma supplies the ordinary spatial smoothness needed for advection and pressure recovery.
TorusEuler.projectedPressure_slice.summary: Preterminal smoothness restricts to every spatial slice

TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.text: Let a linear cutoff commute with the linear divergence operator, and let a linear projection annihilate the cutoff pressure gradient. Suppose $u_t=S_\Lambda V_t$, $V_t+\operatorname{div}(V\otimes V)+\nabla\Pi=R_V$, and $R_u=\mathbb P[u_t+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)]$. Then $R_u=\mathbb P[S_\Lambda R_V+\operatorname{div}((u-V)\otimes u+V\otimes(u-V)+(I-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V))]$. The formal identity works with any real vector spaces, bilinear product and linear operators satisfying these algebraic premises. It does not itself assert $u=S_\Lambda V$, boundedness of a multiplier, or a pressure Poisson equation. In §5.7 those facts identify the objects with the physical cutoff and turn this identity into (5.58).
TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.summary: Derive the three cutoff tensors by bilinear algebra

TorusEuler.projectionJets_fderiv_periodi.text: If `f` is invariant under integer lattice translations, its total Fréchet derivative is invariant under those translations too. The proof uses translation of `fderiv` and equality of the translated functions. No differentiability assumption appears here: this is periodicity of the total derivative expression, not an assertion that an actual derivative exists.
TorusEuler.projectionJets_fderiv_periodi.summary: A periodic function has a periodic derivative

TorusEuler.projectionJets_toUnitTorus_ad.text: The quotient map from Euclidean space to the unit torus sends a vector sum to the sum of its images. This coordinatewise quotient identity lets a Euclidean line be read as a translated torus line. No regularity or periodicity assumption on a field is involved.

TorusEuler.projection_apply_fixed.text: A symmetric projection `hr` satisfies $r(rv)=rv$ for every vector. This extracts idempotence from the bundled hypothesis and identifies the range as a space of fixed vectors. It is used to apply coercivity assumptions that are stated only on the projected subspace.
TorusEuler.projection_apply_fixed.summary: Every projected vector is fixed by the projection

TorusEuler.projection_lattice_neg.text: The real vector associated with the negative integer lattice mode is the negative of the original lattice vector. This elementary compatibility keeps the signs consistent when passing between Fourier characters and homogeneous real symbols. It is used with evenness of the projection symbol to recover real-valued multiplier actions.
TorusEuler.projection_lattice_neg.summary: Negating a Fourier mode negates its real frequency

TorusEuler.pullback_torusField_spatially.text: For an arbitrary function on the label torus, proves spatial periodicity after composition with the quotient map. The target can be any type; continuity and differentiability are unnecessary. The proof uses equality of quotient points under integer translation, so it is a representation fact rather than an analytic estimate.

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.text: For continuous linear maps `J` and `G`, the curl associated with `J.comp G` is the sum of cross products between the transformed coordinate directions and `J` applied to those directions. This is a purely algebraic derivative-map identity. No claim that `J` or `G` comes from a genuine flow is required.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.summary: The pulled-back curl splits into three coordinate cross products

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.text: When the label scale `ℓ` is nonzero, the pulled-back curl equals the sum of three weighted label derivatives multiplied by the inverse-scale curl rows. This is an algebraic identity involving the totalized Fréchet derivative. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for this rewrite; analytic bounds later supply genuine differentiability and coefficient control.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.summary: Weighted coordinate derivatives reproduce the pulled-back curl

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.text: At a time where differentiation on the time set is well defined, assume $J_t$ exists and $G_t=-GM$; identify $J=D_aQ[V]$ and $G=(D_aX)^{-1}$. Differentiating the transported curl gives the curl of $\partial_tQ[V]$, the commutator $[\partial_t,\mathbf d\times]Q[V]$, and the strain contribution. This is the decomposition used after (5.33) to estimate $(\partial_t+M)C[V]$. The inverse deformation evolves according to its flow equation, and the derivatives must exist on the stated time interval.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.summary: Separate the differentiated potential and the coframe commutator

TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.text: For nonzero label scale, applying the inverse coframe’s adjoint to the label gradient equals a sum of weighted label derivatives multiplied by the corresponding pressure rows. The scalar derivative is converted to a vector through the inner-product duality map. This is an identity for arbitrary input functions and linear maps, before regularity assumptions are applied.
TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.summary: The pressure gradient splits into weighted label coordinates

TorusEuler.quotient_iteratedFDeriv_one.text: The half-Hölder quotient formed from the first iterated derivative equals the quotient formed from the Fréchet derivative. The currying equivalence preserves differences and their norms. This is an encoding identity for the derivative field; it does not independently prove existence or continuity of a classical derivative.
TorusEuler.quotient_iteratedFDeriv_one.summary: First-derivative increments have the same Hölder quotient

TorusEuler.quotient_iteratedFDeriv_zero.text: The half-Hölder quotient of the zeroth iterated derivative equals that of the original field. Lean stores a zeroth derivative as a zero-argument multilinear map, and the standard currying equivalence preserves norms of differences. This identity removes that encoding when comparing the order-zero lift norm with ordinary field bounds.
TorusEuler.quotient_iteratedFDeriv_zero.summary: The zeroth derivative preserves Hölder quotients

TorusEuler.radialClamp.text: Defines the auxiliary truncation $x\mapsto R x/\max(\|x\|,R)$ used to obtain an ODE solution on a whole compact interval. For positive $R$, it fixes the radius-$R$ ball and maps every vector into that ball. Its definition itself accepts every real $R$; all geometric estimates below explicitly assume `hR : 0 < R`.

TorusEuler.radialClamp_lipschitz.text: For positive radius $R$, proves a global Lipschitz bound with constant two for the radial truncation in an arbitrary normed real space. The proof separates the change in the vector from the change in its scalar denominator. This estimate permits Picard–Lindelöf to be applied to the truncated linear vector field over the full time interval.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope.text: The formal envelope is $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$, where one particular smooth function $\chi$ equals one for arguments at most one and zero for arguments at least two, with values in $[0,1]$. For $\ell_*>0$, the resulting field is even, equals one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and vanishes for $|a|\ge2\ell_*$. These are the properties prescribed in §5.1; the formalization fixes this cutoff rather than quantifying over every possible choice. The formula is also defined at $\ell_*=0$: division by zero is zero, giving $g\equiv1$. Hence positivity of the radius is essential for the stated localization.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope.summary: Fix a smooth radial cutoff at the chosen label scale

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.text: For the fixed radial cutoff $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$, assume $\ell_*>0$ and $|a|\le\ell_*$. Then $g(a)=1$. The positivity assumption makes $|a|/\ell_*\le1$, where the chosen smooth cutoff is exactly one. This is the plateau property required in §5.1 and used when computing the central gradient. The assertion is only about the spatial envelope in parent labels; it does not assert that the time cutoff is one, or by itself prove that the physical leading wave is active. Other admissible radial cutoffs are not quantified over.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.summary: The chosen positive radius gives an exact unit plateau

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.text: For positive `ell`, the radial envelope at label `a` equals the unit-radius envelope evaluated at $\ell^{-1}\cdot a$. The proof unfolds the envelope and simplifies the norm of scalar multiplication. This identity isolates all radius dependence in a linear rescaling, enabling derivative constants to be chosen from the fixed unit envelope.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.summary: Every positive-radius envelope rescales the unit envelope

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.text: For positive radius, the chosen radial envelope is zero at every point whose norm is at least twice that radius. This is the outer support condition of the localized wave; smoothness is proved separately.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.summary: The envelope vanishes outside its outer ball

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_mem_Icc.text: The chosen radial envelope takes values in the closed unit interval for every real radius and every point. This unrestricted range bound does not supply the intended support geometry when the radius is nonpositive.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_neg.text: The radial envelope has the same value at a point and its negative, since the norm is even. No positivity or smoothness assumption is needed for this identity.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_zero_collar.text: For positive envelope scale `hr`, if some coordinate lies beyond the stated collar threshold, the radial envelope is zero. The threshold simplifies to twice the scale. A coordinate absolute value is bounded by the Euclidean norm, so the outer-radius cutoff lemma applies.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_zero_collar.summary: A coordinate outside the envelope radius forces the cutoff to vanish

TorusEuler.radius_power_small.text: The first-order envelope threshold bounds every smaller radius power.
TorusEuler.radius_power_small.summary: The envelope threshold controls smaller radius powers

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.text: The range of the ambient orthogonal projection `endpointJointConstraintProjection T` is precisely `endpointTorusSpace T`. That space combines zero time mean at almost every label with the weak spatial divergence condition. The statement identifies the projection range; it does not separately reconstruct the displacement or its pointwise endpoint values.
TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.summary: The joint projection range is the endpoint constraint space

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointSubtractMe.text: For hT : 0 < T, the range of time-mean removal equals the kernel of time integration. One inclusion is the zero-integral theorem. For the other, a field with zero integral is fixed by $Q$ and supplies its own preimage. The equality concerns submodules of joint $L^2$, before imposing any spatial divergence constraint.

TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.text: The range of the bounded complex Leray operator equals the Fourier solenoidal submodule. This equality establishes both that every projected field is solenoidal and that every field in that submodule is attained. It concerns Hilbert-space elements, with no additional pointwise regularity claim.
TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.summary: The full Leray range is precisely the solenoidal subspace

TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.text: The range of the ambient real Leray operator is precisely `endpointSpatialSolenoidal`. Thus every output passes the weak gradient tests, and every field passing them is attained by the projection. This identifies the subspace intrinsically before later arguments recognize it through transverse Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.summary: The projection range is exactly the weak solenoidal space

TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.text: The longitudinal rank-one projection is invariant under nonzero real rescaling of its direction.
TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.summary: Longitudinal projection is unchanged by nonzero rescaling

TorusEuler.raw_center_coupling_lower.text: For nonzero vectors `k` and `a`, a normalized first coupling at least $D^{-1}$ implies a raw contraction at least $D^{-1}\|k\|\|a\|$. Multiplication by the positive norm product justifies removing the denominator. The statement itself places no sign restriction on `D`; positive quantitative use is supplied by the center-wave hypotheses.
TorusEuler.raw_center_coupling_lower.summary: Central normalized coupling gives a raw lower bound

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff.text: Defines the real-valued convolution operator by integrating the real part of the finite spectral kernel against a field with values in a real normed space. The Fourier multiplier identification for an even symbol is proved separately by scalar testing. The definition itself accepts arbitrary representatives and does not assert their integrability.

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.text: Almost-everywhere equality of two real normed-space-valued representatives gives pointwise equality of their real convolution cutoffs. The integrands agree almost everywhere at each fixed output point, so integral congruence applies. The declaration explicitly omits the surrounding `CompleteSpace` assumption; it is only a congruence statement for the total integral.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.summary: Real convolution respects almost everywhere equality

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.text: With an even symbol, an integrable field in a real Banach space, and a continuous real linear functional `l`, scalarization of the real cutoff equals the complex scalar Fourier cutoff of `l ∘ g`. Evenness makes that scalar cutoff real. This identifies the operator’s Fourier meaning, beyond its real-kernel definition.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.summary: Testing the real cutoff by a scalar functional

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.text: For an integrable `Vec3`-valued field, the real-kernel convolution equals complexification followed by the complex Fourier cutoff and real projection. The proof commutes the real-part map with an integrable Bochner integral and checks the scalar multiplication coordinatewise. Integrability is essential to this identification as stated.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.summary: The real convolution agrees with the velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.text: This definition casts the three integer frequency components to real numbers and places them in the Euclidean vector wrapper. It supplies the real frequency at which the angular Leray symbol is sampled. The associated norm and inner-product lemmas connect this representation to the earlier complex coefficient formulas.
TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.summary: Integer modes embedded as real Euclidean frequencies

TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency_inner.text: The real inner product of the embedded integer frequency with a vector equals the sum of its integer coordinates times the vector coordinates. This unfolds the Euclidean representation. It is used to show that restricting the complex Leray symbol to real coefficients agrees with the real angular operator.
TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency_inner.summary: The real frequency pairing is a coordinate contraction

TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency_norm_sq.text: The squared Euclidean norm of the embedded real Fourier frequency equals the sum of the squared integer coordinates, `frequencyNormSq k`. This is the real counterpart of the complex Euclidean identity. It ensures that both versions of the Leray formula use exactly the same denominator.
TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency_norm_sq.summary: The real frequency norm matches the coordinate sum

TorusEuler.realFourierMode.text: For an integer frequency in `frequencyBand R`, selects the real part of its complex character when the Boolean is true and the imaginary part otherwise. These scalar functions span the real finite Fourier space. The definition concerns the torus variable alone and imposes no positivity assumption on the band radius.

TorusEuler.realFourierMode_gradientPair_.text: If the real vector `z` is orthogonal to the frequency vector, the Haar pairing of its character-weighted wave with any smooth potential gradient is zero. The proof embeds the amplitude into the complex transverse mode space. This connects a finite-dimensional transversality condition with the weak real solenoidal tests.
TorusEuler.realFourierMode_gradientPair_.summary: A transverse real Fourier mode annihilates every gradient

TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.text:
A real linear measurement viewed as a complex-valued torus function.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.summary: Testing a real Fourier field by a linear functional

TorusEuler.realFourierSpace.text: Takes the real linear span of the sine and cosine components indexed by the finite frequency band. It is a submodule of all real functions on the torus, not a space completed in a norm. Its finite dimensionality lets the Bernstein proof recover vector-valued functions from finitely many real scalar measurements.
TorusEuler.realFourierSpace.summary: The real space of bounded Fourier frequencies

TorusEuler.realHessianEntry.text: Defines a bounded real-linear functional that applies an operator to coordinate direction `i` and reads output component `j`. Keeping that order explicit avoids a transpose ambiguity when comparing a Hessian with mixed scalar derivatives. The input is an arbitrary spatial operator and need not already be known to be symmetric.

TorusEuler.realHessianEntryLift.text: Extracts direction `i`, component `j` from a real operator-valued half-Hölder torus field and packages it as a continuous scalar function. Continuity follows from the input field and the bounded coordinate functional. This prepares the field for entrywise Fourier comparison; no assertion that it is an actual Hessian is part of the definition.
TorusEuler.realHessianEntryLift.summary: View a represented Hessian entry as a continuous function

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a complex operator symbol smooth away from the origin, constructs the fixed-cutoff dyadic operator on half-Hölder fields and realifies it through `X`. The value of the symbol at zero supplies the mean action in the underlying construction. Positive homogeneity is not assumed by this definition; it enters separately when identifying every nonzero Fourier coefficient with the requested symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: Construct the real multiplier using a fixed cutoff

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a symbol smooth away from zero, the constructed real multiplier satisfies an off-support Lipschitz bound when $f$ vanishes on a product-metric ball of radius $r>0$ and the second point lies within $r/4$. The constant is explicit in the annular symbol's derivative mass and the inverse-fourth-power tail. The input factor is the supremum norm $\|f.val.1\|$, not its full half-Hölder norm.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: A real multiplier gains local Lipschitz control

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a smooth, even, degree-zero homogeneous symbol `P`, the real half-Hölder multiplier acts on every real-character moment by `P` at the lattice vector. The hypotheses `hEven` and `hHom` are explicit, and the conclusion includes the zero Fourier mode. This identifies the constructed real operator with the desired projection symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: The real multiplier has the prescribed Fourier moments

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.text: For arbitrary measure `μ`, lift the coordinatewise real-part map to complex vector-valued L² functions. The result is a real continuous linear map into real vector L². It is one of the projection maps used to build the complexification of the entire time-path Hilbert space.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.summary: Take real parts of vector valued L² paths

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.text: The real part of $i v$ is minus the imaginary part of `v` as an L² equality. Representative compatibility reduces the assertion to the corresponding scalar complex identity in each coordinate. It records the sign convention needed to prove that componentwise real-operator extension is complex-linear.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.summary: Multiplication by i turns imaginary paths into negative real parts

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.text: Taking the L² real-part map has the same representative as applying `periodicRealPartVector` pointwise, almost everywhere. The measure is arbitrary and no time-interval assumption is involved. This equality permits integrals and norm identities to use the familiar finite-dimensional real-part formula.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.summary: Path real parts agree with pointwise real projection

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.text: A real L² path is unchanged by first complexifying it and then taking its real part. This equality holds in the quotient space and is proved by representative comparison. It provides the left-inverse axiom of the concrete L² complexification, ensuring that real data retain their identity under embedding.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.summary: Real projection recovers the original real path

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.text: For continuous complex-valued-space field `f`, a real-linear map `Re`, frequency `k`, and complex scalar `c`, the real-character moment of `Re(f)` is half of `Re` applied to the combination of coefficients at $-k$ and $k$. The input need not be real-valued. Both opposite modes are required by the real part of the character.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.summary: Real character moments use both opposite Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.text: Assume `hRe` makes a complex operator compatible with a real operator under `Re`, and `hneg` and `hpos` give the same complex multiplier relation at both opposite frequencies. Then the corresponding real-character moment of `g` is the real operator applied to that of `f`. A single-frequency identity would not suffice for this conclusion.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.summary: Paired Fourier identities transfer a real multiplier action

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff.text: Defines the scalar cutoff by complexifying a continuous real torus function, taking the finite Fourier sum with symbol `ψ` and scale `Λ`, and extracting its real part. It is defined even for scales and symbols outside the analytic cutoff regime. Approximation estimates and the intended symmetric multiplier interpretation require their own hypotheses.

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_add.text: The real scalar cutoff of two added continuous torus functions equals the sum of their cutoffs. Integrability comes from continuity, and the proof distributes through Fourier coefficients, finite summation, and real-part extraction. No symmetry or positivity assumptions on the symbol or scale are needed for this linear identity.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_add.summary: The real scalar cutoff preserves addition

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_coord.text: Taking a coordinate of the real vector cutoff gives exactly the real scalar cutoff of that coordinate field. The identity holds for every real symbol and cutoff scale. It reconciles the componentwise scalar Fourier construction with the bundled vector construction before their derivatives are assembled into a divergence or gradient.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_coord.summary: Scalar cutoff agrees with each vector coordinate

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.text: For a continuously differentiable lifted vector field with a continuous scalar divergence representative, cutting off that representative equals taking the divergence of the vector cutoff. The proof combines the coordinate derivative identities with scalar finite-sum linearity. The statement is valid for arbitrary symbol and scale and does not itself supply norm bounds.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.summary: The real cutoff commutes with vector divergence

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_sum.text: Applying the real scalar cutoff to a finite sum of continuous functions equals the finite sum of their cutoffs. The theorem includes the empty sum and arbitrary symbol and scale. Its role is to pass the cutoff through the three coordinate terms in the divergence of a vector field.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_sum.summary: The real scalar cutoff preserves finite sums

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.text: Turns a complex-linear operator into a real-linear operator by complexifying a real input and taking the real part of the output. The construction is itself a continuous real-linear map on operators. It is used after Fourier reconstruction to obtain a real pressure Hessian from real scalar source data.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.summary: Restrict a complex operator to real vectors

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.text: States the exact evaluation rule for `realSpatialOperatorPart`: complexify the real vector, apply the complex operator, then take its real part. The equality is definitional and holds for every complex operator. No assumption that the operator preserves real vectors is required.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.summary: Evaluate the real part of a complex operator

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.text: Taking the real operator part of the pressure symbol applied to a complex scalar gives the scalar’s real part times the real angular projection. The identity holds for every frequency. It is the algebraic step that converts paired complex Fourier coefficients into the real cosine and sine moment formula.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.summary: Recover the real scalar pressure projection

TorusEuler.realTensorFourierCutoff.text:
The real Fourier cutoff on a tensor field represented in a complex normed space.

Default-value audit (b5): The maps J and R are arbitrary continuous linear maps in the definition. Recovering the original real tensor requires the retraction property R∘J=id, and approximation bounds also require a positive cutoff scale.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff.text:
The Fourier cutoff on real Euclidean vector fields, obtained by complex Fourier synthesis followed by the coordinatewise real projection.

Default-value audit (b5): The cutoff delegates to finite Fourier synthesis and uses an arbitrary real scale in the raw definition. Positive scale, symbol support and regularity are supplied by the cutoff estimates.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Complexifies a possibly noncontinuous real velocity field, applies the complex Fourier cutoff, then takes its real part. The definition accepts an arbitrary function on the torus. Subsequent results relate this representative-level construction to continuous fields and to almost-everywhere classes; meaningful analytic estimates use integrability or essential boundedness.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Applying the real vector cutoff to a representative

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Almost-everywhere equal real velocity representatives give exactly equal cutoffs. The proof passes their equality through complexification, applies the complex cutoff congruence, and then takes real parts. The result is pointwise equality of output functions; it does not require the inputs themselves to have pointwise equal values.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Real velocity cutoffs ignore null-set changes

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: For a continuous real velocity field, the representative-level cutoff agrees with the earlier `realVectorFourierCutoff`. This is an equality of the two operator definitions, not a proof that an arbitrary input is continuous. It allows estimates stated for continuous torus fields to be used with the expanded representative interface.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Agreement with the continuous velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.text: With smooth time-dependent Fourier coefficients in the retained band, smooth odd divergence-free input slices and an even symbol, the cutoff is jointly smooth on the specified time set. Every slice is periodic, odd, divergence free and has no frequencies beyond $2\Lambda$. These are the listed admissibility properties; no bound on the residual or deformation is asserted.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.summary: Smooth coefficient paths produce an admissible next parent

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_add.text: Real vector cutoff preserves addition of continuous torus fields.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.text: For a continuously differentiable scalar torus lift and a continuous vector field representing its gradient, the real vector cutoff of that field is the gradient of the real scalar cutoff. The proof differentiates the finite Fourier sum coordinatewise. This exact identity holds for arbitrary real symbol and scale, independently of the later analytic cutoff bounds.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.summary: The real cutoff preserves the form of a gradient

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.text: The commutation with finite vector field sums, used in tensor divergence.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.summary: Fourier truncation commutes with finite sums

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.text: For a continuous torus tensor whose lift is continuously differentiable, let `d` continuously represent its physical divergence. The real vector cutoff of `d` equals the divergence of the real tensor cutoff. The proof uses each coordinate derivative and a finite sum; no smooth-symbol or positive-scale assumption is needed for this exact identity.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.summary: The real cutoff commutes with tensor divergence

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_zero.text: For every symbol and real scale, applying the real vector Fourier cutoff to the zero continuous field gives the zero field. Every Fourier coefficient and every term of the finite sum vanish. The result is used when a divergence-free field is truncated; it does not require an analytic cutoff bound.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_zero.summary: The real vector cutoff sends zero to zero

TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.text: For any real frequency vector `ξ` and vector `z`, the angular Leray projection of `z` is orthogonal to `ξ`. The proof splits off `ξ = 0` before cancellation of its squared norm. At zero frequency the orthogonality statement is automatic and is consistent with retaining every amplitude.
TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.summary: The angular projection removes the frequency component

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.text: Given a bounded real-linear operator $L$ on half-Hölder fields valued in the complexification, embeds each real input by `X.ofReal`, applies $L$, and then takes `X.re` pointwise. This yields a bounded real-linear operator on real-valued fields. The construction works for arbitrary $L$ and does not require its outputs on real inputs to have zero imaginary part.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.summary: Transport a multiplier to real Hölder fields

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.text: If the complex embedding of $v$ equals $F$ applied to the embedded $f$ plus $G$ applied to the embedded $s$, then $v$ equals the sum of the two corresponding realified outputs. Applying the real-part map proves the equality pointwise. The premise supplies the exact embedded identity, so preservation of the real subspace by each operator separately is unnecessary.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.summary: Transport an embedded multiplier identity to real fields

TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.text: Let $\lambda_n$ be real frequencies with $\lambda_0\ge2$ and $\lambda_{n+1}\ge\lambda_n^2$ for every nonnegative integer $n$. For every $j\ge0$, the series $\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda_{j+k}^{-1}$ converges and is at most $2\lambda_j^{-1}$. The hypotheses imply all frequencies are positive, so the reciprocals are ordinary reciprocals with no zero-denominator convention involved. This numerical result is independent of the Euler equations and does not itself bound velocity differences. Section 8 combines it with the increment estimates and, for higher derivatives, vanishing of the later oscillations. Taking the tail to start at $j=n+1$ gives the last bound in Proposition 8.1.
TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.summary: Squaring growth gives summability and an explicit bound for every tail

TorusEuler.recover_endpointPhysicalVeloc.text: From actual physical jet data, deformation evolution, inverse bounds and $H^\#\le I$, this helper constructs a jointly smooth label velocity with zero endpoint primitive. It also returns the kinetic and mixed coercivity estimates, with constants $D^{-2}$ and $[2D^2(1+L)^2]^{-1}$, and all finite recovered-word families. The hypotheses include $0<T\le1$, $D\ge1$ and $L\ge0$.
TorusEuler.recover_endpointPhysicalVeloc.summary: Physical coefficient jets recover the endpoint velocity

TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.text: Let real numbers $\varepsilon,\tau,x,s,e,Y$ satisfy $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $(1+x^2)s^2=1$ and $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon\tau xs^2/2$. The formal statement proves $x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon\tau Y=x-\varepsilon+2\varepsilon s^2+2\varepsilon\tau s(1+e)$ and $-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY=1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon xs^2$. Multiplying by $s=\cos\varphi$ gives the simplified reference couplings in (2.22). The algebraic statement also permits the negative square-root choice of $s$, since it assumes only its square; the wave application selects $s>0$. Neither smallness of $e$ nor a differential equation is required for the cancellation.
TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.summary: Two polynomial identities remove the apparently large terms

TorusEuler.reflectionParity_of_onSlab.text: A smooth profile satisfying the reflection identity on the slab satisfies it everywhere as a representative. Reflection preserves time, so both sides are zero at off-slab points. This lets later symmetry proofs work on the domain where derivatives and coefficient identities have their physical meaning.
TorusEuler.reflectionParity_of_onSlab.summary: Extend an on-slab reflection law to the representative

TorusEuler.relayAdjointCoordinate.text: For a coordinate index `i`, this continuous linear map sends an endomorphism `A` to $A^*e_i$. It composes the adjoint isometry with evaluation on the unit coordinate vector. These vectors supply the rows appearing in curl and pressure-gradient formulas after pulling derivatives back to label coordinates.
TorusEuler.relayAdjointCoordinate.summary: Extracting a coframe row through the adjoint

TorusEuler.relayCrossLeftCLM.text: This packages $v\mapsto(w\mapsto v\times w)$ as a continuous linear map into the space of endomorphisms of $\mathbb R^3$. Additivity and scalar compatibility come from the cross product, and its continuity uses a norm bound of one. The construction supports derivative bounds by composition with coframe coefficients.
TorusEuler.relayCrossLeftCLM.summary: Cross product as a linear coefficient map

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.text: The map sends $v$ to the continuous linear operator $w\mapsto v\times w$. Its norm is controlled by one, so composing it with the normalized wave-vector profile preserves parent derivative bounds. This public construction supplies the same geometric operation needed in the potential and its time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap_apply.text: For any vector `v`, evaluation of `relayCrossMap` returns `cross3Left v`. The equality is definitional, exposing the concrete cross-product operator after it has been packaged as a continuous linear map. This allows the jet algebra to be identified with the normalized coefficient formulas used in the relay.

TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.text: The map sends a coframe `G` to $\ell^{-1}(G^*e_i)\times\cdot$, the coefficient paired with one scaled label derivative in the curl. It is linear in `G`, so every label derivative of the row is controlled by the corresponding derivative of `G`. The inverse width is kept explicit.
TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled curl row

TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM_apply.text: Applying the continuous linear map `relayCurlRowCLM` to `G` is definitionally the geometric coefficient `hierarchyRelayCurlRow`. The equality aligns a derivative-friendly linear-map representation with the coordinate formula used in the relay norm. It holds for every real width, including its totalized zero-width value.

TorusEuler.relayMaterialUnitBilinear.text: This private continuous bilinear map takes an inverse coframe `G` and strain `M` to the unit-width material relay row. Writing $P_i$ for the unit-width curl-row map, its value is $M\circ P_i(G)-P_i(G\circ M)$. Thus strain acts after the curl row in the first term. The bundled map lets the mixed product estimate account for both coefficient factors.
TorusEuler.relayMaterialUnitBilinear.summary: The unit-width material row is a bilinear map

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.text:
Apply the mean-zero oscillatory pressure construction to the fixed-label strain, covector, forcing and velocity profile. This is a scalar phase profile used by the slow pressure-gradient term.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a normalized phase primitive, not a pressure solution predicate. Smoothness, phase periodicity, nonzero covectors and the transverse momentum equation justify its use as pressure.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.summary: The normalized phase pressure used in the relay

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.text: The normalized phase pressure is linear under simultaneous scalar multiplication of the velocity and forcing slices. Both terms in its pressure slope scale, and so does their zero-mean phase primitive. The coefficients `M` and `k` are held fixed; the theorem does not describe scaling the wave vector or strain.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the phase pressure together

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_of_.text: If `hperp` states $\kappa\cdot F=0$ at every label and phase, the normalized pressure profile agrees with the pressure obtained by replacing `F` with zero. Only the forcing contribution to the pressure slope vanishes. The velocity-dependent term remains, so the conclusion does not assert that the pressure itself is zero.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_of_.summary: A transverse force contributes no phase-pressure slope

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.text:
The actual primitive fields in the relay with the frequency removed from the covector. Each depends only on the indicated fixed-time coefficient and profile data.

Default-value audit (b5): This uses the raw wave potential; nonzero covectors and integrable phase profiles are needed for its physical primitive interpretation. The coefficients and profiles in the construction provide those hypotheses.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.summary: The normalized primitive profile for the relay

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.text: Scaling the velocity slice by a constant multiplies its relay potential by that constant. The normalized wave-vector coefficient is a continuous linear map and the centered phase primitive commutes with scalar multiplication. The equality is pointwise in label and phase, so a time-dependent weight may be treated as constant on each fixed-time slice.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.summary: The potential is linear under simultaneous scaling

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.text:
At fixed label, take the normalized phase primitive of the potential-time source built from M, k, V and f. The definition prepares the primitive used in the linear relay; the solution equation is supplied separately.

Default-value audit (b5): The phase integral is a totalized integral. Smooth phase profiles, the nonzero covector and the time evolution identity must be supplied before identifying this primitive with an actual time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.summary: The phase primitive of the potential-time source

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_add.text: For continuous velocity and forcing slices, the potential-time profile decomposes into its zero-forcing part plus the ordinary potential of `F`. This follows by separating the integrand’s two linear coefficient terms and adding their phase primitives. No transverse condition is needed for this identity; transversality is used when simplifying pressure.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_add.summary: The forcing contributes its own potential

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.text: If both the velocity and forcing slices are multiplied by `r`, the potential-time profile is multiplied by `r`. Its integrand is linear in those two inputs through separate coefficient maps. This identity permits amplitude normalization after the physical time derivative has been evaluated, without introducing a derivative of the weight.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the potential derivative together

TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.text: This map sends `G` to the scalar-to-vector operator $c\mapsto\ell^{-1}cG^*e_i$. It provides the $i$th pressure-gradient coefficient in label coordinates. Packaging the operation as a continuous linear map lets the same coframe derivative estimate control both the pressure row and the curl row.
TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled pressure gradient

TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM_apply.text: Applying `relayPressureRowCLM` to a coframe gives exactly `hierarchyRelayPressureRow`. This definitional equality connects the linear-map construction to the scalar-to-vector coefficient in the pressure-gradient sum. It imposes no invertibility or positivity assumptions; the analytic identities using the coefficient carry those assumptions separately.
TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM_apply.summary: The packaged map is the pressure coefficient

TorusEuler.relayPrimitive_add_continuous.text: For continuous functions into a complete real normed space, the centered phase primitive of their sum is the sum of the two primitives. Continuity supplies integrability on every finite interval and continuity of the resulting indefinite integrals. These hypotheses justify the additivity needed to split forcing from homogeneous relay terms.
TorusEuler.relayPrimitive_add_continuous.summary: Adding continuous inputs adds their phase primitives

TorusEuler.relayPrimitive_const_smul.text: Multiplying an input by a real constant `r` multiplies its centered phase primitive by the same constant. The proof distributes scalar multiplication through both interval integrals and through subtraction of the phase mean. This algebraic identity applies without an extra continuity assumption; it does not claim that the primitive differentiates to an arbitrary input.
TorusEuler.relayPrimitive_const_smul.summary: A constant passes through the centered phase primitive

TorusEuler.relayWordBound_add.text: Two smooth profiles with word bounds `A` and `B` have sum bounded by `A + B` at the same order and scales. The proof packages them as a two-element finite family. This preserves separate velocity and forcing contributions when the normalized potential and pressure are assembled.
TorusEuler.relayWordBound_add.summary: Adding two profiles adds their derivative bounds

TorusEuler.relayWordBound_bdd.text: A `HierarchyRelayWordBound` supplies an explicit upper bound for each admissible derivative-value set used in the supremum norm. Its nonnegative bound controls the set’s inserted zero as well as all derivative norms. These boundedness facts are needed to use conditional real supremum inequalities correctly.
TorusEuler.relayWordBound_bdd.summary: Derivative bounds make every relevant supremum finite
