This identity is used when matching the negative-frequency character in the Fourier-transform convention with the convolution formula at the origin.

TorusEuler.torusQuotient_sub.text: The image of a Euclidean difference is the difference of the two torus images. This exact homomorphism identity aligns translations in Euclidean kernel integration with translations of torus fields. It avoids choosing a fundamental-cell representative each time a convolution is evaluated.
TorusEuler.torusQuotient_sub.summary: The torus quotient respects spatial differences

TorusEuler.torusTranslateField.text: For a torus increment `b`, the constructed field takes the value of `f` at `a+b`. Translation preserves the torus distance, so the same value and square-root increment bounds certify the new bundled field. This is the underlying field construction before it is packaged as a bounded linear operator.
TorusEuler.torusTranslateField.summary: Translate a half Hölder field on the torus

TorusEuler.traceCLM.text: This continuous linear map sums the three diagonal coordinate evaluations of an endomorphism of Euclidean three-space. Packaging trace in this way permits it to commute with differentiation and linear combinations in the cutoff-divergence calculation. The definition applies to every operator, regardless of whether it arose as a derivative.
TorusEuler.traceCLM.summary: The trace bundled as a bounded linear map

TorusEuler.traceCLM_apply.text: For any continuous linear endomorphism, the bundled coordinate functional `traceCLM` agrees with `LinearMap.trace` of the underlying linear map. This identifies the implementation with the coordinate-free trace used in divergence formulas. It is a finite-dimensional algebraic identity and carries no smoothness or invertibility assumptions.
TorusEuler.traceCLM_apply.summary: The coordinate functional equals the intrinsic trace

TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.text: At a point `a`, assume `F` is differentiable with derivative `DF`, has local determinant one, and admits the stated left inverse `G`. Then the trace of the directional variation `DF w` composed with `G` is zero. This extracts the cancellation needed when differentiating a volume-preserving pushforward.
TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.summary: Differentiating a unit determinant gives zero trace

TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq.text: This is pointwise at a label $a$: $X$ is twice differentiable, $v$ differentiable, $\det D_aX=1$ in a neighbourhood and $G(D_aX)=I$. If $X$ preserves volume, $v$ is divergence free in label coordinates and $B=D_aXv$, then $\mathbf d\cdot B=0$. The statement assumes the necessary spatial derivatives and inverse deformation. This identifies the divergence condition in the endpoint formulation with the mean equation (5.11), using the volume-preserving change of variables.
TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq.summary: Volume preservation carries divergence freedom to physical coordinates

TorusEuler.trace_frame.text: For any orthonormal frame and continuous linear operator on three-dimensional Euclidean space, identifies its trace with the sum of the three diagonal frame entries. Trace freeness is not an assumption of this lemma. In the moving-frame proof, the separate hypothesis that the trace vanishes converts $-B_{11}-B_{22}$ into $B_{33}$.

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.text: Assume `F` has a symmetric spatial derivative, determinant one near `a`, and a left inverse `G` at `a`. The trace of the derivative of $Fv$, composed with `G`, equals the divergence of `v`. The extra derivative of `F` has zero trace by the determinant identity, while cyclicity of trace cancels the inverse in the remaining term.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.summary: A volume preserving coframe preserves divergence

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.text: For a twice differentiable spatial map `X`, determinant one in a neighborhood and a left inverse of its derivative give the coframe divergence identity for a differentiable field `v`. Second derivative symmetry is obtained from `hX`, rather than assumed separately. The result is pointwise at the label `a` and does not assert global invertibility of `X`.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.summary: The flow deformation gives the divergence identity

TorusEuler.trace_stationaryShearGradient.text: The constant gradient matrix of the stationary shear has trace zero for every real shear parameter. The proof expands the trace in the Euclidean basis. This algebraic form of incompressibility allows the affine moving-frame equations to be applied when estimating the first coupling throughout the initial wave window.
TorusEuler.trace_stationaryShearGradient.summary: The stationary shear matrix has zero trace

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.text: In finite-dimensional parameter and state spaces, a jointly continuous family solving a smooth vector-field ODE with a smooth initial map is jointly smooth on a positive closed slab. The proof bootstraps using the spatial variational equation and the combined time-parameter derivative. It is a regularity theorem for an existing family, not a global existence result.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.summary: A continuous smooth-flow family is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.text: For a finite-dimensional trajectory family of a smooth time-dependent ODE, assume joint continuity `hYc`, the trajectory equation `hYt`, and smooth initial data `hY₀`. Every time slice is then spatially differentiable; its derivative is jointly continuous and solves the first variational equation within $[0,T]$. The theorem derives regularity of an existing family rather than constructing trajectories.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.summary: A trajectory family has a continuous variational derivative

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.text: Under smooth finite-dimensional ODE data, joint continuity of the trajectory family, and smooth initial values, the spatial derivative of any order `n` exists continuously across the slab. Both the trajectory derivative and the differentiated right-hand side are jointly continuous. The time derivative of the former is exactly the latter, expressed as a within-interval derivative.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.summary: Every spatial derivative satisfies its differentiated ODE

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.text: For a phase-independent mean, transporting through a smooth inverse chart increases only the explicit parent-parameter power in its jet bound. The input frequency exponent `alpha` remains unchanged. Positive frequency suffices; there is no carrier-size or phase-width assumption. The estimate depends on supplied scaled mean jets and weighted derivatives of the actual coframe.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.summary: The mean preserves its frequency exponent under transport

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.text: A phase-independent mean composed with the inverse labels has the same chain-rule estimate with no carrier term. The input supplies scaled jets of the mean, weighted coframe jets, and a number `Q ≥ 1` bounding the label cost alone. The proof specializes the general transported-profile estimate to zero carrier and unit amplitude.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.summary: Phase-independent fields incur only the label derivative cost

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.text: With width $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, carrier length at most $D\lambda$, and inverse label scale bounded by $D^a$, a scaled profile bound of frequency exponent `alpha` gives graph jets with exponent $3n/2+alpha$. Smooth chart and coframe identities and weighted derivative bounds are required. The theorem keeps an explicit parent exponent and restores `gamma` after differentiation.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.summary: Every physical derivative adds the explicit carrier cost

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.text: Given a smooth inverse-label map, its actual coframe field, a bound on weighted coframe jets, and scaled profile jets bounded by `gamma * M`, graph evaluation has a uniform finite jet bound. The supplied number `Q ≥ 1` bounds the combined label and phase cost. The explicit order constant and $Q^n$ record repeated spatial differentiation.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.summary: A profile jet bound becomes an Eulerian jet bound

TorusEuler.transportedProfile.text: Given maps $A(t,x)$, a fixed $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and a profile $f(t,a,s)$, the formal definition is $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$. For the parent flow, $A(t,\cdot)=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$, so it is exactly the evaluation convention of §3.1. The formula itself does not assume that $A$ is an inverse or solves a transport equation. It is defined on all arguments and imposes no regularity, spatial periodicity or label support. Those properties must be established before this evaluated expression is used as a smooth field on the torus.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile.summary: The inverse label map determines both label and phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.text:
At $(t,x)$, assume the inverse label map and profile have their indicated joint derivatives, and that $A_t+D_xA\,U=0$. Let $a=A(t,x)$, $s=k_*\cdot a$ and $\kappa=(D_xA)^Tk_*$. The formal statement gives $D_xf^
atural=D_af\,D_xA+(\partial_sf)\kappa^T$ and $(\partial_t+U\cdot
abla_x)f^
atural=\partial_tf$, with the profile derivatives evaluated at $(t,a,s)$. These are (3.1). Time derivatives are taken within the given time set, which must determine a unique derivative at $t$; a nondegenerate closed interval includes the appropriate one-sided endpoints. Periodicity and nonvanishing of the wave vector are unnecessary for the chain rule.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.summary: Spatial differentiation sees the phase; material differentiation does not

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.text: If the inverse-label map is odd and the profile transforms by a supplied map `R` under simultaneous label and phase negation, its graph evaluation transforms by the same `R` under spatial reflection. The result is algebraic and allows an arbitrary target type and transformation, beyond the later even and odd specializations.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.summary: Spatial reflection reflects both label and phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.text: At a fixed time, suppose $A(t,X(t,a))=a$. For any profile $f$ and any real wave vector $k_*$, the formal statement proves $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$, where $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$. This is the evaluation convention used for the leading oscillation in §3.1. Only the inverse relation at the label in question is required; there is no derivative, trajectory equation, periodicity or nonzero-covector hypothesis. Constancy of the phase along the parent follows by applying this identity with the phase profile itself.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.summary: The profile sees the initial label and its fixed phase

TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.text: This complex subspace is the orthogonal complement of the complex line spanned by the real wave vector embedded in Euclidean coefficient space. At nonzero frequency it is the transverse plane. At zero frequency the span is zero and the transverse space is the whole coefficient space.
TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.summary: Coefficients orthogonal to the frequency span

TorusEuler.transversePlane.text:
The real linear plane transverse to a wave vector.

Default-value audit (b5): At k=0 the kernel of the zero functional is the whole ambient space. The intended codimension-one transverse plane requires k≠0.

TorusEuler.transversePressureIdentity.text: At one time, the wave-vector and forced amplitude derivative equations, together with hperp, the zero derivative of their inner product, imply $\|\kappa\|^2p_s=\langle\kappa,f\rangle-2\langle\kappa,MV\rangle$. The theorem works in any complete real inner-product space. It neither divides by $\|\kappa\|^2$ nor requires a nonzero wave vector, so it does not by itself determine a unique pressure when $\kappa=0$.

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.text: Inserts the proved periodic Leray estimate into the abstract time-uniform residual theorem. It obtains one nonnegative residual coefficient `Cr` before choosing depth `P`, and a tail coefficient `Ct` that may depend on `P`. The inputs require bounded time-indexed Hölder norm ranges. The output estimates the defined projected residual expression; its equality with the physical Euler residual is proved separately.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.summary: The actual Leray residual obeys the uniform truncation bound

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text:
The projected cutoff residual in (5.58) with the Euclidean momentum tensor and its divergence.

Default-value audit (b5): The tensor operations are fixed to the physical ones, but the projection remains an arbitrary function parameter. The actual residual identification chooses the periodic Leray projection and proves its domain conditions.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The projected residual with the physical momentum tensor

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: This algebraic identity rewrites `truncatedEulerProjectedResidual` as the Leray projection of the cutoff input residual plus the divergence of `terminalCutoffStress g g`. It is valid for arbitrary continuous torus inputs and cutoff parameters. The proof expands definitions and cancels tensor terms; it supplies neither an Euler equation nor a bound on the resulting field.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: Express the projected residual using the cutoff stress

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: Specializes the abstract residual bound to the actual Euclidean momentum tensor and its column divergence. A first-order bound for the chosen projection is still an explicit hypothesis. The result controls the second-order cutoff error and first-order residual expression with the common tail budget, while keeping the coefficient of the input residual independent of expansion depth.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The momentum residual has a uniform Hölder estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: For any nonempty index type, applies the slice estimates with one common set of constants and takes real suprema over the family. Boundedness of the input velocity and residual norm ranges is required explicitly. The index can represent time, but no temporal derivative or time continuity is assumed by this norm-aggregation theorem.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The residual estimates hold uniformly over an index family

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text:
The right-hand side of (5.58), formed using the real velocity and tensor cutoffs.

Default-value audit (b5): The projection, tensor pairing and contraction are parameters. This expression is the physical residual only after their concrete identities and the smooth cutoff hypotheses are supplied; it is not a PDE assertion by definition.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The residual after velocity and tensor truncation

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text: Assuming a first-order Hölder bound for `proj`, a bilinear tensor product, a derivative contraction and compatible real-complex maps, obtains uniform bounds for the second-order velocity tail and first-order projected residual. The error is $\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_P)^2$ with `P ≥ 2`. The coefficient on the supplied residual is independent of `P`; this theorem estimates the defined expression, not its identification with a PDE residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The abstract projected residual satisfies the truncation estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure.text: Takes the negative real Fourier pressure potential of the coefficients of a continuous torus vector field `A`, retaining the finite band of radius `r`. In the child construction `A` represents advection. Smoothness and zero mean hold for every input, but the equation with the full divergence of `A` requires the separate band hypothesis.

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.text: If the input torus field represents the advection of the stationary shear, its slice pressure is identically zero for every cutoff radius and shear parameter. The shear advects itself trivially, so the represented source and every Fourier coefficient vanish. This confirms the pressure normalization used by the explicit zero-stage construction.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.summary: The stationary shear has zero normalized pressure

TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.text: If `C ≥ 0` and the next frequency is at least $\max(2,(2C)^2)$, then $C\,\mathrm{next}^{-7/2}+\mathrm{next}^{-5}\le\mathrm{next}^{-3}$. The explicit threshold absorbs the fixed constant and allocates room for both error terms. This is a rate comparison, not an independent bound on any velocity or residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.summary: Two residual terms fit below a third inverse power

TorusEuler.truncatedParent_smooth_slice.text: Restricts a jointly smooth function on a closed time slab to a fixed time belonging to that slab, producing an all-order smooth function on the entire spatial space. The target is any real normed vector space. This restriction needs slab membership but no positive interval length.
TorusEuler.truncatedParent_smooth_slice.summary: Joint slab smoothness gives every spatial slice

TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.text: For the chosen radial envelope $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$ with $\ell_*>0$, the closure of the set where $g\ne0$ lies in $\{a:|a|\le2\ell_*\}$. This is a closed-support statement, so it includes possible boundary points where the function itself is zero. The theorem does not mention the periodic cell. To obtain the sentence in §5.1, also use $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-3}$ and $\mathsf D\ge2$, which give $2\ell_*\le1/4<1/2$; hence the support lies strictly inside the centered unit cell. The envelope acts in label space, before transport to physical space.
TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.summary: The closed support lies inside the ball of twice the radius

TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.text: From a `LaterPrimaryCosts` witness, proves `UniformPhysicalEstimates Unit`. It combines first and later seed estimates, recurrence bounds, pressure geometry, Fourier cutoff constants and residual estimates, then takes maxima and sums to choose common exponents and nonnegative costs. The first case uses zero switches; the later case uses the actual activation profile and its weighted switch bound.
TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.summary: The first and later bounds share one common cost table

TorusEuler.uniform_gronwall.text: For a normed-space curve with a within-interval derivative satisfying the stated affine growth inequality, its norm at every allowed time is bounded by the Grönwall expression at the full terminal time `T`. Nonnegativity of `K` and `ε` allows this replacement. The initial norm bound `hinit` is retained as the parameter `δ`.
TorusEuler.uniform_gronwall.summary: A full-interval bound for vector-valued growth

TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_centeredCell_fir.text: The centered label cell has unique derivatives in the sense of `UniqueDiffOn`. The argument uses convexity and a nonempty interior containing a ball around the origin. This property permits equality of smooth functions on the entire closed cell to identify their ambient derivatives even at its boundary.
TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_centeredCell_fir.summary: Derivatives on the closed cell are uniquely determined

TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.text: For T > 0, the closed time–label–phase slab satisfies the unique-differentiability condition used by within-set derivatives. The positivity excludes a slab reduced to a single time.
TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.summary: The nondegenerate slab determines derivatives uniquely

TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_terminalSlab.text: If `0 < T`, the product $[0,T]\times E$ has unique derivatives in the sense required by Mathlib’s within-set calculus. The interval has unique derivatives even at its endpoints, and the spatial factor is unrestricted. This condition makes the selected joint derivative usable throughout the mixed-to-joint derivative comparison.
TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_terminalSlab.summary: The closed terminal slab has unique derivatives

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail.text: Defines the real constant obtained by integrating $|z|^{-4}$ over the complement of the open unit ball in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This records the finite tail mass used in all later off-support estimates without choosing a numerical spherical-coordinate evaluation. Scaling then gives the radius dependence $r^{-1}$.

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail_no.text: The unit inverse-fourth-power tail constant is nonnegative because its integrand is nonnegative on the integration set. This sign is subsequently needed when multiplying inequalities by the tail constant and replacing Euclidean torus distance by a larger multiple of the product distance. The statement claims neither strict positivity nor an exact numerical value.

TorusEuler.unitPhaseIntegralCLM.text: This bounded linear map integrates a continuous path on $[0,1]$, using its clamped extension to express the phase-average operation. Its norm is at most one. The compact domain supplies the uniform norm, and the map is used to transfer derivatives through phase averaging.
TorusEuler.unitPhaseIntegralCLM.summary: Integrate a continuous profile on the unit interval

TorusEuler.unitPhaseIntegralCLM_apply_eq.text: If a continuous unit-interval path agrees there with an ordinary real-domain profile, integrating the path gives that profile's phase average. The proof uses equality only on $[0,1]$. It therefore permits the two objects to differ arbitrarily elsewhere and does not require a globally continuous or periodic extension of the profile.
TorusEuler.unitPhaseIntegralCLM_apply_eq.summary: The path integral equals the original phase average

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.text:
Product Haar probability measure on the unit three-torus.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.summary: Probability Haar measure on the unit three-torus

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.text: For a nonnegative radius, the Haar measure of the closed ball about any torus point is $(\min(1,2r))^3$, expressed through `ENNReal.ofReal`. The formula uses the product metric on three unit circles. It is not the Euclidean three-dimensional ball-volume formula, and this distinction matters when reading the interpolation constants.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.summary: Small torus balls have an explicit volume

TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.text: Let $v$ be a continuous normed-space-valued field on the unit torus and suppose $\|v(a)-v(b)\|\le H\sqrt{d(a,b)}$ with $H\ge0$. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\|v\|_\infty\le\varepsilon H+\varepsilon^{-3}(\int\|v\|^2)^{1/2}$. Measure is normalized to total mass one. This is the averaging inequality used in Lemma A.2; the exponent three reflects the spatial dimension. The paper writes a full half-Hölder norm and an unspecified constant, whereas this formal estimate uses the supplied seminorm bound and explicitly restricts the small parameter.
TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.summary: Control the supremum by a small Hölder term and energy

TorusEuler.vectorCoordinate.text: Packages one coordinate of a continuous torus vector field as a continuous real torus function. The index belongs to the three-coordinate type, so evaluation always selects a valid coordinate. This lets the scalar cutoff lemmas express the components of the vector cutoff without changing the underlying field.
TorusEuler.vectorCoordinate.summary: View a vector coordinate as a scalar field

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.text: This continuous real bilinear map sends two vectors to the complex tensor with entry $u_i v_j$. Its norm is bounded by the product of the two Euclidean norms using coordinate estimates. On the diagonal it supplies the velocity tensor for pressure, while no symmetry is claimed for two different inputs.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.summary: Real velocities give a bounded bilinear complex tensor

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.text: The entry `(i,j)` of the tensor made from two real vectors is the complex inclusion of `u i * v j`. This definitional identity fixes the coordinate order used in double divergence and the pressure Poisson equation. It introduces no approximation or transpose convention.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.summary: The velocity tensor has the expected coordinate product

TorusEuler.vorticityForm.text: For bounded operators $F,M$ on a real Hilbert space, define $\Omega=F^*(M^*-M)F$. In the three-dimensional application, the adjoints are transposes, $F=D_aX$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$, so this is precisely (4.1). The sign is $M^T-M$, consistent with the paper's velocity-gradient convention. No invertibility, flow equation or Euler equation is assumed in this definition. The time evolution relation with $K=F^*F$ is established separately using $F_t=MF$.
TorusEuler.vorticityForm.summary: Pull back the skew part of a velocity gradient

TorusEuler.waveBump.text: The formal construction fixes $\psi(s)$ by applying a smooth transition function to $1-64s^2$. The resulting even smooth function satisfies $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi(0)=1$, and vanishes for $|s|\ge1/8$, as proved in the same file. Its support therefore lies compactly inside $(-1/4,1/4)$, the interval allowed in the proof of Lemma 3.1. The linked definition specifies this particular bump; it does not quantify over all bumps satisfying the paper's assumptions. Subsequent estimates use its narrower support to obtain the explicit bounds $-h/2\le F_h'\le1$ and $|F_h|\le h/2$.
TorusEuler.waveBump.summary: A particular even bump is supported inside the paper’s allowed interval

TorusEuler.waveBump_even.text: The chosen bump takes the same value at $s$ and $-s$. Its argument depends only on $s^2$, so the identity is exact for all real inputs. Evenness is preserved through the permitted scaled periodization and later makes the integrated normalized slope into an odd wave profile.

TorusEuler.waveBump_scaled_zero.text: For positive `hh`, the scaled bump at $s/h$ vanishes whenever $|s|\ge h/8$. Positivity is used to translate the support inequality through division. This locates the narrow active region within each unit phase cell and underlies the upper bound on its mean.
TorusEuler.waveBump_scaled_zero.summary: Scaling the bump scales its support radius

TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.text: The bump has value one at phase zero because the smooth transition is evaluated at one. This is the normalization needed before subtracting its mean. Dividing the mean-free slope by its value at zero then makes the eventual wave profile derivative equal exactly one there.
TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.summary: The compact bump equals one at its center

TorusEuler.waveBump_zero_of_abs_ge.text: If `hs` gives $|s|\ge1/8$, the bump vanishes. The chosen quadratic argument is then nonpositive, where the smooth transition is zero. The support is narrower than the paper’s allowed quarter interval, leaving a generous zero collar for the periodic copies to fit together smoothly.
TorusEuler.waveBump_zero_of_abs_ge.summary: The bump vanishes outside the inner eighth interval

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.text: If the phase derivative of $\langle\kappa,C\rangle$ equals `-divV`, if `divV` is continuous, and if that scalar component has zero phase mean, obtains $\langle\kappa,C(s)\rangle=-\operatorname{phasePrimitive}(\mathrm{divV})(s)$. The theorem assumes the derivative identity; it does not derive it from commuting spatial operators or a curl construction. No nonvanishing condition on $\kappa$ is needed here.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.summary: Recover the correction along the wave vector

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.text: Let $\kappa$ be independent of phase, let $C(s)$ and a scalar function $d(s)$ be continuous, and suppose $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C)=-d$ for every $s$, with $\int_0^1C=0$. The formal statement proves $\kappa\cdot C(s)=-\partial_s^{-1}d(s)$, where the primitive has zero phase mean. Substituting $d=\mathbf d\cdot V$ gives the second identity of (3.6). This theorem assumes the longitudinal derivative identity; it does not prove that $C$ was formed by a curl. Periodicity and nonvanishing of $\kappa$ are not needed for this integration step.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.summary: Zero phase mean fixes the integration constant

TorusEuler.wavePotential.text: At fixed time and label, the formal definition is $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$, with the covector held fixed during phase integration. The primitive means the integral from zero with its average over $[0,1]$ subtracted. A continuous transverse $V$ and $\kappa\ne0$ give $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]=V$; period one and zero mean of $V$ make the potential periodic. These are separate hypotheses, not requirements of the definition. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the displayed formula gives $Q[V]=0$ at $\kappa=0$; it cannot then recover a nonzero oscillation by its fast curl.
TorusEuler.wavePotential.summary: The normalized phase primitive supplies the potential for a curl

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.text: The expression is defined for every $\kappa$, with reciprocal powers set to zero at $\kappa=0$. Its interpretation as a time derivative requires $\kappa\ne0$. This is the vector inside the phase primitive in (5.33): the three cross-product terms divided by $|\kappa|^2$, together with the correction from differentiating that denominator. It depends only on $M$, $\kappa$, $V$, and $f$. The accompanying derivative theorem supplies the nonvanishing and differential-equation assumptions that give it this interpretation.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.summary: Collect the terms inside the time-differentiated phase primitive

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.text: An algebraic identity splits the potential-time source into its amplitude coefficient applied to v and its vector-potential coefficient applied to the forcing. This does not itself differentiate a time-dependent solution.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.summary: The potential time derivative separates amplitude and forcing

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.text: Replacing the normalized covector `k` by `freq • k` multiplies `wavePotentialTimeSource` by `freq⁻¹`, assuming positive frequency. Strain, velocity, and forcing remain fixed. This is an exact algebraic homogeneity identity, independent of time regularity and valid even for a zero normalized covector because the formula is totalized.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.summary: The time source scales by inverse carrier frequency

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_linea.text: With strain and covector fixed, the time-source expression can be written `A v + B f` for two continuous linear maps. No nonzero-covector hypothesis is needed for this algebraic decomposition, since the formula is totalized. The representation is used to transfer continuity, periodicity, and zero phase mean from the inputs.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_linea.summary: The potential time source is linear in velocity and forcing

TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.text: Let $\kappa\ne0$ and let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $\kappa\cdot V(s)=0$ for every phase. The formal statement proves $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V](s)=V(s)$ for every real $s$, where $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$. Differentiating the normalized primitive removes its additive constant, and the vector triple product gives the result. This is the fast part of the curl in (3.5). The theorem does not require periodicity or zero phase mean; those ensure a periodic potential in the application. The nonzero-covector assumption excludes the default zero value of the quotient.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.summary: Transversality and a nonzero covector give an exact algebraic recovery

TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.text: For the selected first-wave amplitude $\mathbf a(t,a)$, transported wave vector $\kappa(t,a)$ and radial envelope $g(a)$, the formal theorem identifies the phase potential of $g(a)F_h(s)\mathbf a(t,a)$ with $g(a)P_h(s)(\mathbf a\times\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$, assuming $0<h\le1$. Here $P_h$ is the mean-zero periodic primitive of $F_h$, and $s$ is an independent phase variable. The statement concerns this particular first-wave construction; it does not quantify over arbitrary amplitudes and parent flows from §3.1. It allows zero frequency: at $\kappa=0$ the inverse squared norm is assigned zero, so the identity still holds algebraically but does not assert a nonzero wave or an inverse curl relation.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.summary: The phase primitive gives the explicit first-wave potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.text: The identity holds for every phase field and every vector, including zero, because the potential assigns zero to reciprocal powers at a zero wave vector. Rescaling the wave vector by a positive frequency rescales its vector potential by the inverse frequency. This separates the factor $\lambda^{-1}$ from the normalized coefficients $\kappa/\lambda$ and $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$ in the proof of Lemma 5.5. Product, derivative, and phase primitive estimates are then needed to bound the curl correction.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.summary: Normalize the wave vector and extract the small factor

TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.text: The normalized potential of the reversed, negated velocity is the reversed potential of the original velocity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.summary: Reflection of the normalized vector potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_translate_phase.text: For a continuous one-periodic zero-mean profile, translating its phase by `b` translates its normalized wave potential by `b`. The proof compares derivatives and uses the zero-mean normalization to eliminate an additive constant. The covector need not be nonzero for this algebraic integral identity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_translate_phase.summary: Shifting the phase shifts the normalized potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.text: At a fixed time and label, suppose $V(s)=0$ for every real phase. The formal statement gives $Q[V](s)=0$ for every phase, for any covector $\kappa$, including zero. Phase integration and subtraction of a phase mean act only on that label's profile and cannot create a nonzero value elsewhere. This is the potential part of the support assertion following (3.6). The theorem does not itself address $C[V]$: vanishing of the spatial curl outside the support additionally uses locality of differentiation on an open set where the potential is zero.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.summary: Zero input at every phase gives zero potential at that label

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient.text: For a real scalar $c$, phase gradient $\kappa$, amplitude $\mathbf a$ and linear map $M$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $2c(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. In the localized wave, $c$ is the combined cutoff factor $\widetilde\chi g$; at the centre it is one. The definition permits arbitrary real $c$ and does not assert positivity or a differential equation. It assigns zero when $\kappa=0$ because division by zero is zero. The physical pressure calculation uses nonzero $\kappa$, and its sign additionally depends on the coupling and on $c$.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient.summary: A scalar cutoff multiplies the usual wave pressure coefficient

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.text:
Let $\kappa,\mathbf a
e0$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, let $M$ be a linear map and $c\in\mathbb R$. Put $E_{1,+}=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $
u_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$. The formal identity is $-[2c(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2]\,\kappa\otimes\kappa=-2c|\mathbf a||\kappa|
u_+\,E_{1,+}\otimes E_{1,+}$. It is the tensor form of the scalar pressure normalization used for the wave coupling. Nonzero vectors justify the normalizations, but perpendicularity and positive coupling are not assumed. Consequently the identity alone gives neither a sign nor an upper bound for the pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.summary: Normalizing the wave directions expresses the pressure tensor through the coupling

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.text: The positive coefficient used to write the leading pressure as $-cP_h$ equals minus the oscillatory pressure slope for zero source and cutoff-scaled amplitude. This is an exact algebraic identity for arbitrary inputs, including a zero covector under Lean’s totalized division. Nonnegativity and geometric use of the coefficient require additional hypotheses.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.summary: The leading pressure uses the opposite slope sign

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.text: When `freq ≠ 0`, substituting the transported covector, explicit seed, and stationary-shear gradient into the wave-pressure coefficient yields `(c / freq)` times the normalized coefficient. The shear ratio cancels. Nonzero frequency is needed for the inverse-length calculation; the theorem does not extend its stated factorization by removing that hypothesis.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.summary: The first pressure separates scale and frequency

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.text: Let $\kappa\ne0$, $0\le\theta\le1$, and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge0$. For $c_{\mathbf a}=2\theta(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$, the formal statement proves $c_{\mathbf a}\ge0$ and $c_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2\le2|\kappa|\|M\||\mathbf a|$. In Lemma 5.9, $\theta=\widetilde\chi g$ and the localized positive coupling supplies the sign. Together with $F_h\,{}^{\prime}\ge-Ch$, this yields an upper bound for $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h\,{}^{\prime}\kappa\otimes\kappa$. The theorem itself is a pointwise coefficient estimate; it does not include the other Hessian tensors or assert an absolute bound for the leading pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.summary: Positive coupling makes the leading pressure coefficient nonnegative

TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.text: For any real width parameter, the formal definition sets $P_h=\partial_s^{-1}F_h$: integrate $F_h$ from phase zero, then subtract the mean of that integral over $[0,1]$. For $0<h\le1$, the constructed $F_h$ is smooth, odd, periodic and of zero mean, so $P_h$ is a smooth periodic primitive with $\int_0^1P_h=0$. This is the scalar factor in the leading pressure (3.3). The normalization does not generally give $P_h(0)=0$. The definition is assigned values outside the admissible width range as well, but those values carry none of the stated profile guarantees.
TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.summary: The scalar pressure profile is the normalized primitive of the velocity profile

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.text: If a total operator decomposes into four contributions, a one-sided quadratic bound for its leading part and operator norm bounds for the other three add to a one-sided bound for the total. Symmetry is not assumed or needed for this inequality. The theorem preserves the favorable sign of the leading pressure instead of replacing it by its norm.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.summary: Combine one signed bound with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.text: Combines a leading quadratic bound at order $N^{-1/4}$ with norm bounds for geometric, higher oscillatory and mean terms at orders $N^{-3/4}$, $N^{-5/12}$ and $N^{-5/2}$. Since $N\ge1$, all three faster decays are bounded by the quarter power. The nonnegative constants `b`, `c` and `d` justify these exponent comparisons.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.summary: All pressure contributions fit the quarter power upper bound

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.text: A nonnegative pressure coefficient makes the quadratic form of $-c\,\kappa\otimes\kappa$ nonpositive in every direction. The proof reduces it to minus a nonnegative scalar times a square. This sign statement concerns only the leading rank-one contribution; the geometric remainder is bounded separately in operator norm.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.summary: The central rank one contribution is nonpositive

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.text:
Let $0<h\le1$ and let $c,\phi:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. For the constructed profile $F_h$ and primitive $P_h$, write $\kappa=
abla\phi$. The formal statement gives $
abla^2(-cP_h(\phi))=-cF_h'(\phi)\kappa\otimes\kappa-F_h(\phi)(
abla c\otimes\kappa+\kappa\otimes
abla c+c
abla^2\phi)-P_h(\phi)
abla^2c$. All terms are evaluated at the same spatial point. When $c$ is constant and $\phi$ is linear, only the rank-one term remains, recovering the affine pressure calculation in §1.2. The formal identity permits varying coefficients and curved phase, but uses the particular constructed family; it is not a statement for every smooth profile without further hypotheses.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.summary: The Hessian separates the leading rank-one term from coefficient and phase derivatives

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.text: If the transported phase vanishes at the origin, the leading pressure Hessian there is $-c(0)\kappa\otimes\kappa-P_h(0)D^2c(0)$. The mixed and phase-curvature terms vanish because $F_h(0)=0$, while the slope is one. The coefficient-Hessian term remains: a zero-mean primitive need not vanish at phase zero.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.summary: The central Hessian retains a slow coefficient term

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: For $0<h\le1$, $c\ge0$, any phase value $s$ and vectors $\kappa,v\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $v\cdot[-cF_h'(s)\kappa\otimes\kappa]v\le(hc|\kappa|^2/2)|v|^2$ for the constructed profile. It uses the lower slope bound $F_h'\ge-h/2$. With $c=p_{\rm w}$ and linear phase $\kappa=k$, this yields (1.11) with the explicit factor $1/2$. It is an upper quadratic-form bound and permits a large negative eigenvalue. It controls the leading rank-one term only; if the coefficient or phase varies spatially, the additional Hessian terms require separate estimates.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The profile’s lower slope bound controls the positive part of the pressure Hessian

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: For $N\ge1$, cutoff in $[0,1]$, nonnegative coupling and a nonzero covector, the scale bounds on $\kappa$, strain and amplitude yield a quadratic upper bound $2D^3N^{-1/4}|v|^2$. The profile width is fixed to $N^{-1/2}$. This bounds the largest quadratic contribution, not the operator norm of a potentially large negative rank-one tensor.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The signed leading Hessian has quarter power decay

TorusEuler.waveProfile.text: The formal definition is $F_h(s)=\int_0^s S_h(r)\,dr$, where $S_h$ is the periodized scaled bump after removing its phase mean and normalizing its value at zero. It fixes $F_h(0)=0$ for every real $h$. For $0<h\le1$, the slope is smooth, even and has zero integral over one period; the proved consequences are smoothness, oddness and period one of $F_h$. These hypotheses matter: the formula alone is defined for arbitrary widths and does not assert those regularity properties there. The construction realizes the family used in Lemma 3.1, rather than leaving the primitive's additive constant unspecified.
TorusEuler.waveProfile.summary: Integrating the normalized slope fixes the profile at phase zero

TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.text: The profile defined by integrating its slope from zero has value zero at zero for every real scale. The equality uses the integral over a degenerate interval. It is the base-point condition that combines with oddness and unit central derivative in the localized wave construction.
TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.summary: The primitive profile vanishes at phase zero

TorusEuler.waveSlope.text: Let $\psi$ be the chosen even bump and extend $\psi(s/h)$ with period one by reducing the phase to the centered unit cell. If $c_h$ denotes its phase mean, the formal definition is $S_h(s)=(\psi_{\mathrm{per},h}(s)-c_h)/(1-c_h)$. For $0<h\le1$, the proved bound $0\le c_h\le h/4$ makes the denominator positive; the slope is smooth, mean zero and equals one at zero. On $|s|\le1/2$ this is the formula in Lemma 3.1. The formula is also assigned values at other widths: division by zero then gives zero, and no profile conclusions are asserted without the admissible-width hypotheses.
TorusEuler.waveSlope.summary: Remove the bump mean and normalize the central value

TorusEuler.waveSlope_bounds.text: At every phase and for $0<h\le1$, the slope lies between $-h/2$ and one. The lower bound uses the small bump mean and the denominator lower bound; the upper bound uses the bump’s value at most one. These are concrete constants for the inequalities in Lemma 3.1.
TorusEuler.waveSlope_bounds.summary: The slope has a small negative part and unit upper bound

TorusEuler.waveSlope_denom_pos.text: For $0<h\le1$, one minus the bump’s phase mean is strictly positive. The preceding mean bound gives a value at least $3/4$, though this lemma states only positivity. It is the guard allowing division to normalize the slope and cancellation at phase zero.
TorusEuler.waveSlope_denom_pos.summary: The normalized slope has a positive denominator

TorusEuler.waveSlope_even.text: For $0<h\le1$, the normalized slope is even in phase. The bump is even and its mean and denominator are phase-independent scalars. Integrating this even slope from zero will therefore produce an odd profile, which is the symmetry needed for the localized Euler velocity.

TorusEuler.waveSlope_zero.text: For $0<h\le1$, the slope at phase zero is exactly one. The bump value there is one, so numerator and denominator agree; their common value is nonzero by the positivity lemma. This verifies the normalization that prescribes the central gradient of the localized wave.
TorusEuler.waveSlope_zero.summary: The normalized slope equals one at the origin

TorusEuler.waveSwitch.text: The switch is the smooth transition evaluated at $r(t-t_0)$. The definition accepts arbitrary real $r$; activation after $t_0$ with duration $1/r$ requires the positive-rate hypotheses in later lemmas. This scalar factor multiplies the leading wave and its divergence correction without changing their spatial cancellation.

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.text: Let $r>0$ and let $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, where the fixed smooth transition $\theta$ equals one for arguments at least one. If $t\ge t_0+1/r$, then $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$. Since $\tau=r(t-t_0)$, this is precisely the statement that the cutoff equals one for $\tau\ge1$. Positivity of $r$ is essential for this conversion of the time inequality. The theorem applies at the endpoint $t=t_0+1/r$ as well as afterward, and imposes no condition on the amplitude of the wave being switched on.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.summary: The wave is fully present after one normalized time unit

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.text: Write $\theta$ for the fixed smooth transition and define the envelope profile by $\chi(s)=1-\theta(s-1)$. The formal theorem proves $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$ for every real $t_0,r,t$, where $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$. Thus the paper's spatial-envelope profile also gives its time transition. This identity alone does not require $r>0$ and does not state the zero-before-activation branch. With $r\ge0$, the transition is zero for $t\le t_0$, giving that branch, including the activation time itself.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.summary: Identifies the time transition with the fixed envelope profile

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.text: For any $r\ge0$ and real $t_0$, take $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, where the fixed smooth transition is zero for nonpositive arguments. The formal theorem proves $\widetilde\chi(t)=0$ whenever $t\le t_0$. It therefore includes equality at the activation time, while the piecewise display in §6.2 explicitly gives the zero branch only for $t<t_0$. The result also allows $r=0$, in which case the cutoff is identically zero. It does not assert vanishing of every higher oscillatory profile; those profiles require their own initial conditions.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.summary: The cutoff is zero up to and including activation

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.text: There is a constant $C\ge0$, depending only on the fixed smooth transition, such that the following holds. Let $r>0$, $G\ge0$ and let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\gamma(t)|\le G$ on $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$. For $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, the formal theorem gives $|\widetilde\chi'(t)\gamma(t)|\le CrG$ for every real $t$. No continuity or measurability of $\gamma$ is needed; outside that interval the derivative of the cutoff vanishes. Taking $\gamma=1$ and $G=1$ gives $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr$. Taking $G=e^{3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}}$ after the early-gain estimate gives the residual factor following (6.8).
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.summary: Only the weight on the switching interval affects the bound

TorusEuler.weightedGenerator.text: Defines the transformed linear generator $A-(g′/g)I$ for the normalized unknown $x/g$. The inputs are the value `g` and its proposed derivative `dg` at a time. The definition itself does not assert that `dg` is a derivative or that the weight is positive; those assumptions enter the transformation theorems.
TorusEuler.weightedGenerator.summary: The generator after dividing by the amplitude weight

TorusEuler.weightedGenerator_stable.text: Assume every homogeneous solution of `A` satisfies the given weighted forward estimate with constant `K`. Then every solution of the transformed generator satisfies the corresponding unweighted norm estimate. The weight is positive and has the stated within derivative throughout the interval, so multiplying back by it and cancelling its values is legitimate.
TorusEuler.weightedGenerator_stable.summary: Weighted stability becomes ordinary stability after normalization

TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.text: Under the same positive-word and adjacent-jet assumptions, dividing the increment by $\sqrt{\operatorname{dist}(x,y)}$ gives the stated Hölder quotient bound. The hypothesis `hxy : x ≠ y` makes the denominator strictly positive. This theorem covers distinct labels; the jet-range proofs handle equal labels separately using the total division convention.
TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.summary: Divide the increment estimate at distinct labels

TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.text: For positive duration and radius, assume smooth coframe and force, bounded Hölder jet sets, and actual torus derivative words for their product whose negative primitives equal the source words. Each weighted source time norm is bounded by $T\sqrt2$ times the finite product estimate. The argument includes both integration duration and the Euclidean-to-torus Hölder comparison.
TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.summary: The integrated source is bounded by the coframe product

TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.text: The physical center growth estimate gives the fixed-coordinate estimate on the same slab. Reading and lifting coordinates cost the two deformation bounds, so a physical constant `D` becomes `D^3` when both are at most `D`.
TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.summary: Fixed transverse coordinates cost two deformation bounds

TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.text: On a nondegenerate interval, assumes a smooth homogeneous linear ODE, a strictly positive differentiable weight, weighted homogeneous stability on a parameter set, initial jets through order `N`, and positive-order coefficient jets. It bounds all solution jets through `N` by $\mathrm{linearODEWordFactor}(K(r-l)C,N)\,KB\,g(t)$. Finite-dimensional parameter and target spaces allow word estimates to yield operator norms.
TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.summary: Homogeneous stability controls every prescribed parameter jet

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.text: The weighted forward estimate for a forced linear ODE in fixed coordinates, with the exact time integral of the normalized forcing.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.summary: Weighted variation of constants for forced linear evolution

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.text: For a positive differentiable weight, a continuous perturbation bounded by `ρ` changes the weighted forward estimate by $e^{KD}$, where $D$ is the integral of `ρ` up to the observation time. A second conclusion bounds the difference from an unperturbed solution, including the initial mismatch. Both constants and the actual perturbed equations are explicit hypotheses.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.summary: An integrated coefficient error controls weighted propagation

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.text: Compares solutions of the center operator `A` and a nearby operator `A₁` using a positive differentiable weight `g`. If every center solution has weighted growth at most `K`, the interval has length at most one, and the operator gap is at most `d` with $Kd\le1$, the relative error is bounded by the propagated initial mismatch plus $eK^2d$ times the initial relative size.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.summary: Nearby solutions remain close relative to the center

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.text: Assume continuous coefficients and forcing, a continuously differentiable positive weight, $K>0$, and that every central homogeneous solution obeys the stated forward weighted bound. A nearby equation inherits the central weighted propagation estimate when its coefficient differs by at most the reciprocal of the central bound and the interval has length at most one. Variation of constants gives the factor $eK$ multiplying the initial weighted amplitude and the integral of the weighted forcing. Taking $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives (5.23).
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.summary: Weighted variation of constants controls the forced transverse equation

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.text: Assume continuous coefficients on $[a,b]$, a continuously differentiable positive weight, $K>0$, and $b-a\le1$. The central bound must hold for every homogeneous solution. If the central homogeneous equation has weighted propagation bound $K$, a coefficient perturbation of size at most $K^{-1}$ changes that bound to $eK$ on an interval of length at most one. The weight is positive and differentiable. Applied with $K=\mathsf D^3$, this is the nearby-label Gronwall estimate used in the proof of Lemma 5.3.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.summary: Small coefficient variation preserves weighted forward control

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.text: A uniform coefficient comparison with the center gives stability at a label for every pair of ordered times on the slab.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.summary: Near-center coefficient control gives weighted stability

TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.text: For continuous linear coefficients on $[l,r]$, a weighted stability estimate for every solution on that interval also holds for solutions launched at any $a \in  [l,r]$. The proof extends the later solution backward using linear ODE existence and identifies the extensions by uniqueness. Positivity or regularity of the weight is not separately needed because the comparison is already assumed.
TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.summary: Restrict weighted stability to a later launch time

TorusEuler.wordNorm_bounds_of_bdd.text: For an admissible word, boundedness of all jet sets gives a pointwise derivative bound by the finite norm. When the proposition `holder` holds, it also gives the corresponding square-root distance bound. The proof treats coincident points separately before clearing the positive denominator at distinct points.
TorusEuler.wordNorm_bounds_of_bdd.summary: A bounded finite norm controls values and differences
